en: Having bowed to Kṛṣṇa, Rāma, Nṛsiṃha, Vyāsa, and also to the gurus,
the Sūtradīpikā is composed by the one known as Jagannātha Āyatī.
The first quarter of the first chapter.
The Section on the Desire to Know (Jijñāsā-adhikaraṇa)
Oṃ. Now, therefore, the inquiry into Brahman. Oṃ.

Now, after the attainment of the qualifications consisting of study, tranquility, self-control, and so forth; therefore, because the purpose known as liberation exists, or by the grace of Viṣṇu, the meaning is that the inquiry (*jijñāsā*) into Brahman—which is full of attributes—must be undertaken in the form of hearing (*śravaṇa*) and the rest. || 1 ||
Section on Birth (Janmādhikaraṇa) 2.
Oṃ. [Brahman is that] from which there is the birth, etc., of this [world]. Oṃ.

The meaning is this: that from which the birth and so forth—the group beginning with creation and ending with dissolution—of this measured universe, consisting of both sentient and insentient beings, occurs; that alone is Brahman, and nothing else. || 1 ||
The Section on Scripture Being the Source [of Brahman] (Sūtra 1.1.3).
Om. [Brahman is] the source of the Śāstra, Om.

The status of Rudra and others as the cause of the world is not to be inferred. Why? Because [Brahman] has the scripture as its source (*śāstrayonitvāt*). Scripture—consisting of the *Ṛg-veda* and so forth—is the "source," meaning the cause of knowledge, for that which has it as its source is "scripture-source" (*śāstrayoni*). The state of being such is "having scripture as its source" (*śāstrayonitva*); therefore, Brahman is the cause of the world. The meaning is that [Brahman] is to be understood solely through scripture.
The Section on Concordance (Samanvayādhikaraṇa)
Om. That [Brahman] [is the cause of the world], because of its inherence [in all things]. Om.

The word "tu" (but) has the sense of "only. That very [Brahman] called Viṣṇu is indeed Brahman; it is He alone who is primarily the source of all scriptures, not Rudra or others. Why? Because of "samanvaya"—that is, because of the presence of the marks of purport, such as the introductory passages and so forth, which are properly consistent with Him. *Ikṣatyadhikaraṇa* || 5 ||
Oṃ. [The Brahman] is not that which is not based on scripture, because it is seen [in scripture]. Oṃ.

That Brahman is not without sound, nor is it inexpressible by words; rather, it is indeed expressible. Why? Because of "seeing" (*īkṣati*); "seeing" means knowledge. The meaning is: because it is the object of that [knowledge].
If it be argued that [the term "Self"] is used in a secondary sense, we say no, because of the word "Self" (ātman). Oṃ.

If it is argued that the one bound by the qualities of *sattva* and so forth—the *jīva* alone—is [meant] because of the scriptural statement of "seeing" (*īkṣati*) in the words "He [sees] from this," we say no. Why? Because of the word "Self" (*ātman*). The meaning is that in the object to be seen, there is the hearing of the word "Self" in the phrase "one should see the Self. || 2 ||
Oṃ. Because liberation is taught for one who is devoted to That, Oṃ.

For one who is devoted to That—the knower of the Supreme Self—there is the teaching of liberation; since liberation is heard in such passages as "He by whom [Brahman] is known," the meaning is that the individual soul (jīva) is not the primary referent of the word "Self. || 3 ||
Oṃ, and because there is no statement that it is to be abandoned, Oṃ.

Because of the statement regarding its being something to be abandoned, and because Brahman is not primarily taught here as having the nature of being abandonable for the sake of liberation—on the contrary, there is the statement that it is not to be abandoned, namely, "Know [Him]"—that which is denoted by the word *ātman* is not secondary; rather, the meaning is that it is Viṣṇu himself, who is devoid of qualities (*nirguṇa*). || 4 ||
Oṃ, because of deep sleep, Oṃ.

Because of its dissolution into itself—since the term "dissolution" (apyaya) denotes the state of merging—and because the Śruti states that "it dissolves itself," this [Brahman] is indeed devoid of qualities (nirguṇa) and not figurative. For this very reason, it is the meaning expressed by the word [Brahman]. || 5 ||
Oṃ, because of the commonality of destination, oṃ.

The meaning is that there is no one other than Viṣṇu who is established as the cause in other Vedic branches, because of the "equality" (sāmānya)—that is, because of the scriptural teaching of a single form for the knowledge of the birth of various beings. || 6 ||
Oṃ, and because it is heard [in scripture], Oṃ.
Furthermore, because it is stated in the Śruti, "The God is one," the meaning is that Brahman is not inexpressible by words. || 7 ||
Section 6: The Topic of that which Consists of Bliss (Ānandamaya-Adhikaraṇa)
Oṃ, [the Self] consists of bliss because of repetition; Oṃ.

Viṣṇu alone is denoted by such terms as "consisting of bliss" (ānandamaya) and so forth, and not Prakṛti or others. Why? Because of repetition; that is to say, because the word "Brahman" is heard in every section concerning the one consisting of bliss and so on. || 1 ||
"Oṃ. If it be argued that [the Self] is not [denoted by the word 'person'] because of the word 'modification,' we say no, because of abundance. Oṃ.

If it is argued that [the term] "consisting of bliss" (*ānandamaya*) and so forth refers to Viṣṇu because it is a word denoting a modification—meaning because it contains the suffix *mayaṭ* which signifies a modification—[we reply: no. Why? Because of abundance; the meaning is that the suffix *mayaṭ* expresses fullness as stated in the rule for the word *prācurya*. || 2 ||
Oṃ, and because its cause is designated [in scripture], Oṃ.

The word *ca* (and) denotes conjunction. The meaning is that the one consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya*) is indeed Viṣṇu, because of the designation of the reason known as "being the impeller of the world" for Him, and because it is stated in the Śruti text, "Who indeed could breathe? [Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.7]. Thus, the one consisting of bliss is Viṣṇu alone. || 3 ||
Oṃ, and it is proclaimed as being exactly according to the words of the mantra; Oṃ.

Since the Brahman described in the words of the mantra—"Brahman is truth, knowledge, and infinite"—is celebrated and established by means of terms such as "consisting of bliss" (ānandamaya), the meaning is that Brahman alone is what is denoted by the terms "consisting of bliss" and so forth. || 4 ||
Oṃ. It is none other, because [otherwise] it would be impossible. Oṃ.

The other [category] consists of the four-faced Brahmā and so forth. Why? Because it is untenable; the meaning is that they cannot be the object of the knowledge that produces liberation, as stated in the passage, "The knower of Brahman attains the Supreme. || 5 ||
Oṃ, and because of the designation of difference, Oṃ.

And because distinguishing attributes such as having a face like a bird and so forth are mentioned for the one consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya*), the meaning is that the other [the Self within] is not the one consisting of bliss. || 6 ||
Oṃ. And because of desire, there is no dependence on inference. Oṃ.

Because there is no inference that accords with the scriptures on non-duality (advaita), and because mere inference proceeds according to one's own desire (icchā), there is no need for inference; the meaning is that one should not rely on "dry" (śuṣka) inference regarding objects beyond the senses. 7.
Oṃ. And [the Lord] teaches his union with this [body]; Oṃ.

The word "ca" (and) in the *Yuktisamuccaya* [indicates] that because in this section concerning the one consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya*), the Śruti teaches—that is, establishes—the connection, namely the union or relationship of this individual soul (*jīva*) even with liberation through the one consisting of bliss and so forth; therefore, for this reason as well, the one consisting of bliss and so forth is Brahman alone, and not the body and so forth—this is the meaning. || 8 ||
The Section Concerning the One Residing Within (Antasthatvādhikaraṇa)
Oṃ. [The one within is Brahman] because of the teaching of its attributes. Oṃ.

The one within—"the one who has entered within"—is indeed Brahman heard within the heart, and not Indra or others. Why? Because of the teaching of its attributes (*taddharmopadeśāt*). This means that because attributes of Viṣṇu—such as residing in the midst of the milk-ocean, abiding in the ocean of dissolution, and being the seed of the cosmic egg—are taught in the passage beginning with "within the ocean," etc., regarding that one heard within. [End of Section 8: The Topic of Ākāśa]
Oṃ. [The word "ether" (ākāśa) denotes Brahman] because of its characteristic marks; Oṃ.

The "ether" (ākāśa) mentioned here is Viṣṇu alone, who is denoted by the word "ether," and not the well-known physical ether. Why? Because of its characteristic marks (liṅga); that is to say, because the characteristic marks of Viṣṇu, such as being "higher than the high" (parovarīyastva) and so forth, are heard in the Chāndogya Upaniṣad with respect to this ether.
Section 9: The Topic of the Vital Breath (Prāṇa)
Oṃ, for this very reason, [it is] the vital breath; Oṃ.

When it is said, "Thou indeed becamest Prāṇa," that Prāṇa is Viṣṇu alone and none other. Why? For this very reason; that is to say, precisely because of the mark (liṅga) of being the Lord of Śrī in the passage, "And Śrī [is] thine. Thus ends the section on Light (Jyotir-adhikaraṇa). || 10 ||
Oṃ. [The Brahman is] light, because of the mention of its feet. Oṃ.

The "Light" is indeed Brahman, which is denoted by the word "Light," and not anything else. Why? Because of the mention of its feet—that is, because of the mention of the ears and so forth as its feet. The meaning is that from the passage, "My ears are [wide open]," it is heard that the Light is entirely beyond the reach of the ears and other senses.
|| Section on the Designation by Name || 11 ||

"Oṃ. If it be argued that [the Self] is not [meant here] because of the mention of the metre, we say no; for there is a declaration of the fixing of the mind [therein], and such is seen [in other passages]. Oṃ.

Because of the designation as a *chandas*. Now, it may be argued that since the word "Gāyatrī" found in the *Chāndogya* Śruti denotes a meter (*chandas*) consisting of twenty-four syllables, Viṣṇu is not the one expressed by the word "Gāyatrī. This is not so. Why? Because there is indeed a scriptural vision to that effect; for there exists the Śruti passage, "He sings and protects," which establishes that Viṣṇu is denoted by the word "Gāyatrī" on the basis of his being the agent of singing (*gāna*) and protecting (*trāṇa*).

Therefore, since it might be argued that the designation of Viṣṇu by the term *gāyatrī* is useless, it is said: "In the same way," and so forth. "In the same way" means because of the scriptural statement regarding the fixing of the mind on Viṣṇu; that is, because He is designated in the mind for the purpose of meditation (*upāsanā*) as possessing the grounds for the application of terms such as *gāyatrī*. Thus, the sense is that there is no pointlessness [to the designation]. || 1 ||
Om. And because the designation of the quarters beginning with "the origin of beings" is appropriate, it is thus; Om.

The word "thus" (evam) is to be repeated. It is only thus that it is logical that Brahman is denoted by the term *gāyatrī*. Why? Because the designation of its quarters as consisting of "beings" (*bhūta*) and so forth is appropriate only in this way. This is because of the statement, "One quarter of Him is all beings; His three quarters are the immortal in heaven," and because such a description of possessing parts consisting of beings and the immortal is possible only in the case of Viṣṇu and impossible elsewhere. This is the meaning. || 2 ||
Om. If it be argued that [the meditations] are not identical because of the difference in instruction, we say no, because there is no contradiction in either case. Om.

If it is argued that [the Brahman referred to] in the *Gāyatrī* and the *Jyotiṣ* [passages] are not one because of differences in instruction—due to the difference in scriptural texts teaching contradictory attributes, such as being situated in heaven (*dyusthatva*) in the passage "His immortal three-quarters are in heaven" (*tripādasyāmṛtaṃ divi*), and being beyond heaven (*paratva*) in the passage "beyond heaven" (*paro divaḥ*)—and therefore these two are not the single entity called Viṣṇu but rather distinct, [we reply: no. Why? Because there is no contradiction even though both scriptural passages intend to establish the same unity; the meaning is that there is no contradiction when the twenty-one worlds are intended [by the term "heaven"]. || 3 ||
The section concerning the vital breath as the substratum at the end of the quarter: 12.
Oṃ. [The word *prāṇa* refers to Brahman] because it follows [as the subject] in that manner. Oṃ.

Likewise, the Prāṇa mentioned in the Aitareya Upaniṣad in the passage "Tāvā etāḥ," like the Prāṇa mentioned in the Taittirīya Upaniṣad in the passage "Tadvai tvam," is indeed Viṣṇu alone. Why? Because of the continuous presence [of his characteristics] (anugamāt). This means that because the marks of Viṣṇu—such as being the deity to be meditated upon and so forth—and the word "Brahman" are heard repeatedly [in these contexts]. || 1 ||

If it be argued that [the Upanishads] are for the purpose of instruction regarding the self and so forth, we say no, because in this [text] there is an abundance of connection with the inner self. Om.

The genitive case is used in the sense of the accusative. If it is argued that because Indra taught himself to Viśvāmitra—the speaker of a thousand *bṛhatī* verses—by instructing him regarding his own self as the vital breath (*prāṇa*), this vital breath must therefore be Indra and not Viṣṇu, [we reply: "No," is the remainder [of the sūtra]. This is repeated. The term "because of the subsequent agreement" (*anugamāt*) carries over from the previous context. Thus, for the reason of the aforementioned agreement, the vital breath is not Indra. Nor is there any contradiction with the instruction [if this were the case].

Why? Because in this context, the Lord’s abundant internal connection—His awakening to many bodies in the forms of Indra, Viśvāmitra, and others—is stated; that is the meaning. Or rather, because in this Indra there exists an abundance (*bhūmā*), a multiplicity, of the connection—that is, the immersion—of the *adhyātman*, the superior Self; that is the meaning. || 2 ||
Oṃ. Or rather, instruction [is given] through the study of the scriptures, as in the case of Vāmadeva. Oṃ.

The word *tu* (but) has the sense of *eva* (indeed). It is like Vāmadeva: just as the sage Vāmadeva, with the intention of referring to the Inner Ruler (*antaryāmī*), declared his own identity with Manu, Sūrya, and so forth, saying, "I was Manu," in the same way. By the vision of the Teacher (*śāstradṛṣṭyā*)—the Teacher being the Inner Ruler because He governs all—the teaching, namely the designation "I am Prāṇa," is made solely with that intention; it does not mean [identity] through oneness. || 3 ||

"Om. If it be argued that [the self] is not [the one taught here] because of the characteristic marks of the individual soul (jīva) and the chief vital breath (mukhya-prāṇa), we say no; because of the threefoldness of meditation, and because that [threefoldness] is possible here due to its being resorted to. Om.

If it be argued that [the subject here] is not Viṣṇu but another Prāṇa, because of the mention of marks of the individual soul (jīva)—such as having a lifespan of a hundred years—and marks of the chief vital air (mukhyaprāṇa)—such as the dialogue with the senses and the gods, as well as the statements "so many [breaths] in a hundred-year life" and "they did not injure one another"—we say no. Why? Because of the "consequent connection" (anugama). Nor is there a contradiction of the marks; for it is possible that those marks refer to the Inner Controller (antaryāmī), and so forth must be supplied. To the question, "For what purpose is the Inner Controller mentioned? it is said: "Because of the threefold nature of meditation" (upāsātraividhyāt).

Because the meditation on Brahman is threefold—distinguished as internal, external, and all-pervading—and because this threefold nature is relied upon, stated, and connected within this context; that is to say, because those qualified aspirants possess the fitness for these three types of meditation. Thus, the sense is that it is appropriate to describe the Inner Controller (Antaryāmin) by means of various terms according to the distinction between those respective qualified aspirants for the purpose of meditation. || 4 ||
Thus ends the first quarter of the first chapter in the Sūtradīpikā composed by Śrī Jagannātha Yati. || 1 || 1 ||
Section on Omnipresence || 1 ||
Oṃ, because of the teaching of what is established everywhere. Oṃ.

The word "that" (tat) carries over from the previous context. In all cases—referring to earth and the other elements—the entity being described is indeed Brahman, known as Nārāyaṇa, and nothing else. Why? Because of the teaching of what is well-known; that is to say, because in the case of the omnipresent entity, the word "Brahman"—which is well-established in the Śrutis and other sources as denoting Nārāyaṇa—is heard [in the text] as "this very one is Brahman. || 1 ||
Om. And because the qualities intended [by the scripture] are possible [in Brahman], Om.

The word *ca* (and) is used for conjunction or emphasis. Regarding the term "all-pervading" (*sarvagata*), the word "by scripture" (*śrutyā*) is to be supplied as the remainder. Thus, because the qualities such as "not being heard" and so forth—which are intended hereafter, which are suitable to be stated as residing in the all-pervading one, and which will be mentioned—belong only to Viṣṇu due to His fitness, and because they are logically possible in Him alone and impossible elsewhere, the meaning is that Viṣṇu alone is all-pervading. || 2 ||
Oṃ, because [the self] cannot be logically established [as being identical to the body], it is not the body. Oṃ.

The word "tu" (but) has the sense of "eva" (indeed). "Śārīraḥ" means the individual soul (jīva), or else the sun. Why is it not omnipresent? Because of impossibility; that is to say, because it is impossible for a single individual soul to reside in all bodies. || 3 ||
Oṃ, and because of the designation of the agent and the action, Oṃ.

The meaning is that since [the scripture] teaches "self" as the object (*karman*) with respect to an all-pervading entity, and designates the living being (*jīva*) as its agent (*kartṛ*), which is contradictory to that [all-pervasiveness], and because this has already been stated, the living being is not all-pervading. || 4 ||
Oṃ. [The self exists] because of the specific nature of sound. Oṃ.

The meaning is that in the sentence "em eva brahma," because the word *brahman* is accompanied by the qualifying particle *eva*, which has the sense of restriction (*avadhāraṇa*), the word *brahman* does not refer to the individual soul (*jīva*). || 5 ||
Oṃ, and because of mindfulness, Oṃ.

The word "ca" (and) signifies conjunction. The meaning is that the term "Brahman" does not refer to the individual soul (*jīva*) not only because it is so stated in the Śruti, but also because of the existence of such Smṛti passages as "I am the Self, O Guḍākeśa. Thus, the term "Brahman" does not refer to the individual soul. || 6 ||

"Oṃ. [The Lord is not the individual soul] because of His having a small abode and because of the designation of that [smallness]; if it is argued 'no,' [it is not so] because He is to be perceived as such, and because He is like the ether. Oṃ."

Because of its having a small abode; because it is stated that the omnipresent reality has a small location in the form of the space within the hearts of all living beings in the passage, "In all beings"; because of its designation as such; because that [reality] is designated by means of the marks of that [individual soul], such as its shadow and so forth; and because it has been so stated. If it is argued, "No, it is Brahman alone that is omnipresent," [the answer is: "If you say no, why? Because those [attributes] are possible only in Viṣṇu"—this is the remainder of the sense. Nor is there any pointlessness, because it is to be understood in this way.

Thus, because Viṣṇu alone is the object of worship in the form of having a small abode and so forth, there is no futility [of the scriptures]; this is the intended meaning. Furthermore, since the Śruti, Liṅga, and other marks refer to Brahman, there is no contradiction with them; this is the intended meaning. To the question, "How can the all-pervading Viṣṇu reside in a small place?", it is said: "like space" (vyomavat). The meaning is that just as space, though all-pervading, resides in a single location such as a house, so too does Viṣṇu. || 7 ||
If it be argued that there is no attainment of the state of enjoyment [of the fruits of action], we say: No, because of the difference in nature. Om.

If it is argued that Brahman is not omnipresent because of the objection that, like a human being, if It were present within the bodies of all living beings, It would necessarily undergo experience—that is, experience identical to theirs—this is not so. Why? Because of "distinction" (*vaiśeṣyāt*), meaning that Viṣṇu possesses a specific excellence of power. Thus, the sense is that He does not undergo experience identical to that of the individual souls. || 8 ||
|| Section on the Non-Eater || 2 ||
Oṃ, the Self [exists], because of the inclusion of both the moving and the non-moving; Oṃ.

The Self (attā) is Viṣṇu alone, who is the consumer of all as stated in the phrase "He eats everything," and not Aditi. Why? Because of the inclusion of the moving and the unmoving; the meaning is that in the scriptural text, the entire phenomenal world consisting of sentient and insentient beings is designated by the word "all" as that which is eaten. || 1 ||
Oṃ, and because it is manifest, Oṃ.
And because of the context concerning Viṣṇu in the passage beginning with "There is nothing whatsoever here," the meaning is that Viṣṇu alone is the Eater. || 2 ||
The Section on the Cave (Guha-adhikaraṇa) || 3 ||
Oṃ! Having entered the cave, we two are indeed the Selfs, because of the vision of that; Oṃ.

The word *tat* (they) follows by a modification of the grammatical number [from dual to plural]. Based on the etymology "those who measure (*mā*) the self (*ātman*)," the two selves referred to by the word *pibantau* ("drinking") in the scriptural text "the two drinking the *ṛta*" are indeed the two forms of Viṣṇu known as the Inner Self (*antarātman*) and the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), and not the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Lord (*īśvara*). Why? Because of the phrase "having entered the cave," which means because they have both entered the cave of the heart. By the word *hi* ("because"), he indicates that the mark of residing in the cave of the heart is well-known from the scripture, "He who knows."

He states the proof for His abiding in the cave of the heart within the body by way of His twofold nature: "Because that is seen. The meaning is: because that fact—that Hari, by virtue of His twofold nature, abides in the cave of the heart—is stated in the Śruti, "His dharmas are on all sides. || 1 ||
Oṃ, and because of the qualification, Oṃ.

The word *ca* (and) is used for the purpose of collecting arguments (*yuktisamuccaye*). By the use of the singular number in the qualifying term "the bridge" (*yaḥ setuḥ*), the meaning is that there is only one protector; and because he is qualified by such attributes as being the son of Sutīkṣṇa and being Brahman, he is Viṣṇu alone, not the individual soul (*jīva*). || 2 ||
|| Section on the Intermediate State || 4 ||
Oṃ. [The soul exists] as an intermediate state, because of its re-arising. Oṃ.

"He who is within the eye"—the one described by this scriptural text as being internal, situated within the eye, is Viṣṇu alone and not Agni. Why? Because of the logical consistency (upapatti); for qualities such as immortality and the term "Brahman" are heard in reference to the Internal One, and these qualities are applicable to Viṣṇu alone—this is the meaning. || 1 ||
Oṃ, and because of the designation of place and so forth, Oṃ.

Because of the designation of both the power of the eye, which has become the abode of Brahman, and the power of Brahman that presides over it—and because it is stated, "He pours either clarified butter or water"—the meaning is that Viṣṇu alone resides within the eye. || 2 ||
Oṃ, and precisely because it is designated as "Excellence in Bliss," Oṃ.

The word *ca* (and) is used for conjunction. Because of the specific mention of bliss: since in the context beginning with "Kaṃ brahma," Viṣṇu alone is specifically designated as the one within the eye by being called full bliss, how much more so is He [the one] in the ether (*khaṃ*) by virtue of His full knowledge? This is the meaning. || 3 ||
Oṃ. And because the scripture describes the path for one who has heard the Upaniṣads. Oṃ.

The meaning is that Viṣṇu alone is the internal eye, because he is the one by whom men who have heard the Upaniṣads and meditated upon this knowledge as taught therein attain their goal; for it is stated in the Śruti, "He leads them to Brahman," regarding the attainment (gati) of the two—the effected Brahman (kārya-brahman) and the supreme Brahman (para-brahman)—by which wind (vāyu). Thus, Viṣṇu is the internal eye. || 4 ||
Oṃ. It is not the other, because of instability and impossibility. Oṃ.

The other fire is not the internal eye, but Viṣṇu alone. Why? Because of the impossibility of an infinite regress (*anavasthiti*). For if the fire were the controller of another living being (*jīva*), then since that [fire] would likewise be a living being without distinction, one would have to admit yet another controller for it, leading to an infinite regress as the same logic would apply to each subsequent one. Furthermore, the meaning is that it is impossible for a living being such as fire to be the controller of another living being. || 5 ||
The Section on the Inner Ruler (Antaryāmy-adhikaraṇa) 5.
Oṃ. [The Inner Controller is the Supreme Self], because its attributes are designated in relation to the intermediate, the divine, and so forth. Oṃ.

The Inner Controller (antaryāmī) mentioned in the scripture as "This is the Self, the Inner Controller" is Viṣṇu alone, and not the Pradhāna or other such entities. Why? Because of the designation of His attributes within the contexts of the divine, the personal, and the elemental (adhidaiva, adhyātma, and adhibhūta). That is to say, because there is the designation—that is, the statement—of those attributes of Brahman, such as being unknown [even] to Him, which are declared in the scripture: "Whom the earth does not know. || 1 ||
Oṃ, and it is not [the Self] taught in the Smṛtis, because there is no description of its attributes [therein]. Oṃ.

The word "ca" (and) is used for conjunction. "Smārta" refers to that which is stated in the Smṛti of Kapila. [The object of the inquiry is] neither the Pradhāna nor the individual soul (jīva), because they are not the inner ruler (antaryāmī). Why? Because there is no mention of their attributes; that is to say, because there is no statement of those attributes belonging to the Pradhāna and the individual soul, such as consisting of the three guṇas, being subject to transmigratory existence, and so forth. || 2 ||
Oṃ. For both [schools] indeed study this as the embodied one through distinction. Oṃ.

The particle *ca* serves to draw forward the negative particle *na*. For (*hi*) because both—the Mādhyandinas and the Kāṇvas—study and recite [the text] as distinct from Antaryāmin; therefore, the meaning is that the embodied soul (*jīva*) is not Antaryāmin. || 3 ||
The Section on "Invisibility" (Adṛśyatvādhikaraṇa) || 6 ||
Oṃ. [The Self] possesses qualities such as invisibility and so forth, because of the teaching of its attributes. Oṃ.

The one characterized by qualities such as invisibility is Viṣṇu alone—not primordial matter (prakṛti) or anything else—who is denoted by the word *akṣara* (the Imperishable) as qualified by attributes such as invisibility mentioned in the scripture, "That which is invisible... Why? Because of the mention of His attributes; that is to say, because the attributes of Viṣṇu, who is the object of the higher knowledge (*paravidyā*) concerning the Ṛgveda and so forth, are stated in the scripture beginning with the words, "By which... (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 1.1.6). || 1 ||
Oṃ. And because of the distinction and the designation of attributes, it is neither of the other two. Oṃ.

The word *ca* (and) denotes conjunction. The other two are the two primordial natures (*prakṛti*). Furthermore, Viriñca (Brahmā) and Rudra do not possess the qualities of being invisible and so forth. Why? Because of the distinction of attributes and because of the designation [of difference]. Each of the two reasons is to be connected respectively with each of the two propositions. [The first reason is] because of the attributes such as omniscience; [the second is] because of the statement that Viriñca and Rudra arose from the Imperishable (Akṣara) which possesses the qualities of invisibility and so forth, in the passage beginning with "From that, this... [Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 2.1.2]. 2.
Oṃ, and because of the assignment of form, oṃ.
The meaning is that Viṣṇu alone possesses the qualities such as invisibility, because the passage beginning with "When the seer sees" establishes His unique golden form. || 3 ||
The Section Concerning Vaiśvānara (Adhikaraṇa 7).
Oṃ. Vaiśvānara [is the Supreme Self], because of the distinction of the common term; Oṃ.

Vaiśvānara—He who is denoted by the words Vaiśvānara and so forth occurring in the passage beginning with "But he who [meditates on] this," is Viṣṇu alone and not Agni. Why? Because of the specification of a common term; that is to say, because the word Vaiśvānara, which is common to both Agni and Viṣṇu, is specified by the word "Self" (ātman) in the Śruti text, "The Self, indeed, as Vaiśvānara. || 1 ||
Oṃ, it may be argued that what is being remembered would constitute inference; Oṃ.

Thus, the Vaiśvānara-nature of Viṣṇu, which is recorded in the Smṛti as "Having become Vaiśvānara, I [entered]," and which is being remembered here, would serve as an inference—that is, it would be the means of inferring—that the Vaiśvānara-vidyā has the Blessed Lord as its object, as stated in the Gītā. This is the meaning. || 2 ||

"Oṃ. If it be argued that [the Self] is not [the inner controller] because sound and the other objects are established within [the body], we say no; for there is instruction [to the contrary] based on what is seen, because [such a location] is impossible [for the Self], and they also study [the texts] describing Him as being of human form. Oṃ."

The word "ca" (and) in the *Yuktisamuccaya* signifies a conjunction. The meaning is: [Vaiśvānara is not Viṣṇu] because of words such as "fire," because of the indicative mark (*liṅga*) of being the locus of the fire-oblation, and because of his abiding within the body as the digester. If it be argued that Vaiśvānara is not Viṣṇu but indeed Agni, we say no. Why? Because there is instruction regarding him as having been seen in such a manner; that is to say, because there is instruction regarding him through the teaching of meditation, characterized by names such as "fire," as well as by indicative marks and ritual actions.

And thus, since the scriptural texts and indicative marks (liṅgas) concerning Agni and others have scope for application within Viṣṇu, the sense is that there is no contradiction with them. Furthermore, because the attributes mentioned here—such as being the Self and being Brahman—are impossible in Agni and the others, Vaiśvānara is indeed Viṣṇu alone. Moreover, because the Chandogas study and declare this Vaiśvānara to be "of the form of a person" (puruṣavidha), possessing qualities identical to those of Nārāyaṇa as propounded in the Puruṣasūkta; for this reason also, he is Viṣṇu alone.
By the word "ca" (and), it is indicated that the fact that the Puruṣasūkta refers to Viṣṇu is established by many authorities. || 3 ||
Oṃ, for this very reason, there is neither deity nor elemental being; Oṃ.

The deity is in the form of Agni and so forth; nor is the term *vaivānara* denoting the elemental fire (*tejobhūta*) that is identified with that [deity]. Why? Precisely for the reason stated above, namely, because of the word *ātman* and other such reasons which leave no room for other interpretations. This is the meaning. || 4 ||
Oṃ. Jaimini [holds that] there is no contradiction even with direct perception; Oṃ.

"Directly," that is, in the primary sense (*mukhyavṛttyā*). Even though Brahman is denotable by words such as "fire" (*agni*) and so forth, there is no contradiction; the meaning is that the teacher Jaimini declares that there is no contradiction of those respective words with respect to fire and the like, due to other causes such as ignorance (*ajñāna*) and so on. || 5 ||
Oṃ. "Because of manifestation," says Āśmarathya. Oṃ.

The meaning is that the teacher Āśmarathya holds the view that because Brahman is manifested within fire and the other elements when the meditation on Brahman has been performed, there is a restriction regarding the recitation of the hymns (sūktas) dedicated to fire and the rest, based on that manifestation. || 6 ||
Oṃ, Bādari [holds that liberation comes] from constant mindfulness; Oṃ.

The meaning of Bādari’s view is that because those who worship specific hymns (*sūkta*) and so forth remember Brahman specifically within Agni and the other deities through such recollection (*anusmṛti*) and mental application (*anusandhāna*), there is a fixed distribution (*vyavasthā*) of the hymns to Agni and the rest. || 7 ||
"Oṃ, [the fruit of knowledge is] attainment [of all desires], so Jaimini thinks, for thus scripture shows; oṃ."

For indeed, because the well-known scripture beginning with "as that" (taṃ yathā) shows it in such a way, it establishes the view of Jaimini. Therefore, following the scripture that accords with his own statement, Jaimini says that there is a restriction regarding the hymns and so forth, with the intention of [teaching] the attainment of Agni and others as the cause for those who meditate on the hymns dedicated to Agni and the rest, through the process of identification (sampatti). This is the meaning. || 8 ||
And they designate him as "Oṃ" in this context. Oṃ.

The word *ca* (and) serves to remove doubt. Since they thus enjoin Viṣṇu as residing within [the fire and other elements]—establishing Him through such passages as "He who dwells in the fire"—therefore the doubt, "How can the attainment of fire and so forth result from the worship of Viṣṇu in fire and so forth? is removed. Why? Because by the term "fire" (*agni*), the intended meaning is precisely the attainment of the Lord who resides therein. || 9 ||
Thus ends the second quarter of the first chapter in the *Sūtradīpikā* composed by the venerable Jagannātha Yati. 1.2.
|| Chapter on the Heaven and Earth [Adhikaraṇa] || 1 ||
Oṃ. The abode of heaven, earth, and so forth is Brahman, because of its own word. Oṃ.

The abode of heaven, earth, and so forth—referred to in the passage beginning with "in whom"—is Viṣṇu alone, the support of all things such as heaven and earth, and not anyone else. Why? Because of the word "own" (sva). The word "own" (sva) is the term "own"; the meaning is: because of the word "Self" (ātman), which denotes Brahman and is not [merely] grasped by the word "own. || 1 ||
Oṃ. [The Brahman is the cause] because it is designated as that which is to be approached by the liberated. Oṃ.

The abode of heaven, earth, and so forth is none other than Viṣṇu, but Viṣṇu alone. Why? Because of the designation of it as that which is to be approached by the liberated. This [term] emphasizes the state [of being]. The meaning is that since the entity which is the abode of heaven, earth, and so forth is described as "the bridge to immortality," it is to be reached by the liberated, and such a status is impossible for anything else. || 2 ||
Oṃ. There is no inference [of the existence of the Lord], because there is no word for Him. Oṃ.

Or, "ānumānam" means "based on inference. Rudra, Pradhāna, and so forth—imagined as the support of all by means of the Āgamas of the Pāśupatas and others, whose authority is established through inference—are not the abode of heaven, earth, and so on. Why? "Because of the absence of its word" (atacchabdāt); that is to say, because of the absence of any characteristic mark (liṅga) such as the wearing of ashes or ferocity, which would indicate them. || 3 ||
Oṃ, and the breath-bearer, Oṃ.
For this very reason, the individual soul (jīva) also is not the abode of heaven, earth, and so forth; such is the meaning. || 4 ||
Oṃ. Because of the designation of difference. Oṃ.
The meaning is that there is no identity between the two, because their difference is stated in the phrase "another Lord. || 5 ||
Oṃ, because of the context, Oṃ.

Because passages such as "another who does not eat" belong to the context of Viṣṇu; here, only the difference of the individual soul (jīva) from Viṣṇu is stated, and not its difference from anything else—this is the meaning. || 6 ||
Oṃ, and because of abiding and eating, Oṃ.

The meaning is that the identity of the Lord (Īśa) and the individual soul (Jīva) cannot be asserted on the grounds of the two reasons stated in such passages as "Two birds..."—namely, the state of not partaking in the fruits of karma and the state of partaking in them, respectively. || 7 ||
The Section on the Plurality [of Worlds] (Bhūmādhikaraṇa) 2.
Oṃ. The Infinite [is Brahman], because of the instruction given concerning the state of perfect serenity. Oṃ.

The term *bhūman* (the Infinite) refers to Viṣṇu alone, who is described as "full" in the scriptural passage, "That which is indeed *bhūman*. Why? Because by the statement, "The bliss of that *bhūman* [is what they call bliss]," it is declared that *bhūman* consists of perfect bliss, which is denoted by the word *samprasāda*. Furthermore, because of the teaching of superiority (*adhyupadeśāt*), for *bhūman* is designated as being superior even to Name and the rest, being the most excellent among the deities presiding over Name and so forth. This is the meaning. || 1 ||
Oṃ, and because of the occurrence of the Dharma, Oṃ.

Because of the hearing of attributes such as being all-pervasive (*sarvagatatva*) in the passage beginning with "That indeed is below," and because those [attributes] are logically possible for Viṣṇu alone, the meaning is that Viṣṇu alone is the Infinite (*bhūman*). || 2 ||
Section on the Imperishable (Akṣarādhikaraṇa) 3.
Oṃ. [Brahman is] imperishable because it supports up to the ends of space. Oṃ.

The Imperishable (akṣara) denoted by the word "akṣara" in the phrase "That indeed is this" is Brahman alone, not the material cause consisting of consciousness (citprakṛti). Why? Because of its supporting everything up to the ether (ambarāntadhṛteḥ); the meaning is that in this Imperishable, as stated in the passage "in this very Imperishable," there is heard the mention of its being the sustainer of all things ending with space (ākāśa). || 1 ||
Oṃ, and that [is so] because of the authoritative instruction; oṃ.

Why is this so? Because that support of the ends of space occurs through the *praśāsana*—that is, by the mere command—of Viṣṇu, as stated in the scripture beginning with "Of this [breath]... For this reason as well, Brahman alone is denoted by the word "Akṣara"; it does not mean the non-intelligent primordial matter (*prakṛti*). This is the meaning. || 2 ||
Oṃ, in those things excluded from other natures, oṃ.

Furthermore, because the scripture states, "neither gross nor subtle," thereby describing the absence—i.e., the exclusion—of the natures of other entities (anyabhāva), such as grossness and so forth, which are distinct from Viṣṇu, the meaning is that Brahman alone is the Imperishable (akṣara). || 3 ||
|| The Section on the Six Subjects || 4 ||
Oṃ. He [is Brahman], because of the mention of Him as the object of the act of seeing. Oṃ.

"That which is denoted by the words 'Being' (sat) and so forth occurring in this context is Viṣṇu alone, not the Pradhāna. Why? Because of the designation of the object of the act of seeing (īkṣatikarma-vyapadeśāt); that is to say, because there is the mention of the action called 'seeing,' characterized by the words 'It thought' (tadaikṣata), which indicate a conscious agent. || 1 ||
|| The Section Concerning the Small [Space] (Daharādhikaraṇa) || 5 ||
Oṃ, [the teaching] on the small [space] from the later [sections], oṃ.

Viṣṇu alone is the one residing in the small space (*dahara-ākāśa*) within the heart-lotus mentioned in the passage, "In that small lotus is the abode," and not the individual soul (*jīva*) or others. Why? Because of the subsequent [attributes], meaning because of the qualities such as freedom from sin (*apahata-pāpmatva*) and so forth stated in the subsequent passage beginning with, "That Self which is free from sin... (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.7.1). || 1 ||
Oṃ; for it is seen by means of both motion and sound, and by its mark, Oṃ.

By the two reasons of "going" (*gati*) and "word" (*śabda*)—namely, the state of being reached by one who sleeps and the word "Brahman" heard in the passage, "Every day they go to this world of Brahman"—the one situated within the small lotus is indeed Brahman. Furthermore, because in the scripture stating "And the spokes," there is likewise the state of being reached by one who sleeps; for the characteristic mark (*liṅga*), well-known as residing in Viṣṇu, which consists in having a world that rests upon the ocean called Araṇya, serves as the means of proof. It has been stated that [this mark] is seen in the one situated in the heart-lotus.
Therefore, the meaning is that the one situated in the small lotus is Viṣṇu alone. || 2 ||
Oṃ. And because its greatness, consisting of support and so forth, is perceived in this [earth]. Oṃ.

Furthermore, because it is heard in scripture that the one residing in the heart-lotus is the support of all—based on the text, "He is this bridge, the sustainer"—Viṣṇu alone is the one residing in the heart-lotus. Moreover, because the greatness described in the Chāndogya Upaniṣad as residing in the heart-lotus, such as being the Lord of all and so forth, is recognized in this Vājasaneyaka passage, "He is the Lord of all," through its being heard [therein]; and also because of the agreement of their designations, Viṣṇu alone is the one residing in the heart-lotus. Now, if it is asked why Viṣṇu alone is [meant] even by virtue of the designation, it is said: "Of this," and so forth.
"Of this greatness of Viṣṇu"—the meaning is: simply because it is heard in this statement from the Vājasaneyaka [Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad]. || 3 ||
Oṃ, and it is well-established; Oṃ.

And because of the well-known scriptural statement, "The small, sinless one," which establishes that Viṣṇu resides within the heart-lotus, the meaning is that He alone is the one situated in the heart-lotus. || 4 ||
Om. If it be argued that he [is the one referred to] because of a reference to another, we say no, because of impossibility. Om.

Because of the reference to the other: since the individual soul (jīva), which was described as "attaining manifestation in its own form," is referred to and grasped by the word "this Self" (*eṣa ātmā*) as being the Self residing within the heart-lotus; if it is argued that the one residing in the heart-lotus is the individual soul alone—no. Why? Because of impossibility: the meaning is that qualities such as freedom from sin (*apahatapāpmatva*), which are heard in scripture as residing in the one situated in the heart-lotus, are impossible in the individual soul independently. || 5 ||
Oṃ, if it is argued that [the soul] is from the north, then its true nature has indeed been manifested; Oṃ.

The word *tu* (but) has the sense of *eva* (only). The word *na* (not) is to be supplied as the remainder. This is because of the subsequent passage, "He moves about there," from which the qualities such as having true desires are perceived of the individual soul (*jīva*). From that very [passage], freedom from sorrow and so forth are possible. If it is argued that this [individual soul] alone is the one residing in the heart-lotus, we say no. Why? Because in that sentence, by the force of the subsequent phrase "by his own [nature]," it is the liberated soul whose nature has become manifest that is being taught, not the mere individual soul. Furthermore, the liberated soul does not possess qualities such as being free from sin by its own nature. Therefore, even for him, there is no residence in the heart-lotus; this is the meaning. || 6 ||
Oṃ, and the reference is for another purpose; Oṃ.

The word *ca* has the sense of *eva* (only). The reference (*parāmarśaḥ*)—namely, the word *eṣaḥ* ("this") occurring in the sentence "This is the Self"—has another meaning; the meaning is that it refers only to the Supreme Self spoken of as "the highest light," and not to the individual soul (*jīva*). || 7 ||
If it be argued that [the Brahman] has limited hearing, that has already been answered. Om.

If it be argued that because of the mention of its abiding in a small place—namely, the description of the "small" (*dahara*) for one of little learning—the Jīva alone resides in the heart-lotus, [the answer is] "No," this is the remainder [of the sense]. Why? Because that which was stated—that is, the abiding in a small place—is stated in the passage "because it is to be perceived thus" (*nicāyyatvāt tathā hi darśanam*); it is said there that even though Viṣṇu is all-pervading, this is mentioned for the sake of meditation, and it is also stated in the Śruti: "The Self within the heart" (*ātmāntarhṛdaye*). This is the meaning. || 8 ||
|| Section on Imitation (Anukṛtyadhikaraṇa) || 6 ||
Oṃ. And because of its imitation of that [world], Oṃ.

The word *ca* (and) denotes conjunction. The term *tasya* (of that) is a citation of the scriptural passage. *Anukṛtiḥ* means imitation. Thus, Brahman alone is [the subject], being apprehended in a manner favorable to the purpose of knowledge, as expressed in the request, "How indeed may I know That? Why so? Because of "imitation": for in the remainder of the sentence, "Everything shines after Him as He shines," there is heard the statement that the sun and other luminaries are agents of the activity called illumination following the activity of the Blessed Lord; and because of the scriptural declaration that "By His light all this shines," meaning that the entire world is illuminated by the radiance of the Supreme Self. || 2 ||
|| The Section on the Dwarf Incarnation (Vāmanādhikaraṇa) || 7 ||
Oṃ. He is known from the word alone. Oṃ.

Viṣṇu alone is established by the word "Īśāna" in the passage, "Īśāna of the past and the future"; he is determined as such in reality, and not Vāyu. Why? Because of the word itself—meaning, precisely because of the unambiguous scriptural mention of Vāmana in the phrase, "Vāmana in the middle. || 1 ||
Oṃ. But with respect to the heart [of the matter], it is because the qualification belongs to human beings. Oṃ.

The word *tu* has the sense of *eva* (only/indeed) and the sense of *api* (also/even). Thus, the statement that Viṣṇu, although omnipresent, is "the size of a thumb" is made with reference to the heart.

This is said with reference only to the space within the heart, which is the size of a thumb. The meaning is that Viṣṇu’s nature is not to be understood as limited by that measurement. Now, an objection is raised: since animals and the like lack thumbs, how can this statement regarding being "only that much" (thumb-sized) be applicable to all qualified seekers? To this it is replied: "Because the qualification belongs to human beings. Thus, because the meditation on this knowledge has humans as its qualified practitioners, and because the application of this knowledge is possible for them, there is no fault even though animals and the like lack thumbs; this is the intended sense. || 2 ||
The Section Concerning the Deities (Devatādhikaraṇa) 8.
Oṃ. Bādarāyaṇa [maintains that] even above that [the Brahmaloka], [liberation is possible], because it is possible. Oṃ.

Even above that [the human state], there is eligibility for the knowledge of the Vedas for those humans who are fit for divinity—not only during their human stage, but even after they have attained the status of gods and so forth. Why? Because it is possible; for even they possess the specific intelligence and other qualities that constitute the basis for eligibility. This is the meaning of what the venerable Bādarāyaṇa declares. (Sūtra 1)
If it be argued that there is a contradiction regarding action, we say no, because we observe the attainment of various [results]. Om.

If it be argued that there is a contradiction regarding the beginninglessness of the gods and others in relation to ritual action—namely, with respect to rituals such as sacrifices performed in previous kalpas, where a contradiction arises known as "futility caused by the absence of an intended object"—we say: no. Why? Because of the attainment [of divinity] by many; for we observe that many worthy human beings attain the status of deities, as stated in the Śruti: "Wherein the ancients... (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 1.2.9). This is the meaning. || 2 ||
If it be argued that [the world] is merely sound, we say no; because of its power, as established by both perception and inference. Om.

The term "contradiction" (virodha) carries over from the previous context. [Objection: If the gods were to have a beginning and an end, there would be a contradiction known as the lack of authority (*apramāṇya*) regarding the Word, namely the Veda, because the words of the Veda—established by scripture as eternal—would at times be devoid of a referent. This is the sense of the objection. [Reply: This is not so. Why? Because of the Vedic statement, "As the Creator [ordained]... (RV 10.190.3). Likewise, it is established by perception and inference. It is established by the perception of great beings; and by the inferential marks (*liṅga*) proving the production of the gods through a continuous stream (*pravāha*). Furthermore, because their production—denoted by the word *prabhava*—is understood to occur necessarily at every Kalpa, what has been stated is logical. This is the sense. || 3 ||
Oṃ, and for this very reason, there is eternality. Oṃ.

Therefore, precisely because of the eternity of the Veda as asserted by the proponent of the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣin), the eternity of the stream of deities who are its denotata is established through the principle of "otherwise inexplicability" (anyathānupapatti); this is the meaning. || 4 ||
Oṃ. And because name and form are the same, there is no contradiction even in the case of returning, on account of what is seen [in scripture] and from Smṛti. Oṃ.

Even though there is no recurrence of the gods who were liberated in a previous kalpa within their own stations, there is no contradiction—meaning there is no contradiction known as the invalidity of the Veda which establishes that [recurrence]. Why? Because of the identity of names and forms (*samānanāmarūpatvāt*); for even the gods produced in this present kalpa possess names and forms identical to those of the former [gods]. And thus, since the object to be established is also of a single uniform nature, the Veda that reveals it does not lose its authority; this is the sense. To the question "How is it that they are of a single uniform nature?", it is said: "On account of perception and tradition" (*darśanāt smṛteśca*).
The meaning is: because of the Vedic revelation, "as before," and because of the Smṛti statement, "without beginning or end. || 5 ||

Oṃ. Jaimini [maintains] that there is no entitlement [to the knowledge of Brahman] for those who have not undergone initiation, because [the means of knowledge such as the Upaniṣads] do not apply to the Madhu-vidyā and similar meditations. Oṃ.

In the case of the *madhu* and other such [vidyās]—namely, the *madhu-vidyā* and others taught in passages such as "That sun, indeed, is the honey of the gods"—the teacher Jaimini maintains that there is no qualification for the gods, meaning an absence of eligibility. Why? Because of impossibility; the meaning is that their desire, their fitness for those [results], and so forth, are incompatible. (6)
Oṃ, and because of its existence in light, Oṃ.

Because [the gods] exist within the light—that is, within knowledge—since all things are included therein as its objects, it is not fitting for the gods, who possess perfected knowledge, to have a desire for knowledge; thus, the meaning is that they have no qualification even for the sciences of liberation (mokṣavidyā). || 7 ||
Oṃ. But Bādarāyaṇa [holds that] there is indeed [the existence of the soul], for Oṃ.

For indeed, even among the gods there exists a specific excellence of the prior manifestation to be accomplished through knowledge (*vidyā-sādhya-apūrva-prakāśa-viśeṣa*), and there is also a distinction regarding the fruit of liberation (*mokṣa-phala*). Therefore, the meaning is that one considers the "existence" (*bhāvam*)—that is, the presence of qualification—for the gods. However, it should be understood that Jaimini’s opinion intends that the gods have no qualification for the sake of the fruit of knowledge already attained.
[This concludes] the section concerning those other than Śūdras (*apaśūdrādhikaraṇa*).
Oṃ. For it is indicated by the hearing of contempt for that [suffering] and by the fleeing from it; Oṃ.

This refers to the grief of Śuka upon hearing of that king named Pautrāyaṇa’s disregard—specifically, upon hearing the swan’s expression of contempt, "What a wretched man he is! Even so, from what cause does this grief arise? To this it is said: "For it is indicated... For (hi) because it is indicated—that is, known—by the subsequent sentence, "As he was just rising... Therefore, the grief arises from this very cause. The king was addressed as "Śūdra" by the seer Raikva.

The meaning is that it is not with the intention of [denying] inferiority of caste. And thus, the sense is that one should not consider the eligibility of a Śūdra for Vedic knowledge on the strength of this indicative mark. || 1 ||
Oṃ. And because of the understanding that he was a Kṣatriya, and because of the indicative mark of Caitraratha later on, Oṃ.

The particle *ca* (and) serves to aggregate another indicative mark (*liṅga*). For, in the subsequent sentence—of which "by what is heard" (*śrutena*) is the ellipsis—the [subject] is Caitraratha by virtue of the indicative mark consisting in his connection with a chariot yoked with mules, derived from the word *citra*. And because he is understood to be a Kṣatriya through that indicative mark as a signifier, that is, from the knowledge of his being a Kṣatriya, the meaning is that Pautrāyaṇa is not a Śūdra. || 2 ||
Oṃ, [this is established] because of the grasping at formative forces and because of the expression of their non-existence; Oṃ.

The word *ca* (and) serves to conjoin the predicate. Because of the reference to the sacraments (*saṃskāra*) in the passage, "One should initiate a Brāhmaṇa into the study of the Veda; one should teach him," and because the absence of sacraments is stated by the phrase "he is neither [fit for] fire nor sacrifice," the meaning is that he has no entitlement to the knowledge of the Vedas. || 3 ||
Oṃ. And because there is activity [of the mind] even when that [object] has been determined to be non-existent.

The word "ca" (and) is used in the sense of emphasis (*avadhāraṇe*). That is to say, only when there is a determination of his lack of that [status], namely, the ascertainment that the person named Satyakāma is not a Śūdra, does [the objection hold]. This is because Gautama proceeded with his initiation; from this indicative mark (*jñāpaka*), it follows that the sacrament (*saṃskāra*) is not appropriate for a Śūdra—this is the meaning. || 4 ||
Oṃ. [The soul is not Brahman] because of the prohibition of hearing, studying, and understanding its meaning, and because of the Smṛti. Oṃ.

Because of the prohibition against hearing, studying, and ascertaining the meaning [of the Veda] for a Śūdra—since hearing the Veda, its study, and the determination of its meaning are forbidden by the rule, "In the case of hearing [the Veda], the ears are to be filled with tin and lac"—and because of the Smṛti, specifically the prohibitive Smṛti stating, "There is no fire-sacrifice for a Śūdra," the meaning is that he has no entitlement to Vedic knowledge. || 5 ||
The Section on Trembling (Kampanādhikaraṇa) 10.
Oṃ! Because of trembling, Oṃ!

"The great fear is the thunderbolt"—here, that which is denoted by the word "thunderbolt" (vajra) is Viṣṇu alone, and not Indra's weapon. Why? Because of the mention of the mark of being the cause of all motion, as expressed by the word "trembling" in the passage "everything trembles. This is the meaning. || 1 ||
The Section on Light (Jyotir-adhikaraṇa) 11.
Oṃ. From the vision of light, Oṃ.

"He who is this inner light"—the one denoted by the word "light" (jyotis) is Viṣṇu alone, not the individual soul (jīva). Why? Because of the scriptural vision [of Him as such]; the meaning is that there is a Śruti stating, "Viṣṇu alone is the light" (Caturvedaśikhā). || 1 ||
|| Section on Space || 12 ||
Om. Space [is distinct from Brahman] because it is designated as having a different meaning and so forth. Om.

The ether (ākāśa) mentioned in the Śruti passage, "Indeed, [He] is named Ākāśa," is Viṣṇu alone; it is not the unevolved ether (avyākṛtākāśa). Why? Because of the designation of a different meaning and so forth; that is to say, because in the statement "That which is between them," there is described a distinct nature for Viṣṇu consisting in His being devoid of name and form, as well as His being Brahman and Immortal, which are included by the word "and so forth" (ādi). || 1 ||
|| Section on Deep Sleep (Suṣupti-adhikaraṇa) || 13 ||
Oṃ. [This is established] by the distinction between deep sleep and departure [from the body]. Oṃ.

"That which he sees there whatsoever" refers to the Supreme Self alone as the seer of dreams and so forth mentioned in the Śruti, and not the individual soul (jīva). Why? Because the reason—"for this person is unattached" (*asaṅga*)—must be supplied from outside [the sentence], based on the indicative mark (*liṅga*) of non-attachment thus stated. Now, one might object that the statement of non-attachment could also apply to the individual soul by virtue of its non-difference from the Lord; therefore, it is said: "In deep sleep," and so forth.

And likewise, in the sections concerning deep sleep (*suṣupti*) and departure (*utkrānti*), it is stated with distinction—that is, as a difference—that the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Lord (*īśvara*) are distinct, in the passages: "He is embraced by the conscious Self" (*prājñenātmanā saṃpariṣvaktaḥ*) and "mounted by the conscious Self" (*prājñenātmanānvārūḍhaḥ*). The meaning is that there is no identity between the two. || 1 ||
The Section on the Brāhmaṇas || 14 ||
Oṃ. [The refutation] of the words "Lord" (pati) and so forth. Oṃ.

"This is the eternal greatness of the Brāhmaṇa"—the Viṣṇu, and not Viriñca (Brahmā), is the "Brāhmaṇa" mentioned in this Śruti. Why? Because of words such as "Lord" and so forth; that is to say, because of scriptural passages expressing lordship and other qualities, such as "the Lord of all. || 1 ||
Thus ends the third quarter of the first chapter in the Sūtradīpikā composed by the venerable Jagannātha Yati. 1.3.
Section on those who rely on inference (Ānumānikādhikaraṇa) || 1 ||
"Oṃ. If it be argued that for some [the Self] is also inferential, we say no; because [the scripture] shows that it is grasped as being presented through the metaphor of the body. Oṃ.

The word *api* has the sense of *eva* (only/indeed); *ca* is used for the conjunction of traditional authorities (*smṛti*). And thus, because that which is inferential—that is, postulated by the inference of the Sāṃkhyas, such as Pradhāna and so forth—is expressed by words like "the Unmanifest" (*avyakta*) occurring in the statements of certain Vedic branches, such as "From the Unmanifest, the Puruṣa," therefore it is not logical that Viṣṇu is denotable by all words.

If this is argued, we say no. For Viṣṇu alone is denoted by words such as "the Unmanifest" (*avyakta*), and not the *pradhāna* or other such principles. Why is that? Because the scripture states, "The Unmanifest" (*Pippalāda-śruti*), and the traditional law (*smṛti*) states, "The Unmanifest, the Imperishable. [The word] "darśayati" means that it demonstrates and establishes that Viṣṇu alone is denoted by words such as "the Unmanifest. This is the meaning. [Objection: How then is the usage of words like "the Unmanifest" applied elsewhere? To this it is said: "In the form of a body," and so forth. The suffix *kap* is used here in a derogatory sense.

And likewise, [the terms] are understood as being applied through a metaphorical identification with the body. Just as the body is dependent upon the person, so too—on the ground of its dependence upon the Supreme Self—the Unmanifest and other such entities are metaphorically designated by words like "Unmanifest" (*avyakta*) and so forth, because they are essentially bodiless and are considered contemptible when compared to the body. Thus, the meaning is that the conventional usage of terms like "Unmanifest" for *prakṛti* and other things is due solely to their connection with the Supreme Self. || 1 ||
Oṃ. But that [mind] is subtle because of its worthiness; Oṃ.

Because that which is subtle is indeed subtle and is denoted by the word "unmanifest" (avyakta). Why? Because it is fit for that; that is, because that subtle entity possesses the fitness to be the ground for the application of the term "unmanifest. Furthermore, subtlety belongs to Viṣṇu alone. Therefore, the meaning is that He alone is denoted by the word "unmanifest. || 2 ||
Om. [The individual soul exists] as something purposeful because it is dependent on Him. Om.

And the word "ca" (and) occurring here [in the sūtra] is understood from the previous context. The entire collection of words denoting "supreme," "suffering," "bound," and so forth, applies to the Supreme Self alone; it is meaningful—that is, it possesses a purposeful ground for application (*pravṛttinimitta*)—and is not useless. Why? Because they are dependent on Him; that is, because those attributes such as being supreme or inferior, which reside in *pradhāna* and other things, are dependent upon the Lord. Thus, the meaning is that it is indeed appropriate to employ words like "supreme" and "inferior" with respect to the Lord, even by way of His being the owner of the grounds for application residing in other things. || 3 ||
Oṃ, and because it is not stated that [the self] is an object of knowledge, Oṃ.

The meaning is that Viṣṇu alone is denoted by the words "the Unmanifest" (avyakta) and so forth occurring here, because of the statement that Viṣṇu alone is to be known for the sake of liberation—"Know Him alone as the One"—and because such [knowability] is not stated for others; on the contrary, they are said to be things to be abandoned with the word "abandon. || 4 ||
If it is argued that [the syllable] "oṃ" means "he speaks," no, for he is wise. Oṃ!

[Objection: But does not the Kaṭha Upaniṣad statement, "without beginning or end," speak of the Pradhāna, thereby establishing that even this [Pradhāna] is an object of knowledge? [Reply: No. Why? Because the one designated by the word "Prājña" (the Wise One) is the Supreme Self alone that is being expounded there, not the Pradhāna. Therefore, the meaning is that its status as an object of knowledge is not to be accepted. || 5 ||
Oṃ, from the source, Oṃ.
The meaning is that, by the force of the context, it is the *prājña* alone who is to be established here among the three forms of Viṣṇu. || 6 ||
Oṃ. And thus there is both the presentation and the question regarding these three alone. Oṃ.

In the *Yuktisamuccaya*, the word "ca" (and) is used after "yataḥ" (since), and the word "eva" (only/just) refers to the threefold nature of the manner [in which the questions were asked]. Thus, since [it was] only in this way—namely, regarding only these three, consisting of the propitiation of the ancestors, heaven, and the fire of the Supreme Self—that the question concerning them was posed by the seer Naciketas to Yama; and since only their presentation and the corresponding answers are seen here in this section, the meaning is that the Pradhāna is not what is being expounded here. || 7 ||
Oṃ, and like the Great One, Oṃ.

The word *ca* (and) serves to include the Dārṣyaṇtika view. The meaning is that just as the word *mahat* occurring in the passage beginning with "the great, all-pervading Self" refers exclusively to Viṣṇu and not to the *mahat-tattva*, so too it is with words such as *avyakta*. || 8 ||
Oṃ, [the fire-altars] are like the cups, because there is no distinction; Oṃ.

As in the case of the *camasa*, just as the word *camasa*—though well-known as a sacrificial vessel—is understood by the force of the scriptural text "This is that head" (*idaṃ tacchiraḥ*) to denote the head, so too, although words such as *avyakta* (the unmanifest) are well-known to refer to the *pradhāna* (primordial matter) and other such entities, they denote Viṣṇu alone. Why? Because of the scriptural text "Names [belong to Him]" (*nāmāni*). But even so, why do they denote Viṣṇu? To this it is said: "Because there is no distinction" (*aviśeṣāt*). This means that because of the scriptural text "All names [belong to Him]," there is no distinction from the text "This [is that head]. (9)
Section 2: The Topic Beginning with "Light" (Jyotir-upakrama-adhikaraṇa)
Oṃ. But [the soul] begins from light, for so it is taught by some. Oṃ.

The word *tu* has the sense of *eva* (only). [The term] *jyotis* refers only to Brahman, which is denoted by the word *jyotis* and others mentioned in such scriptural passages as "One should sacrifice with *jyotis*"; it does not refer to the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice and the like. Why? Because (*hi*), for this reason, certain followers of specific Vedic branches (*eke śākhinaḥ*) recite and read [this passage] in the section beginning with "This [sacrifice]... and continuing with "These indeed...", thus establishing that Hari alone is the denotation of all words. This is the meaning. || 1 ||
Oṃ. And because of the instruction regarding mental construction, there is no contradiction, as in the case of honey and so forth. Oṃ.

The word *ca* has the sense of "and" (*evārthe*) or "also" (*samuccaye*). And thus, as in the case of honey and so forth—just as there is no contradiction even though the words "honey" and so on found in the Madhu-vidyā and other contexts denote Viṣṇu.

The contradiction known as the absence [of those qualities] arises from the absence of words denoting worldly honey and so forth. Likewise, even if it is accepted that the Supreme Self is denotable by all words, there is no contradiction with the absence of karma and the like. Why? Because, having accepted that words have the functions of etymological derivation (*yoga*) and conventional usage (*rūḍhi*) elsewhere, one must supply the phrase: "because it is admitted that in the case of the Lord, they function through great etymological derivation (*mahāyoga*). And why is that? "Because of the teaching of figurative designation (*kalpanopadeśāt*)," since the fact that Viṣṇu is denotable by all words was stated for the purpose of meditation (*upāsanā*), which is designated by the term "figurative designation," as in the passage, "The vital breath is the *ṛc*s."

And the meaning is that this is impossible without the *mahāyoga-vṛtti* (great etymological application), which consists in possessing the primary and secondary qualities of all words and their meanings. || 2 || [End of] the Section on the Non-Inclusion of Numbers. || 3 ||
Oṃ. [The Brahman is] not [the cause], even because of the inclusion of a specific number, due to the diversity [of the elements] and because of the surplus [of qualities]. Oṃ.

Because of the inclusion of a number, as indicated by the plural expression "in whom the five five-people (pañcajanāḥ)" [RV 10.89.15]; and also because of the designation of a relationship between a substratum and its contents in the phrase "in whom. There is no contradiction in Viṣṇu being denoted by words such as "five-people," because of His manifold nature, that is, because the Lord exists in many forms. Furthermore, because of the surplus: the meaning is that the form of the substratum mentioned as "in whom" and the form of the contents mentioned as "the five-people" are non-different yet possessed of distinction. || 1 ||
Om. [The five breaths] beginning with prāṇa [are meant here], because of the supplementary statement. Om.

The five classes of beings (*pañcajana*) mentioned as being of the nature of the Blessed Lord should be understood as the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) and so forth—the second set specified by the names of smell, sight, hearing, food, and mind. Why? Because of the remainder of the passage (*vākyaśeṣa*). And they are indeed specific forms of the Blessed Lord. Why? Because of the remainder of the passage beginning with "the breath of breath" (*prāṇasya prāṇam*), which establishes that the quality of being the life-force of the vital breath and the like is impossible for anyone other than Viṣṇu. This is the meaning. || 2 ||
Oṃ! For some, food does not exist; [it exists] as light. Oṃ!

In the branch (śākhā) of certain [sages] such as Kaṇva and others, even though it is not explicitly stated that the Lord exists in the form called "Food" (anna), the meaning is that the completion of the number five should be understood by means of "Light" (jyotis), which is the form of the Lord known by that name. || 3 ||
Section 4: The Topic of Space (Ākāśādhikaraṇa)
Oṃ. And because [Brahman] is designated as the cause in relation to ether and the other elements, as stated [in scripture]. Oṃ.

In passages such as "From the Self, space was produced; from space, air," Viṣṇu alone is present within space and the other elements, denoted by words like "space" which signify intermediate causes that possess the nature of being both effects and causes. He is spoken of as the cause (by the word *ca*) and as the effect (by the word *vāyu* etc.), but not as a mere elemental entity (*bhūta*). Why? Because of the statement regarding his being designated [as such]: in passages such as "He who is unheard from here," Viṣṇu is described as being designated by a certain form, namely, by his state of being unknown and so forth. The meaning is that he is described in the passages concerning space and the rest—such as "whom space does not know"—precisely as one endowed with that very form. || 1 ||
|| Section on Attraction (Samākarṣādhikaraṇa) || 5 ||
Oṃ, from the complete drawing forth, Oṃ!

The meaning is that there is no consequence of the loss of linguistic usage elsewhere, because the word—which primarily denotes the Supreme Self by its own primary function—is drawn from that [primary sense] and its capacity to denote another object is admitted. || 1 ||
Oṃ. [The Self is Brahman] because it is designated as the world. Oṃ.
The meaning is that because one understands from worldly usage that words denote the world, it is logical that their conventional application (prasiddhi) therein is established. || 2 ||
If it be argued that [the term "breath"] refers to the individual soul (jīva) and the chief vital air (mukhya-prāṇa) because of indicative marks and so forth, that has already been explained. Om.

And in the passages, "When the living self (jīva) leaves one branch of this [tree]," and "For the worlds are led by the wind," because of the indicative marks (liṅga) of the living self and the chief vital breath (mukhya-prāṇa)—that is, because of the hearing of these two indicative marks—one might argue that both of them should also be the primary denotations of those respective words. If this is said, it is not so. Why? Because the meaning is: since that collection of sentences has been explained as being directed toward their respective inner rulers (antaryāmin). || 3 ||
Oṃ, but Jaimini [holds that the name] has another purpose, on account of both a question and an explanation; and for this reason, some [Vedic schools] even recite it [differently]. Oṃ.

The word *tu* has the sense of *eva* (only/indeed). By this, it is also logical that words [originally] referring to Viṣṇu are drawn elsewhere to establish [the nature of] ritual action (*karman*) and so forth. Why? Because that is for another purpose—namely, for the sake of knowledge of the Supreme Self (*paramātman*). If one asks how that is so, the teacher Jaimini considers it to be established by both a question and an explanatory statement: from Śaunaka’s question, "In whom? (*kasmin nu*), and from Aṅgiras’s statement, "There are two kinds of knowledge," as well as from the statement, "How indeed? (*kathaṃ nu*).* *Note: The Sanskrit terms have been transliterated using IAST diacritics as requested.*

Furthermore, certain followers of particular Vedic branches explicitly state, "He who does not know that [other]," thus teaching that knowledge of other things is for the sake of knowing the Supreme Self; the meaning is: "for this reason as well. || 4 ||
Oṃ, because of the connection of the statements, Oṃ.
The meaning is that, with a view toward the concordance of all scriptural statements regarding Brahman, the Veda must also propound ritual action and so forth. || 5 ||
Oṃ. Āśmarathya [holds that] the mark [of the Self] is the fulfillment of the promise. Oṃ.

The exposition of ritual action and so forth is by means of the Veda; for it is the means of establishing the initial proposition. Since knowledge alone is the cause of liberation and nothing else—thus establishing the meaning of the proposition "There is no other path"—the Veda serves as the proof. Therefore, the teacher Āśmarathya considers that its exposition is appropriate because of its utility toward that [knowledge]. This is the meaning. || 6 ||
"Oṃ! Auḍulomi maintains that [the soul] has already been drawn out from its state of being. Oṃ.

The meaning is that the teacher Auḍulomi considers it entirely appropriate for the Veda to teach ritual action and so forth as a means to knowledge for the sake of liberation; for since the qualified seeker—who desires liberation through knowledge—is about to depart [from this world], action and the like must still be performed as a cause for attaining such knowledge. Thus, their presentation by the Veda as a means to the knowledge aimed at liberation is indeed justified. || 7 ||
Oṃ. "Because of [the Lord's] abiding [in the individual soul], so says Kāśakṛtsna. Oṃ.

The meaning is that the teacher Kāśakṛtsna considers that because all actions and so forth abide in the Blessed One as their universal substratum, the Veda teaches the nature of the actions and so forth—which serve as the superstrata—in order to make known the Blessed One’s status as the substratum of action and the rest. It should be understood that there is no contradiction among these views, as they pertain to different authorities. || 8 ||
|| Section on Primordial Matter (Prakṛtyadhikaraṇa) || 6 ||
Oṃ. And [Brahman] is the material cause, because there is no contradiction between the initial proposition and the illustrative examples. Oṃ.

The Lord is not denoted by masculine terms alone, but is also denoted by feminine terms such as *prakṛti* (Nature) and so forth, as stated in the passage beginning "She is this Nature. Why? Because only in this way is there no contradiction between the initial proposition (*pratijñā*) and the illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*). That is to say, it is because there is no conflict between the proposition, "Come, let me enter into these two," and the example, "as [rivers enter] the ocean"; otherwise, there would be a contradiction between them. || 1 ||
Oṃ, and because of the teaching regarding covetousness, Oṃ.

The meaning is as follows: from the *abhidhyā* (the will) of the Lord; from the instruction in the Śruti, "But Māyā... (*Māyāṃ tu...*), where it is stated that [the Lord] is denoted by the word *prakṛti*; and because the Lord, who is non-different from that will, is also denoted by that same word. || 2 ||
Oṃ, and there is the direct transmission of both; Oṃ.

The word *ca* is used for emphasis (*avadhāraṇe*). "Directly" means without the mediation of a door. Because both are mentioned—in the statement "This is that person" (*paiṅgi-śruti*), which declares that He is denotable by the words for both Nature (*prakṛti*) and Spirit (*puruṣa*)—the meaning is that it is necessary for the Lord to be denotable by such terms as "Nature" and so forth. || 3 ||
Oṃ. [The world] is not from a self-made cause, because of transformation. Oṃ.

The meaning is that Viṣṇu alone is denoted by the word "prakṛti" (primordial nature), because he effects the transformation of primordial nature and impels it, and because through his own self-activity he makes himself manifold. || 4 ||
Oṃ, for it is indeed sung as the womb; Oṃ.

For indeed, because the Lord is proclaimed and established by the Śruti text "yad-rūta-yonim" as the source (yoni) and as the progenitor of offspring from His own body; therefore, the meaning is that He is denotable by feminine gendered words such as *prakṛti* and so forth. || 5 ||
By this, the section concerning the *savara* [sacrifice] has been explained. || 7 ||
Oṃ. By this, all [sections] have been explained; they have been explained. Oṃ.

By this very reason stated previously, all words such as "void" (śūnya) and so forth are explained; the meaning is that they primarily denote the Blessed One himself. This repetition at the end of the chapter is for the purpose of confirming that the meaning set forth from the beginning of this chapter until its conclusion is exactly thus. || 1 ||
Thus ends the fourth quarter of the first chapter in the *Sūtradīpikā* composed by the venerable Jagannātha Yati. 1.4.
Thus the first chapter is completed.
The First Pāda of the Second Adhyāya.
Section on Smṛti (Tradition) || 1 ||

Oṃ. If it is argued that this leads to the fault of leaving no room for other Smṛtis, we say no, because that would lead to the fault of leaving no room for other Smṛtis [that are consistent with the Vedas]. Oṃ.

Because it would entail the fault of leaving no room for the Smṛtis; that is, by leaving no scope for Smṛtis such as those of the Pāśupatas and others regarding Viṣṇu’s status as the creator of the world and so forth, there would arise the fault of contradicting them if the Śrutis were intended to establish Viṣṇu as the cause—namely, the attainment of the fault known as invalidity.
