Therefore, it is argued that it is not logical for the Śrutis to have Viṣṇu’s causality as their purport, but rather that they must have the causality of Śiva and others as their purport. To this, we say: No.

Why? Because of the consequence of the fault of leaving no room for other Smṛtis. Since the Pañcarātra and other Smṛtis are more powerful than other Smṛtis—such as the Pāśupata and others—due to their agreement with Śruti and because they were composed by Viṣṇu and others who are the most omniscient among Rudra and the rest, there would be no room for them [the Pañcarātra etc. regarding the agency of Rudra and others over the world. Consequently, there would be the fault of invalidity (aprāmāṇya) for the contradictory Śaiva and other Smṛtis, as they would have no scope. The meaning is that, by accepting a superior connection [with Śruti] for those [Pañcarātra etc.], the contradiction [by the Śaiva Smṛtis] becomes irrelevant. || 1 ||
Oṃ, and because others are not perceived, Oṃ.

The term "non-perception" (*anupalabdhi*) is repeated. The word "and" (*ca*) indicates the acceptance of the perception of some [limited] result. Thus, because of non-perception—that is, because of the transcendence of the senses—there is no perception, i.e., no direct observation, of other distinct results suitable for perception, nor of the results mentioned by the Pāśupatas and others, even when the performance or abandonment of the practices prescribed by them has been carried out. Therefore, the meaning is that their lack of authority (*aprāmāṇya*) alone is logical. || 2 ||
Oṃ. By this, Yoga has been answered. Oṃ.

By this very reason previously stated—namely, that [the self] is characterized by being a consumer of the fruit [of actions]—yoga, meaning the Yoga-śāstra, is refuted; the sense is that it is rejected. || 3 ||
Section 2: On the Absence of Non-Differentiation in Characteristics.
Oṃ. Because this [Brahman] is devoid of defining characteristics, its suchness is established through the Word. Oṃ.

This scripture, along with the Smṛtis that follow it, does not lack authority like the Śaiva and other such Smṛtis. Why? Because of its distinctness—namely, its distinction from others known as intrinsic validity (*svataḥ-prāmāṇya*). Furthermore, because the Śruti possesses the distinction of being eternal, and because the Smṛti possesses the distinction of following the Śruti, there is no lack of authority; "being so" means possessing the aforementioned distinctions. This is ascertained from the word [of the Veda], from the traditional teaching: "O Virūpa, she is eternal through speech. || 1 ||
Oṃ, it is indeed seen; Oṃ.

The word "tu" (but) is for the purpose of specification. For, the fruit declared by the Śruti and other authorities is seen—that is, perceived—by those specific qualified persons who are fit for that fruit; therefore, the meaning is that there is no lack of authority [in the scripture]. || 2 ||
Section 3: The Topic of the Possessor of the Conceit (Abhimānin)
Oṃ. But [the term "Self"] refers to that which presides over [the body], because of the specific [usage] and the inclusive [usage]. Oṃ.

The word *tu* (but) is used for emphasis. In expressions such as "the clay spoke," there is a designation (*vyapadeśa*) of the presiding conscious being (*abhimānin*), meaning that the speech is attributed to a sentient entity and not to the insentient matter itself. Why? Because it would contradict reason to say that an insentient thing speaks; therefore, the Veda does not lose its authority.

Now, one might ask: since the possessor of egoity (abhimānin) cannot be disembodied and must therefore possess a body, how can his non-perception [in certain states], his capacity for speech by means of another object as a substrate, and his presiding over multiple objects of egoity be possible? To this it is said: "Distinction" (viśeṣa) means capacity (sāmarthya); "concomitance" (anugati) means pervasion of all objects of egoity. By these two, everything is made possible—this is the meaning. || 1 ||
Oṃ, and it is indeed perceived; Oṃ.

Furthermore, the capacity [of the mantra] with respect to the presiding deity is perceived by yogis; therefore, for this reason as well, there is no contradiction with non-perception—this is the meaning. || 2 ||
Topic 4: On the Non-existent (asat) as the Locus.
Oṃ. If it be argued that [the world] is non-existent, we say no, because [the scripture] consists merely of a negation. Oṃ.

If it is argued that "non-existent" refers only to the prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) of the universe, and therefore God is not the creator of the world—no, for what reason? Because it is a mere negation; the meaning is that it is the object of a cognition of negation by its very nature (*svarūpataḥ*), without possessing the character of an absence (*abhāvadharma*). || 1 ||
Oṃ. [The doctrine is] untenable because, on account of [the soul's] merging [into Brahman], the same undesirable consequence would follow. Oṃ.

"At dissolution" means at the time of reabsorption (*apīti*). "Because that would follow" means because it would follow that [the world] consists of mere non-existence. "The state of being an agent of what is non-existent" means it is improper—that is, illogical—[to hold such a view]. || 2 ||
Oṃ. But this is not so, because of the existence of counter-examples. Oṃ.

The word "tu" (but) serves to emphasize. It is not tenable that all things are non-existent during the dissolution (*pralaya*). Why? Because at that time, the existence of all categories of entities (*padārtha*) is indeed observed; the meaning is that they exist. || 3 ||
Oṃ, and because of the faults in one's own position, Oṃ.

The meaning is that his position is not tenable because of the fault [inherent] in his own side—that is, in the position that everything is non-existent at the time of dissolution—and also because of the fault known as the "inclusion within the example" (dṛṣṭāntāntarbhāva). || 4 ||
Oṃ. If it is argued that, because reasoning lacks a firm foundation, the object of inference must be otherwise, even so, there follows the consequence of the impossibility of liberation. Oṃ.

"Because reasoning is unestablished," that is, because reasoning—characterized by the absence of illustrative examples (*dṛṣṭānta*) and so forth—is unestablished and lacks definitive certainty. "In another way," meaning even in a manner other than that stated by the proponent. If it is argued that "the object of inference may be established by a counter-reasoning (*pratitarka*) in yet another form," the answer is "no"—this is the ellipsis. Why? Because even so, if this were the case, and reasoning in general were not a valid means of knowledge (*apramāṇya*), there would follow the consequence of no liberation (*anirmokṣaprasaṅga*); that is, there would be the consequence of the loss of even liberation, which is accepted by all proponents of philosophical systems as the very purpose of their respective scriptures.

The meaning is: why? Because for one who is in disagreement, it must be established by means of inference alone, and thus it is possible for that [inference] as well to be stated as lacking authority in the same way. || 5 ||
Oṃ, by this, those disciples who are not yet formally accepted are also explained; Oṃ.

By this—namely, by the reason consisting in the presence or absence of supporting examples regarding one's own and opposing positions—the remaining views, including those concerning the soul (*jīva*), time (*kāla*), inherent nature (*svabhāva*), and agency (*kartṛtva*), have been explained, rejected, and refuted; that is to say, they are devoid of Vedic authority and are contrary to it. || 6 ||
|| Section on the Enjoyer (Bhoktr-adhikaraṇa) || 5 ||
If it be argued that there is no distinction because of the attainment of the state of being the enjoyer, we reply: it would be as in the world. Oṃ.

[Objection: Because the enjoyer—the individual soul (jīva)—attains the state of Brahman, as is heard in the scriptural passage, "In the supreme, imperishable, all become one"; therefore, there is no distinction between the two, meaning an absence of difference. Consequently, it is not logical that Brahman, which is non-different from the limited individual soul, should be the cause of the world. [Reply: This is not so. Why? Because "as in the world" (lokavat): just as in the world the statement regarding the becoming one of one body of water with another body of water is made, so too here, based on the unity of location and other such factors, the statement that the individual soul and the Lord "become one" would be a figurative expression of unity. Therefore, the aforementioned defect does not apply. || 1 ||
The Section on the Originative Injunction (Ārambhaṇādhikaraṇa) 6.
Oṃ. There is non-difference [of the effect] from that [cause], on account of the words concerning "originating material" (ārambhaṇa) and so forth. Oṃ.

The non-difference from That—that is, the non-distinction of that independent cause from Brahman—must be asserted. Why? "From the word *ārambhaṇa* and others"; this means: from the passage beginning with *ārambhaṇa*, which implies the substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*) and so forth as indicated by the result [of the inquiry], namely, "In the beginning, what was there? and from logical arguments such as independence (*svātantrya*). || 1 ||
Oṃ. And because [the object] is perceived when there is a mental state, Oṃ.

Because, if there were the existence (bhāva) of an independent means other than God—that is, if such a thing were perceived (upalabdhi)—then [the aforementioned] consequence would follow; therefore, for this reason as well, there is no independent means. This is the meaning. || 2 ||
Oṃ, and because of the existence of what follows, Oṃ.

The word *ca* is used in the sense of emphasis (*avadhāraṇe*). Since that which has no independent means of proof exists [only] because of [the authority of scripture], the statement "He was born from the waters" is intended for that very purpose; thus, there is no contradiction with it—this is the meaning. || 3 ||

"Om. If it be argued that [the Self] is not [the cause] because of the designation of non-existence, we say no; for there is another attribute [intended], as is evident from the remainder of the passage. Om."

Because there is a designation of non-existence, [it is argued that] "non-existence did not exist," since it is stated that something else was non-existent; therefore, the existence of another is not tenable—if this is said, we reply: no. Why? Because that negation is joined with a specific attribute of another property, such as dependence (asvātantrya) and so forth. How is this known? From the remainder of the sentence (*vākyaśeṣa*). The meaning is: from the remaining part of the sentence, "Darkness existed. || 4 ||
Oṃ. [The self is distinct from the body] because of reasoning and because of another scriptural passage. Oṃ.

Just as one who goes out to strike with a staff during a dissolution (pralaya) does not suffer lameness due to his own skillful play (līlā), so too it is appropriate for the Blessed Lord—who relies on means under His own control—to act through His divine play. This is established by another scriptural passage and by the specific traditional teaching (āgama) that "even though He is capable [He acts thus]"; therefore, what has been stated is correct. || 5 ||
Oṃ, like a cloth, oṃ.
The meaning is that the creation of the universe, like the weaving of a cloth, must be accomplished by means of other instruments distinct from the agent. || 6 ||
Oṃ, just as the vital breaths and so forth [arise], Oṃ.
Just as the vital breath, body, senses, and so forth are not independent, so too are other means such as primordial nature (prakṛti) and the like; this is the meaning. || 7 ||
Section 7: The Topic of Designation as Something Else (Itaravyapadeśādhikaraṇa)
Oṃ. Because of the designation of [the Self] as something other, there would follow the defect of not performing what is beneficial and so forth. Oṃ.

The words “iti” and “yadi tarhi” are to be supplied as the remainder [of the sentence]. Because of this designation, since it is stated in the Śruti, “arising from the individual soul (jīva),” that very soul is the agent, not the Lord. If that is so, then there follows the contingency of defects such as the non-performance of what is beneficial; that is, the contingency arises that the non-performance of what is beneficial and the performance of what is harmful, which reside in the individual soul, would constitute defects. The sense is that these two would not exist [as defects] if the soul were independent. Yet these two do exist in the soul; therefore, the meaning is that the individual soul is not an independent agent. || 1 ||
Oṃ, moreover, because of the teaching of distinctions, Oṃ.

The word "tu" (but) serves to exclude equality with the individual soul (jīva). Brahman, however, is superior to the individual soul. Why? Because in such passages as "the hearer, the thinker," etc., specific attributes such as being a hearer are stated; this is the meaning. || 2 ||
Oṃ. And like a stone and so forth, that [transformation] is impossible. Oṃ.

The word *ca* has the sense of the word *api*. "Like stone and so forth" means like rock and the like. "Even though the individual soul (*jīva*) is conscious" means even if it possesses sentience; "the impossibility of that" means the impossibility of its being an agent by itself due to its lack of independence. || 3 ||
"Oṃ. If it be argued that [the soul does not enter the Supreme], because we see the withdrawal [of the organs at death], we say: no, for it is like milk, Oṃ."

Because we observe the completion [of the work] by means of the individual soul (*jīva*), it might be argued that the individual soul alone is the agent, and thus the previously stated agency of Brahman does not hold. If this is said, we reply: no. Why?

Because—as in the case of milk, which is seen among cows—the agency for the completion of what was begun by the individual soul is actually the agency of the Supreme Self (*paramātman*). By the word "for" (*hi*), the scriptural authority of the passage "Food" (*anna*) is indicated as proof for this point. || 4 ||
Oṃ. Even as among the gods and others, so also in the world, Oṃ.

It is logical that even for an Īśvara of such a nature, there should be invisibility, just as in the case of gods and others. To the question "How is this so?", it is said: "In the world. The meaning is that in the world—that is, in the universe—the power of invisibility and so forth is observed even in beings such as *piśācas*; what then need be said regarding the Lord of All? || 5 ||

Om. [If Brahman were to transform into the world] entirely, it would follow that it is subject to total destruction, or else there would be a contradiction with the scriptural texts concerning its partlessness. Om.

The word *vā* indicates the introduction of a fault by way of an alternative position (*pakṣabheda*). If it is accepted that the individual soul (*jīva*) possesses inherent agency and acts with its entire capacity, then there would be the consequence of total engagement (*kṛtsnaprasakti*), meaning there would be the undesirable implication of engaging in all activities—such as the grasping of grass—with its full power. Furthermore, if, in order to avoid this, one accepts that it acts only through a single part (*ekadeśena*), then there would be a contradiction with the scriptural statement regarding its being partless (*niravayava*); the meaning is that there would be a conflict with the *Bhāllaveya* Śruti which states, "It is eternal and partless. || 6 ||
The Section on the Scriptural Basis of Śruti (Topic 8).
Oṃ. [The validity] of the Śruti [is established], because it has the Word as its source. Oṃ.

In the view that God is the agent, however, there is no defect consisting of a contradiction with the arguments stated regarding the view that the individual soul (*jīva*) is the agent—such as [the objection] beginning with "the consequence of the whole [of the world] being affected. Why? Because of scripture itself; for there is the scriptural text from the Paiṅgi-śruti: "He who is that [agent] which is opposed [to reason]. Now, one might ask: how does this much resolve the contradiction with reason? To this it is said: "Because it has its root in the Word (*śabda*). Since God and His attributes have the Word alone as their means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*), they do not fall within the scope of reason; therefore, a contradiction with reason does not apply to them. But it is not so in the case of the individual soul. The meaning is that the soul can be known through other means of knowledge as well. || 1 ||
Oṃ, and likewise within the self; for indeed, they are manifold. Oṃ.

The first word *ca* (and) is used for emphasis; the second is for conjunction. The word *hi* indicates well-known fact. Thus, from the word *hi*, [it follows that] within the Self there is only the Lord. In this way, there exist various and inconceivable powers—well-known from scripture through the phrase "possessing diverse powers"—which dispel all contradictions with reasoning; these powers reside in the Lord, not in the individual soul (*jīva*). Therefore, the meaning is that the contradiction with reasoning applies only to the position of the individual soul, not to the position of the Lord. || 2 ||
Oṃ, and because of the faults in one's own position, Oṃ.

The word *ca* (and) has the sense of restriction (*avadhāraṇe*). Thus, since the scripture stating "those defects" mentions only the defect of contradiction with reasoning regarding the position of the individual soul (*jīva*), that [position] must not be led to a state of being free from defects; rather, the meaning is that only the position of the Lord (*īśvara*) is to be understood as being free from defects. || 3 ||
Oṃ, and she is endowed with all [perfections] because of seeing that; Oṃ.

For the deity known as the Supreme Self (Paramātman) is not only generally possessed of diverse powers; rather, She is "endowed with all" (sarvopetā), meaning She possesses powers regarding all objects at all times. Why? Because of the scriptural revelation (śruti) stating, "She is joined with all," as seen in that [text]. Therefore, the meaning is that one should not suspect any contradiction with reason regarding the Lord (Īśvara). || 4 ||
If it be argued that [the world] is not [produced by Brahman] because of its being subject to modification, we reply: that has already been answered. Om.

"No," [the objection] continues. Because of being devoid of instruments; for from the scriptural statement, "Without hands or feet," it is understood that the Lord is devoid of the sense organs such as hands and so forth. If it is argued that "no"—that is, the Lord's status as an agent is not tenable—then we say no. Why? Because that has been stated: by the scripture beginning with "Not there, nor of him," the fact of His being devoid of instruments is declared to pertain to the domain of natural (material) senses; therefore, this is the meaning. || 5 ||
|| Section on Purpose || 9 ||
Oṃ, [the Lord is] not [the cause], because [the world] possesses a purpose, Oṃ.

The activity of the Lord at the beginning of creation is not for the sake of some purpose of His own. Why? Because He possesses a purpose [in the sense that He has nothing further to attain]; the meaning is that, being perfect bliss, He has already attained all that is to be attained. || 1 ||
Oṃ, as in the world, His activity is mere sport; Oṃ.

The word "tu" (but) is used in the sense of "evātha" (indeed, on the other hand). "As in the world" means that, just as in the world there is the activity of intoxicated persons and so forth, so too is the activity of the Lord. "Līlākaivalyam" means that it consists solely of sport; the meaning is that it does not have the pursuit of some purpose for Himself as its objective. || 2 ||
The Section on Inequality and Cruelty (Sūtra 34–39). || 10 ||
Oṃ. [The Lord is] not subject to partiality or cruelty, because He has regard for [the merit and demerit of beings]; for thus Scripture shows. Oṃ.

If it is admitted that the independent Lord, as the bestower of fruits, depends upon the karma of living beings, then the two faults of partiality and cruelty—which would otherwise attach to Him as an uneven and merciless giver of results—do not exist. Why? Because He is dependent; that is, because it is accepted that the Lord is dependent upon karma. Why is that? Because the Śruti, in the words "By merit, [one attains] merit," shows—that is, establishes—this; such is the meaning. || 3 ||
Oṃ. If it be argued that [the world] did not exist because there was no differentiation of karma, we say no, because [karma] is beginningless. Oṃ.

To avoid the faults of partiality (*vaiṣamya*) and cruelty (*nairghṛṇya*), it is specifically denied that there is no action to be taken into account by the Lord. Why? "Because of non-distinction" (*avibhāgāt*); because that action is not distinct from things that lack independence—that is to say, because of their dependence. If it is argued that, in this way, partiality and the like cannot be avoided due to the dependence on action that is under [the Lord's] own control, we say no. Why? "Because of beginninglessness" (*anāditvāt*); the meaning is that the succession of actions is beginningless.

Likewise, if it is accepted that Īśvara causes the successive actions to be performed by the *jīva* in dependence upon each preceding action, then because the action itself becomes a necessary condition, the aforementioned fault does not apply; this is the intended meaning. || 4 ||
Oṃ, it both arises and is perceived; Oṃ.

Even when the Lord depends upon karma, His independence is established and indeed remains consistent, because karma itself is under His control. Now, one might object that dependence on karma—which is itself under His control—would result in the emergence of partiality; to this it is said: "And it is perceived. The meaning is that through the scriptural text, "He causes [them] to act," such partiality is known not to be a defect. || 5 ||
Chapter Eleven: The Section on the Arising of All Dharmas.
Oṃ, and because all phenomena arise [from conditions], Oṃ.

The meaning is that since all attributes—consisting of the presence of qualities, the absence of defects, and so forth—are logically established, and because [these] are appropriately applicable to Brahman through its independence and other characteristics, one should not suspect any contradiction with reason regarding its being full of all qualities. || 1 ||
Thus ends the first quarter of the second chapter in the Sūtradīpikā composed by the venerable Jagannātha Yati. 2.1.
The Section on the Impossibility of Creation (Racanānupapattyadhikaraṇa) || 1 ||
Oṃ. And because the formation [of the world] is impossible, there is no inference [proving the existence of a creator]. Oṃ.

That which is inferred is called *anumāna*. The *pradhāna* (primordial matter) postulated by the Sāṃkhya through inference is not the creator of the world. Why? Because of the impossibility of its [creative] arrangement; that is to say, because, being insentient (*jaḍa*), the spontaneous activity of the *pradhāna* is impossible, and because there is no evidence for the spontaneous activity of an unconscious entity. || 1 ||
Oṃ, and because of activity, Oṃ.
Furthermore, because activity is observed only in that which possesses volition, such as "I am doing," the Pradhāna is not the creator of the world; this is the meaning. || 2 ||
Oṃ, milk was poured out there as well; Oṃ!

The word "api" (even/also) is intended to include the activity of sentient beings. If it is argued: "Just as the activity of insentient milk and water is observed, let the activity of the Pradhāna be likewise," we say no. Why? Because even in the case of milk, water, and so forth, their activity ultimately proceeds from the Lord alone; the meaning is that there is no activity originating from themselves. || 3 ||
Oṃ. And [the self is not the agent], because [agency] does not persist in the absence [of the body] and because [the self] is independent. Oṃ.

Because there is no establishment of existence apart [from Him], since the Śruti text "not without [Him]" (na ṛte) makes it known that no action whatsoever exists apart from the Lord; and because for that very reason the doctrine of the atheistic Sāṃkhya—that insentient matter alone acts spontaneously—is unauthoritative; therefore, since that [doctrine] is disregarded by the wise due to its independence [from scripture], the meaning is that there is no contradiction with Viṣṇu’s status as the agent. || 4 ||
|| Section on Non-existence Elsewhere || 2 ||
Oṃ. And because [the cause] does not exist elsewhere, it is not like grass and so forth; Oṃ.

Just as rain is merely a cooperative cause (*sahakāri-mātram*) for the effects such as grass and shrubs produced from the earth, so too is the Lord (*īśvara*) the sustainer (*anugrāhaka*) for the effects such as the Great Principle (*mahat*) produced from primordial nature (*prakṛti*); He is not independent. Thus, the position of the Theistic Sāṃkhya (*seśvara-sāṃkhya*) is also not tenable. Why? Because of its absence elsewhere: because the world does not exist apart from the Lord—without His impulsion—and because the Lord bestows existence and other qualities upon primordial nature. This is the meaning. || 1 ||
|| The Section on Acceptance (Abhyupagamādhikaraṇa) || 3 ||
Oṃ. Even if [the existence of the object] were admitted, it would be non-existent; therefore, Oṃ.

The word "no" (na) carries over from the previous [verse]. Even if the inferior [opponents] do not accept [the definition], since they do not accept their own treatise as a *siddhānta*, our desired conclusion is established. Even if they do accept it, there would be self-contradiction because, due to the absence of a [real] object (*artha*), they would be admitting the non-existence of the subject matter (*viṣaya*) and the purpose (*prayojana*), which are pervaded by the state of being a *siddhānta*. Thus, that position is also not tenable; this is the meaning. || 1 ||
Section 4: The Topic of the Man and the Stone.
If it be argued that [the soul] is like a person [driven by a stone], we say: "No, even in that case. (Oṃ)

If it is argued that, just as an insentient body moves toward carrying stones and so forth due to its connection with a person, so too does the insentient *prakṛti* act due to its connection with a sentient being—this is not so.
Why? Because even in that case of the body’s activity, agency belongs solely to the sentient Lord (*īśvara*). Thus, there is no lack of an illustrative example; this is the meaning. || 1 ||
Oṃ. [The Self is not the agent] because the status of being a possessor of limbs is untenable. Oṃ.

If it is admitted that the Puruṣa is the subordinate member (aṅga), then the statement "the member is the principal" (aṅgam aṅgī) would be untenable because it would imply that the status of being the principal (aṅgitva)—that is, predominance—belongs to the subordinate. The meaning is that there is no illustrative example for the position that the agency of Prakṛti is subservient to the Puruṣa. || 2 ||
|| Section 5: On Inference Otherwise || 5 ||
Oṃ, and because there would be a lack of cognitive capacity in the case of inference otherwise. Oṃ.

The word "ca" (and) serves to draw back the phrase "because of the impossibility of being the principal" (*aṅgitvānupapatteḥ*). Just as in the case of the previous position, even though there is a means for inferring the agency of the Person (*puruṣa*) as subordinate to Primordial Matter (*prakṛti*) by way other than that [of the Sāṃkhya], the meaning is that it is precisely because of the impossibility of being the principal due to the absence of the power of action—that is, because the conscious individual soul (*jīva*), being devoid of knowledge, lacks the power of activity necessary for its connection with a body. || 1 ||
Oṃ. And because of contradiction, [the doctrine] is inconsistent. Oṃ.
The meaning is that the doctrine of non-divinity (anīśvaravāda) is inconsistent and illogical because it involves contradictions and is opposed to all scripture, tradition, and reasoning. || 2 ||
The Section on the Vaiśeṣikas. 6.
Oṃ, [it is] like the great and the long, by means of the short and the circular; oṃ.

In the Vaiśeṣika view, just as from the largeness and length residing in dyads (tryaṇuka) and so forth, the dimension [of largeness and length] residing in quadrad (caturaṇuka) and so forth arises; likewise, the meaning is that from the shortness and sphericity—namely, the dimensions of shortness and sphericity residing in both the dyad and the atom—the production of the dimensions residing in the triad and the dyad would also occur. Otherwise, the production of the effect would not occur even from largeness and length. This is the sense of the word "vai" (indeed). Therefore, the intention is that the Vaiśeṣika doctrine is untenable. || 1 ||
Oṃ. In either case, there is no karma; therefore, that [bondage] is absent. Oṃ.

Because, in either case—whether the will of God (īśvarecchā) is eternal or non-eternal—it is not possible for action to arise in the atoms; therefore, due to that absence [of action], there would be an absence of the composite bodies beginning with the dyad (dvyaṇuka). This is the meaning. || 2 ||
Oṃ. And because of the admission of inherence and so forth, there would be an infinite regress due to their being equal [in requiring further relations]. Oṃ.

Because the Vaiśeṣikas accept *samavāya* (inherence) on the grounds that the parts (*avayava*) and the whole (*avayavin*), and so forth, are distinct; because they admit the relation of inherence; and because of the equality [of this situation], since there is an equality of distinctness even between the inherent (*samavāyin*) and the non-inherent (*asamavāyin*). Furthermore, if one accepts inherence in those cases as well, it leads to an infinite regress (*anavasthiti*); and because of this infinite regress, their doctrine is untenable—this is the meaning. || 3 ||
Oṃ, and because it exists eternally, Oṃ.

The word "ca" (and) serves to aggregate the defects. Since causes such as the will of God (*īśecchā*) and atoms (*paramāṇu*) exist eternally—that is, at all times according to the Vaiśeṣika doctrine—there would be the production of effects constantly and always; it would not be the case that they occur only occasionally. This is the meaning. || 4 ||
Oṃ. And because [the pradhāna] possesses form and other qualities, there would be a contradiction, as [such qualities] are observed [to belong to the Self]. Oṃ.

Furthermore, according to the Vaiśeṣika doctrine, because the atoms of earth, water, and fire possess color and other qualities, the opposite would follow—that is, they would possess impermanence, which is the reverse of permanence. Why? Because of observation; the meaning is that there is a pervasion (vyāpti) such that "whatever possesses color and other qualities is impermanent," as this is observed in the case of jars and the like. || 5 ||
Oṃ. And because there would be faults in either case, Oṃ.

In the Vaiśeṣika doctrine, in both ways—that is, in either of the two positions regarding the permanence or impermanence of atoms—there is a fault. The meaning is that, as in those cases, because of the presence of the fault consisting in the absence of the production of that [effect] due to the absence of a cause for the permanence of all things, that position is not tenable. || 6 ||
Oṃ. And because of non-possessiveness, there is absolute lack of longing. Oṃ.

Because the Vaiśeṣika doctrine lacks acceptance of the Vedas and other authoritative sources, and because it is contrary to them; the meaning is that one must show absolute disregard and lack of respect for it. || 7 ||
|| The Section on the Aggregate (Samudāyādhikaraṇa) || 7 ||
Oṃ. Even if both types of causes were present in a collection, that [result] would not be attained. Oṃ.

Because, even if one accepts that the "aggregate" (samudāya)—which consists of the number of plurality (anekatva-saṃkhyā) within an aggregate of atoms—is caused by many atoms joined together, or if one accepts it as being caused by many atoms situated at a distance; from what [source would it arise]? The ellipsis is: "because of defects such as mutual dependence (anyonyāśraya)," as has been established in the *Ṭīkā*. Therefore, the Buddhist position—that the pot is merely a collection of atoms (*paramāṇu-puñja*) and not a composite whole (*avayavin*)—is also untenable. || 1 ||
If it is argued that [the world] exists because of mutual causality, we say no, because [those factors] are merely the causes for the arising [of each other]. Om.

[Objection: "But surely, even if the quintuple aggregate of atoms exists eternally, there is no inconsistency regarding dissolution (*pralaya*) in our position. Why? Because the conventional usage of those [aggregates] and so forth arises from mutual cognition (*itaretara-pratyayatva*). That is to say, it is based on the relative cognition (*apekṣā-buddhi*) that 'this is this and that. Thus, at a time when such a cognition is absent, since the conventional usage of the aggregate and so forth does not exist, dissolution is logically established. [Reply: This is not so.

Why? Because atoms are causes merely for the production of their own aggregates; the meaning of the word "merely" (*mātra*) is that from them, even the production of relative cognition (*apekṣābuddhi*) and so forth is not possible. Thus, the meaning is that in the doctrine of momentariness, linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*) and the like, which are based upon those [aggregates], can never occur. || 2 ||
Oṃ, because of the cessation of the former upon the arising of the latter, Oṃ.

The particle *ca* (and) is used both for emphasis (*avadhāraṇa*) and for conjunction (*samuccaya*). The word "not" (*na*) is understood from the preceding context; the phrase "by virtue of capacity" (*sāmarthyāt*) is the ellipsis. Thus, not only is the conventional usage of a "collection" (*samudāya*) untenable in the theory of momentariness, but moreover, the production of specific effects is also illogical. Why? Because when a subsequent [moment] arises, the cause possesses the capacity to produce an effect similar to itself; therefore, having first produced something similar to itself, the cause would subsequently have to produce a dissimilar effect. To the question, "What is the fault in this? he says: "In the subsequent... and so forth.

And thus, when the subsequent [moment] arises—meaning, when there is the production of an effect similar to itself—it is only upon the cessation of the preceding one, that is, the destruction of the prior cause, that it is impossible for it to produce an effect dissimilar [to itself]. This is the meaning. || 3 ||
Oṃ. Otherwise, there would be a contradiction of one's own thesis or [the simultaneous existence of cause and effect]. Oṃ.

In the doctrine of momentariness (*kṣaṇikavāda*), the production of an effect at every moment is not tenable. Why? Because if one accepts that an effect arises even when its cause is absent, there would be a contradiction of one's own proposition (*pratijñoparodha*). Having previously asserted that "it is an effect" (implying it has a cause), to now accept the opposite would result in the loss of consistency with established doctrine (*siddhāntavyavahāra*). Alternatively, if one accepts that an effect arises only when its cause is present, it follows that simultaneity (*yaugapadya*)—the coexistence of effects with their causes at the same time—would result. This is the meaning. || 4 ||
Oṃ! There is no attainment of analytical cessation or non-analytical cessation because there is no interruption. Oṃ!

Thus, according to the doctrine of momentariness (*kṣaṇikavāda*), there is no attainment of analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) or non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*). This means that the attainment—i.e., the occurrence—of these two cessations, which consist respectively in the destruction of each moment and the destruction of the continuum, is impossible. Why? Because of non-interruption (*avicchedāt*). The meaning is that, according to that system, even when an effect arises, non-effects remain uninterrupted. || 5 ||
Oṃ. And because there are faults in both cases, Oṃ.

Whether one adopts the position that the effect necessarily arises whenever the cause is present, or the position that it does not, there exists a fault—namely, the fault known as the non-arising of the specific effect from the specific cause. Therefore, the meaning is that the position of momentariness is not tenable through presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) by relying on either of these two positions. (6)
Oṃ. And [the soul] is in space, because there is no distinction; Oṃ.

In the sense of "whatever [is cited]": when momentariness (*kṣaṇikatva*) is being established in the world by means of the reason "existence" (*sattva*) using the example of a lamp, there arises the contingency of also establishing non-momentariness (*akṣaṇikatva*) by means of the example of space (*ākāśa*). Now, one might object that the example lacks the property to be proven (*sādhyavaikalya*); to this it is replied: "because there is no distinction in the case of space. This means that, as a prover of momentariness, no specific dimension (*parimāṇaviśeṣa*) mentioned by the opponent is observed in space. Thus, this reason is one whose counter-argument is equally valid (*satpratipakṣa*); the point is that momentariness is not established by it. || 7 ||
Oṃ, and because of mindfulness, Oṃ.
The meaning is that because of the recognition "this is that very same thing," which contradicts [the premise], it is not logical to prove momentariness by means of the reason "existence. || 8 ||
Topic 8: The Non-Existent as the Substratum.
Oṃ. [The effect] does not arise from the non-existent, because such a thing has never been observed. Oṃ.

It is not logical for that which is non-existent—that is, empty—to be the creator of the world; why? Because there is a lack of valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), such is the remainder of the sentence. Why is that? Because it is never observed; for nowhere is a non-existent thing seen to function as a cause. Therefore, the meaning is that there is likewise an absence of inference and scripture [regarding such a creator]. || 1 ||
Oṃ, and thus there is accomplishment even for those who are indifferent; Oṃ.

The meaning is this: if it is thus accepted that an effect can arise from both the existent and the non-existent, then even from indifferent things—such as sky-flowers and the like, which are not objects of the cognition of what is to be rejected or accepted—the production of effects such as fragrance would follow. The word "ca" (and) implies the further point that, conversely, if this were not the case, the production of an effect from even the void (śūnya) would be impossible. || 2 ||
Oṃ. [The world] is not non-existent, because it is perceived. Oṃ.
The non-existence of the world is not "unreal" (asat). Why? Because it is perceived; the meaning is that it is cognized as being existent (sat). || 3 ||
Oṃ. And because of the difference in nature, [the world] is not like a dream and so forth. Oṃ.

The world, like a dream and so forth, is non-existent, just as the state of being awake superimposed upon the objects of sleep is non-existent. Why? Because of their difference in nature (*vaidharmya*); that is to say, because the state of being awake in a dream possesses a distinct characteristic called "sublatability" (*bādhyatva*), whereas that [characteristic] is absent in the [waking] world. || 4 ||
Section 9: On Non-apprehension (Anupalabdhi)
Oṃ, there is no existence, because it is not perceived. Oṃ.

The nature of the world is not even of the essence of cognition; why? Because it is unperceived, meaning that there is no experience of non-difference between cognition and the object of cognition. || 1 ||
Oṃ, and because of momentariness, Oṃ.
The meaning is that because cognition lasts for only a single moment while the world is enduring, there is no identity between the two due to this contradiction. || 2 ||
Oṃ. And because [the world] is impossible in every way, Oṃ.
The meaning is that because it is untenable in every respect, and because the Buddhist extreme is devoid of reason and contradicts [reason], it is not to be accepted. || 3 ||
|| There is no locus in a single [entity]. || 10 ||
Oṃ. [The doctrine of the Self as a single, partless whole] is not tenable, because of the impossibility [of its attributes coexisting] in one [substratum]. Oṃ.

The sevenfold nature asserted by the Jainas is not tenable with respect to a single entity. Why? Because it is impossible; that is to say, because they cannot possibly coexist in one place due to their lack of epistemic validity. These seven modes should be understood as follows: existence, non-existence, both existence and non-existence, distinctness from existence, distinctness from existence while being existent, distinctness from non-existence while being non-existent, and distinctness from both existence and non-existence while being both existent and non-existent. || 1 ||
Oṃ, and thus the non-totality of the self; Oṃ.

And thus, if the size of the self were admitted to be coextensive with the body, it would follow that the self is non-omnipresent (ākātsnyam). Specifically, for the living being (jīva) who was previously limited to the body of an ant and has now attained the body of an elephant or a donkey, there would be incompleteness—that is, a lack of fullness—due to its no longer measuring the size of that [new] body. Likewise, it should be understood that for the self which has attained the body of an elephant, there would be non-omnipresence and even excess when it attains the body of an ant. || 2 ||
Oṃ. Nor can there be non-contradiction even through figurative interpretation, because of transformation and other reasons. Oṃ.

Nor is it tenable to say that there is no contradiction—that is, no aforementioned defect—even by accepting that [the self] possesses the dimensions of its respective bodies through successive stages (*paryāya*) or in sequence. Why? Because such succession (*paryāya*) is not tenable. And why is that? Because of the consequences of modification and so forth; for in that case, since the entity would differ according to the difference in its dimensions at those respective times, the self would incur the state of being subject to change. Consequently, the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of defects such as impermanence and the impossibility of liberation would follow. This is the meaning. || 3 ||
Oṃ. And because of the persistence of the final state, and because both [the soul and the body] would be eternal, there would be no distinction; Oṃ.

The particle *ca* (and) from the preceding sūtra is understood here as well. The phrase *antyāvasthiteḥ* (because of the final state) recurs. The word *ca* is used either for emphasis (*avadhāraṇe*) or for conjunction (*samuccaye*). Thus, this being the case, if it is admitted that the self has the same dimensions as the body, the consequence (*prasaṅga*) is that there would have to be a "final state" (*antyāvasthiteḥ*); this is the remainder of the sense. The meaning is that even in liberation (*mokṣe*), one would have to admit the continued existence of a body for the self that exists [there]. Why? Because of the "final state"—that is, because the final dimension, which is that of the liberated state, must necessarily be admitted.

The sense is that without a body as a delimiting factor (avacchedaka), the existence of the delimited dimension (avacchedyaparimāṇa) is impossible. He says "finally" (antya) to explain why there must be a dimension: the sense is that since liberation (mukti) consists in the persistence of the very nature of the soul (mauktikātmasvarūpa), its existence as such-nature would be impossible without a dimension. To the objection, "Let there be a body even in liberation; what of it?", he replies, "Because both are eternal."

The meaning is that if this were so, it would follow as a consequence that both the body and the self existing at the time of liberation are eternal. To the question, "Let the eternity of the liberated body be granted; what follows from that? he says: "And therefore, there would be the eternity of everything"—this sentence of the objection must be supplied. For this very reason, the word "and" (*ca*) has the sense of conjunction. The meaning is that there would be the eternity of all present bodies. Why? To this he says: "Because there is no distinction" (*aviśeṣāt*).

The meaning is that there is no distinction between the bodies of those who have been liberated and those of the present insofar as their status as "bodies" is concerned. Therefore, the implication is that it is not logical for the self to possess the dimensions of the body. || 4 ||
The Topic of the Lord.
11. Oṃ. On account of the inconsistency of the Lord [being the cause], Oṃ.

It is not logical that Paśupati, the husband [of Umā], is the cause of the world. Why? Because of inconsistency; that is to say, because he would be subject to defects such as dependent origination and so forth. || 1 ||
Oṃ. And because a relationship is untenable, Oṃ.
The meaning is that because Śiva is bodiless, a connection with the world is logically untenable; therefore, he cannot be the agent [of creation]. || 2 ||
Oṃ. And because the superintendence [of a creator] is untenable, Oṃ.

The meaning is that because everything perishes at the time of dissolution (pralaya), and because it would be impossible for Paśupati to have a substratum such as the earth at the time of renewed creation, he cannot be the creator of the world. || 3 ||
If it be argued that [the Self] possesses a cause like [the body], we say no, because of [the absence of] experience and so forth. Om.

If it is argued that there is no such fault because the collection of instruments (sādhanajāta) belonging to Paśupati is like an instrument, like a body, equal to a body, and equal to its locus, we say: no. Why?
Because of [the consequences] such as experience (bhoga), meaning due to the faults consisting in the arising of the experience of pleasure and pain produced by the body, death, and so forth. || 4 ||
Oṃ, [the Lord] is either finite or lacks omniscience; Oṃ.

The meaning is that since, on the two alternatives of Śiva having a body or not having one, there would respectively follow finitude, perishability, and non-omniscience (rather than omniscience), therefore that [position] is not tenable. || 5 ||
Section on Origination (Utpattyadhikaraṇa) 12.
Oṃ, because origination is impossible, Oṃ.

Power (*śakti*) is not the cause of the world. Why? Because of the impossibility of origination; that is to say, because it is impossible for offspring to be produced from mere females designated by the term "power. || 1 ||
Oṃ, and there is no instrument for the agent. Oṃ.

Since the instrument—the means for knowledge and so forth—does not belong to either the agent or to Śiva, who is the bestower of power, it follows that he does not possess the status of being a bestower of power through that instrument; such is the meaning. || 2 ||
Oṃ. Or, if consciousness and so forth exist, there is no negation of that [self]. Oṃ.

Or, if it is admitted that Śiva possesses consciousness and so forth—that is, the existence of knowledge, will, and the rest—then there would be "no refutation of that," meaning no refutation or rejection of that Śaiva position; rather, it would amount to tacit approval, and yet that [position] has already been refuted. This is the meaning. || 3 ||
Oṃ, and because of contradiction, Oṃ.
Furthermore, because it contradicts all the Śrutis and Smṛtis, the Śākta doctrine is improper and untenable; this is the meaning. || 4 ||
Thus ends the second quarter of the second chapter in the Sūtradīpikā composed by the venerable Jagannātha Yati. || 2 || 2 ||
Section on Space (Viya-dhikaraṇa) || 1 ||
Oṃ, space is not [the cause], because it does not pervade; Oṃ.

Space (viyat) is not unproduced; rather, it is indeed produced from the Lord. Why? Because of the absence of scriptural statement (aśruteḥ); that is to say, because there is no scriptural passage regarding the non-production of space. || 1 ||
Oṃ, it exists indeed; Oṃ.
The meaning is that regarding the origin of space, there indeed exists the scriptural text: "From the Self, space was produced. || 2 ||
Oṃ. Because a figurative sense is impossible. Oṃ.

The scriptural statement, "This space is indeed beginningless," is figurative; it refers to a secondary kind of beginninglessness. Why? Because of impossibility; that is to say, if it were taken in its primary sense, it would be inconsistent with the numerous scriptural texts concerning the origination [of space]. || 3 ||
Oṃ, and because of the word [in the scripture], Oṃ.

The meaning is that, by the force of the scriptural statement "Now, indeed, they are eternal," the scriptural texts concerning their beginninglessness must be understood in a figurative sense. || 4 ||
Oṃ. And there may be [the same word] for one [thing], like the word "Brahman. Oṃ.

Regarding the focus [on the meaning]: just as in the case of the word *brahman*, where that single word *brahman* has its primary sense (*mukhyatva*) in Viṣṇu and a secondary sense (*amukhyatā*) in the individual soul (*jīva*), so too the word denoting eternality would have its primary meaning (*mukhyārthatā*) in Brahman; this is the intended sense. || 5 ||
Oṃ. There is abandonment of the thesis because there is no distinction from words. Oṃ.

If one were to state that space (*ākāśa*) is primarily unproduced, there would be a contradiction of the initial proposition (*pratijñāhāni*), namely, the proposition that Viṣṇu is the creator expressed in the text, "He created all this. Why? Because of non-distinction (*avyatirekāt*); that is, because space is not distinct from the referents of the word "all. Furthermore, since from these words and from clear scriptural texts such as "The Self, verily, was this," it is determined that Brahman alone is primarily unproduced and not anything else; therefore, what has been stated is logical—this is the meaning. || 6 ||
Oṃ, as long as there is a distinction [between things], it is like the world; Oṃ.

The word *yāvat* is used in the sense of restriction (*avadhāraṇe*). *Yāvadvikāram* is an indeclinable compound. The particle *tu* has the sense of *ca* (and). Thus, the rule is established: "Insofar as there is modification—that is, a thing that is indeed subject to change—it possesses division," meaning it possesses limited power denoted by the term "division," and nothing else. Therefore, "as in the world" (*lokavat*) means just as in the world; just as in the world, for instance, a jar or similar object is admitted to be a modification because it is divided, so too for space and the rest, their state of being modifications is established by the reason of their being divided. From that very fact, it follows that they are also "beginningless" (*sāditva*) [in the sense of having a beginning in time]. This is the meaning. || 7 ||
The Section Concerning Mātariśvan. 2.
The Section Concerning Space (Viya-dadhikaraṇa) || 1 ||
Oṃ. Space does not exist [as a substance], because it is not heard [in scripture]. Oṃ.

Space (viyat) is not unproduced; rather, it is indeed produced from the Lord. Why? Because of non-hearing—that is to say, because there is no scriptural statement regarding the non-production of space. || 1 ||
Oṃ, it exists indeed; Oṃ.
Regarding the origin of space, the meaning is that the scriptural authority is precisely the Śruti text: "From the Self, space was produced. || 2 ||
Because a secondary sense is impossible. Om.

The scriptural statement, "Or this ether is without beginning," is figurative, meaning it refers to a non-primary kind of beginninglessness. Why? Because of impossibility; that is to say, if it were taken in its primary sense, it would be inconsistent with the numerous scriptural texts concerning the origination [of ether]. || 3 ||
Oṃ, and because of the word [in scripture], Oṃ.

The meaning is that, by the force of the scriptural statement, "Now, indeed, they are eternal," the scriptural mention of [the elements] being non-originated is to be understood in a figurative sense. || 4 ||
Oṃ, it belongs to each one individually, like the word "Brahman"; oṃ.

The word "ca" (and) is used for emphasis. Just as in the case of the word "Brahman," where the single word "Brahman" has its primary meaning (*mukhyatva*) in Viṣṇu and its secondary meaning (*amukhyatā*) in the individual soul (*jīva*), so too the single word denoting eternity would have its primary sense (*mukhyārthatā*) in Brahman; that is the meaning. || 5 ||
Oṃ. There is a loss of the thesis because there is no distinction from words. Oṃ.

If one were to assert that space (*ākāśa*) has no primary origination, there would be a contradiction of the initial proposition (*pratijñāhāni*); namely, the contradiction of the proposition that Viṣṇu is the creator, as stated in the text: "He created all this. Why? Because of non-distinction (*avyatirekāt*), since space is not distinct from the referents of the word "all. Furthermore, because of these words and from clear scriptural passages such as "The Self, indeed, this [was in the beginning]," it is determined that primary non-origination belongs to Brahman alone and not to anything else; therefore, what was said is logical—this is the meaning. || 6 ||
Oṃ, as long as there is differentiation, it is like the world; Oṃ.

The word *yāvat* has a restrictive sense (*avadhāraṇa*). *Yāvadvikāram* is an indeclinable compound. The particle *tu* has the sense of *ca* (and). Thus, the rule is established: "Insofar as there is modification—that is, a thing that is indeed undergoing change—it possesses division," meaning it possesses limited power denoted by the term "division," and not anything else. Therefore, "as in the world" (*lokavat*) means like in the world. Just as in the world, for instance, a jar or similar object is accepted as being a modification because it is divided, so too the fact of being a modification is established for ether and the rest by the reason of their being divided. From that very fact, it follows that they are also beginningless (*sādi*); this is the meaning. || 7 ||
|| Section on Mātariśvan || 2 ||
Oṃ, by this, Mātariśvan is explained. Oṃ.
By this aforementioned reason—namely, being differentiated and so forth—the Mātariśvan, the primary wind, is explained; that is to say, he is stated to possess an origin. || 1 ||
|| Section on Impossibility || 3 | Oṃ But [the existence] of that which is real is impossible, because it is logically untenable. Oṃ.

The word *tu* (but) is used for emphasis. Regarding the existent Viṣṇu, there is simply no possibility of origination—that is, no birth at all. It does not mean that origination from the non-existent (*asat*) is to be asserted on the basis of the Śruti text, "From the non-existent, the existent was born. Why? Because it is logically untenable. Therefore, the meaning is that since origination from the non-existent is impossible for Viṣṇu, [He is eternal]. || 1 ||
The Section on Light (Tejo’dhikaraṇa) 4.
Oṃ, [the Self] is of the nature of light; for thus it has been said: Oṃ.

Fire is of the nature of fire; therefore, it is produced from Brahman alone and not from air. Why? Because the Śruti, "That [Brahman] created fire," speaks in that manner—that is, it declares it according to the method described above. This is the meaning. || 1 ||
The Topic on Non-Obstruction || 5 ||
Oṃ, the waters, Oṃ.

Here too, the phrase "for thus it says" (tathā hy āha) continues from the previous context. And so, water has its origin from Viṣṇu alone, and not from anything else. Why? Because the meaning is: for the Śruti says, "This is indeed Brahman," and therefore [it is so]. || 1 ||

Section on Earth: 6.1.10–23. The Sūtras: 10. On account of the word "earth" (pṛthivī) and so forth, [the opponent argues that] it is the gross earth. 11. And because of the mention of what is not mentioned [in the Upaniṣadic texts]. 12. But [it is] Brahman, on account of the supporting [of the worlds]. 13. And because of the subsequent [passage]. 14. And because of the designation of its own nature. 15. And because of the impossibility of that [supporting] in the case of the other. 16. And because of the connection with the subject matter. 17. And because of the teaching of its qualities. 18. And because of the teaching of the entering. 19. And because of the designation of the two. 20. And because of the teaching of the greatness. 21. And because of the teaching of the entering [into the heart]. 22. And because of the teaching of the measure. 23. And because of the teaching of the going and returning. The Commentary: Now, a doubt arises regarding the passage, "That which is the subtle essence, this whole world has that as its self; That is the Truth; That is the Self; Thou art That, O Śvetaketu" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.8.7). Here, the term "subtle essence" (sūkṣmam) refers to the earth, water, fire, air, ether, food, and so forth, which are the effects of the five elements. The question is whether this "subtle essence" is the gross earth or the Supreme Brahman. The opponent maintains: It is the gross earth. Why? Because of the word "earth" (pṛthivī) and so forth. In the preceding section, the earth is introduced as the object of meditation: "In this city of Brahman, there is a small lotus-palace, and within it, a small inner space" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.1.1). Then, after describing the earth, water, fire, air, ether, and food, the text concludes: "That which is the subtle essence, this whole world has that as its self. Since the context concerns the earth and its derivatives, the "subtle essence" must be the earth itself. Furthermore, the mention of things not previously mentioned—such as the "small inner space"—supports this view. The Siddhāntin replies: But it is Brahman, on account of the supporting of the worlds. The phrase "this whole world has that as its self" indicates that the "subtle essence" is the support of all things. Such supporting is possible only for the Supreme Brahman, who is the cause of all. Moreover, the subsequent passage—"That is the Truth; That is the Self; Thou art That"—identifies the "subtle essence" with the Self and teaches the identity of the individual soul with it. This is impossible in the case of the non-intelligent earth. Additionally, the text designates its own nature by saying, "It is neither coarse nor fine," thereby distinguishing it from the material elements. Furthermore, the entering of the Self into the heart and the teaching of its measure (the size of a thumb) confirm that the "subtle essence" is the Supreme Brahman. Therefore, the "subtle essence" is indeed the Supreme Brahman.
Oṃ. [The Self is] not the earth, because of its specific authority, its form, the word "other," and so forth. Oṃ.

"The earth [became] earth itself; they created food"—such is the Śruti. Thus, by the word "food" (anna), that which is not commonly known as food is meant. Why? Because of the context, the form, another word, and so forth. This means: because of the context denoting the elements (bhūta-prakaraṇa) expressed by the word "context," because of the hearing of the black form mentioned by the word "form," and because of the specific word—namely, the specific scriptural statement, "The earth indeed is food. The meaning of the word "and so forth" (ādi) refers to arguments such as: there is no lack of authority for a sentence that is free from defects due to its being of non-human origin (apauruṣeya). || 1 ||
The Section Concerning Contemplation Thereof (Tadabhidhyānādhikaraṇa) || 7 ||
Om, but he [the individual soul] [arises] from that very meditation on Him, because of the indicative mark; Om.

The word *tu* (but) is used for emphasis. By the word *abhidhyāna*, desire (*icchā*) is expressed. By the pronoun *tat* (that), Viṣṇu is understood. Thus, He—Viṣṇu alone—is the agent of dissolution, not Rudra. Why? Because of the scriptural statement, "From meditating upon Him" (*tad-abhidhyānāt*). The meaning is: precisely because of that very mark (*liṅga*) consisting of the desire to dissolve beginningless bondage—which is characterized by a specific desire to withdraw [the world] and is indicated by the word in the form of meditation upon that Viṣṇu, which serves as the proof of His being the dissolver of the world beginning with Sādi. The particle *eva* (alone), however, according to the method of the Bhāṣya, indicates the argumentum ad absurdum (*kaimutya*): "How much more so from the Śrutis? || 1 ||
|| Section on the Reversal of the Argument || 8 ||
But the sequence is established by way of reversal; therefore, it is logical. Oṃ.

The word *tu* (but) is used for emphasis. The phrase "from this" (*ataḥ*) is repeated. "From this" means from the order of origination (*utpatti-krama*). "In reverse" (*viparyayeṇa*) means by way of inversion. "Order" (*kramaḥ*) refers to the order of dissolution (*laya-krama*), and not the order of origination. Why? Precisely because of that very scripture stating "due to this reversal" (*vyutkramāt*). Furthermore, this reversal is logical and appropriate. Why? Because it is reasonable that those things which have originated earlier possess greater capacity than those which originate later, and thus their remaining for a longer duration of time is justified. This is the meaning. || 1 ||
|| Section on the Intermediate State || 9 ||

Oṃ. If it be argued that consciousness and the mind [dissolve] in succession within the intermediate state because of their respective characteristics, we say no, because there is no distinction [between them]. Oṃ.

Consciousness (*vijñāna*) and the mind (*manas*) are the principles of consciousness (*vijñāna-tattva*) and the principle of mind (*manas-tattva*). Without [the former], that is, independently; elsewhere, there is dissolution either in sequence or out of sequence, but not even for those two. Why? Because of the indicative mark (*liṅga*): in the passage "and from the mind, consciousness," although the mind has already arisen prior to consciousness, the statement of its dissolution earlier—in "one should restrain speech in the mind"—is seen as providing proof. If this is argued, we say no. Why? Because there is no distinction. The meaning is that there is no specific authoritative evidence (*pramāṇa*) regarding the order of dissolution being the same as the order of origination for the principles of consciousness and mind. || 1 ||
Om. But [the designation of the Self as] "moving and non-moving" must be figurative, based on its connection with them, because [the Self] exists when they exist. Om.

"Based on the moving and the non-moving" means common to the objects of knowledge consisting of the senses, their functions, and the [objects] denoted by the terms "moving" and "non-moving. As for the designation of that [knowledge], there is the scriptural usage, "And from the mind, consciousness. However, this is figurative (*bhākta*); it refers only to the objects of knowledge consisting of the functions of sleep, which are a single part of the referents of the terms "mind" and "consciousness," and not to the [ultimate] reality itself. For what reason? Because it exists only when that [sleep] exists (*tadbhāvabhāvitvāt*).

Its recurrence occurs because, with respect to that object denoted by the terms "moving and non-moving"—namely, the sentient and insentient—it arises from being permeated by that state, that is, by the state of the mind, through mental perception. Therefore, the observation of the aforementioned mark (liṅga) does not constitute a sublation; this is the meaning. || 2 ||
|| Section on the Self (Ātmādhikaraṇa) || 10 ||
Oṃ. The Self does not [arise from the elements], because it is not heard [to do so] in scripture, and because of its eternity according to those [scriptures]. Oṃ.

The Self, which is the Supreme Self, does not dissolve; for there is no scriptural authority for its dissolution, as such a dissolution is nowhere heard of in the scriptures. Furthermore, because of those [scriptures] such as "He is eternal and devoid of qualities," and because Viṣṇu's eternity is understood from them, the meaning is that there is no destruction of Him. || 1 ||
|| Section on Knowledge || 11 ||
Oṃ, for this very reason [the Self] is omniscient; Oṃ.

One who knows is a "knower" (jña), which refers to the individual soul (jīva) as well. Therefore, the soul is indeed produced from Viṣṇu. Why? Because of the very scripture of Kāṣāyaṇa, which states: "For this very reason, they are produced as non-perishing entities. This is the meaning. || 1 ||
Oṃ, and because of the connection, Oṃ.

The meaning is that even though the individual soul (*jīva*) is eternal from beginningless time, it is logical that its "origination" consists in its dependence upon the Lord and its possession of a body; therefore, the soul is indeed subject to origination. 2. || Section on Departure (Utkrānti-adhikaraṇa) || 12 ||
Oṃ, [homage] to those who possess the power of departing, going, and returning. Oṃ.

Therefore, because of the reasons consisting of the departure of the body from this world as stated in such passages as "he [goes] from here," and the going to another world and the returning to this world, the soul (jīva) is indeed atomic (aṇu) and not all-pervading (vibhu); this is the meaning. || 1 ||
Oṃ, and by means of one's own self for the two following [sections], Oṃ.

The word *ca* has the sense of *eva* (only). The individual soul (*jīva*) possesses departure and so forth only by its own self—that is, by the independent Supreme Self alone and through His impulsion, not by itself. Why? Because of the subsequent [passages]: from the force of the later statement, "By this very self... for He [leads] this individual soul," as found in the *Pauṣyāyaṇa* [Brāhmaṇa]. This is the meaning. || 2 ||
"Oṃ. If it be argued that [the soul] is not atomic because of its being associated with desires, we say no, because of the reference to the other [state]. Oṃ.

[Objection: But surely the individual soul (*jīva*) is not atomic. Why? Because of the absence of scriptural authority for that; for we hear from scripture a pervasiveness that contradicts atomicity, namely, "The selves are indeed all-pervading. [Reply: This is not so. Why? Because of the context of the other, that is, because this occurs within the section concerning the Supreme Self (*paramātman*). Thus, since the scriptural statement regarding pervasiveness has the Supreme Self as its subject matter, it does not sublate the doctrine of atomicity; such is the meaning. || 3 ||
Oṃ. And because of its own word and its measurement, Oṃ.

The word *ca* (and) denotes conjunction. The meaning is that the scriptural statement regarding pervasiveness (*vyāptatva-śruti*) refers not only to Viṣṇu by the force of the context, but rather—because of the word *ātman*, which is grasped by its own term within the sentence of the Kāṣāyaṇa [Upaniṣad], "For this is the Self risen above the power of measurement," and because of the indicative mark (*liṅga*) of being immeasurable (*aparimitatva*) from the word *unmāna*—the scriptural statement regarding pervasiveness refers exclusively to Viṣṇu and not to the individual soul (*jīva*). || 5 ||
If it be argued that there is a distinction because of its specific location, we say no; for this is admitted [by us], since [the soul] resides in the heart. Oṃ.

[Objection: Is it not reasonable that a drop of sandalwood paste should pervade the body? Why? Because of the particularity of its location (*avasthitivaiśeṣyāt*), meaning that it is properly situated in a specific region of the body; whereas for the individual soul (*jīva*), it is not so, because that [particularity] is absent. [Reply: No. Why? Because of the scriptural statement, "For he is in the heart" (*hṛdi hy eṣaḥ*), which implies that the soul is also properly situated in the heart, while its improper situation in other parts of the body is admitted. || 6 ||
|| Section on Negative Concomitance (Vyatirekādhikaraṇa) || 13 ||
Oṃ, there is distinctness, just as in the case of possessing fragrance; and thus it demonstrates. Oṃ.

The word *ca* ("and") is intended to include the Smṛti statement, "in the inconceivable. "Like fragrance" means as in the case of fragrance. Just as there is a separation or distinction of the flower's fragrance from its own parts, so too is a separation of the atomic individual soul (*jīva*) from its own parts by the power of the Lord (*īśa-śakti*) logical. Why is this established? Because the Śruti (Śāṇḍilya) shows it to be so; thus the meaning is "for this very reason. || 1 ||
|| A Separate Topic || 14 ||
Oṃ. [The self is distinct from the body] because it is taught separately. Oṃ.

The individual soul (jīva) is separate and distinct from the Supreme Self (paramātman). Why? Because of the teaching; the meaning is that it is so because of the scriptural revelation (śruti) in the Kauśika Upaniṣad: "He is distinct and inconceivable. || 1 ||
Oṃ, but because its essence consists of those qualities, it is designated by that [name], as in the case of the Intelligent One (the individual soul). Oṃ.

"As in the case of the Wise One," that is, as in the case of Brahman; just as in the Wise Brahman there is the statement of non-difference with the world in the text, "All this, indeed, is Brahman," so too is that designation [of non-difference] applied to the individual soul (jīva). Thus, the declaration of identity with Brahman in the text "That thou art" is logical. Why? "Because its essence consists of those qualities"; the meaning is that it is due to the fact that the nature of the individual soul consists of qualities such as knowledge and bliss that are similar to the qualities of Brahman. || 2 ||
As far as the subject matter extends. 15.
Oṃ. And because it exists as long as the personal existence [lasts], there is no fault, since that is what is seen. Oṃ.

And because the individual soul (*jīva*) exists as long as the Supreme Self exists—that is to say, because it is eternal—there is no fault. There is no fault regarding the lack of authority of the scripture which teaches the connection with merit and demerit, namely, "He [is] without beginning. Why is this so? Because that eternity is seen; for it is stated in the *Āgniveśya* Śruti that "the *jīva* is eternal," and because of the two *Smṛti* texts from the *Bhārata* stating that the self, the *jīva*, is eternal. || 1 ||
The Section on Masculinity (Puṃstvādhikaraṇa)
Om. But because of the possibility of manifestation for that which already exists, just like virility and so forth; Om.

The word *tu* has the sense of *eva* (only/indeed). Just as in the case of masculinity (*puṃstva*) and so forth—where, although the capacity for the production of offspring exists equally in males, females, and others, its manifestation occurs only at a specific time—so too, because this [jīva] already exists even prior to liberation by virtue of being the very nature of the Self (*jīvasvarūpa*), there is the possibility of the manifestation of its knowledge, bliss, and other attributes; and since it is joined with that manifestation as the instrumental cause in liberation, the scriptural statement of the Paiṅgins, "He becomes blissful," is justified. Thus, there is no contradiction with the capacity [of the jīva] regarding its nature as bliss and so forth; the meaning is that the jīva is indeed of the nature of bliss and the rest. || 1 ||
Oṃ. Otherwise, there would follow the consequence of either its constant perception or its constant non-perception, or else the necessity of one or the other being restricted. Oṃ.

The word *vā* signifies an alternative restriction (*vyavasthitavikalpa*). "Apprehension" (*upalabdhi*) means experience. Otherwise, if one were to accept that the individual soul (*jīva*) has bliss and so forth as its essential nature while refusing to accept the existence of a veil (*āvaraṇa*), it would follow that there must be either constant apprehension or constant non-apprehension. The connection [of the alternatives] is as follows: for those fit for liberation, there would be a constant experience of bliss; for those fit for darkness (*tamas*), there would never be an experience of bliss, but rather only the experience of suffering inherent in their own nature.

Thus, for middle-class humans, there is a restriction to one or the other of the two experiences of pleasure and pain; that is, the restriction would indeed be one of equality [between the two]. This means it is due to the obstruction caused by a veil. Therefore, the sense is that a veil for the individual soul (jīva) must be admitted. || 2 ||
|| Section on Agency || 17 ||
Oṃ. [The Lord] is the agent, because the scripture would otherwise be purposeless. Oṃ.

The individual soul (jīva) is also the agent. Why? Because only when that is the case is the purpose of the scripture fulfilled; that is to say, the scripture consisting of injunctions and prohibitions possesses its intended utility, whereas otherwise it would result in futility. || 3 ||
Oṃ, because of the instruction on the [four] abodes, Oṃ.

Even in the state of liberation, because the agency of dwelling is stated in the passage, "Eating, playing," the individual soul (jīva) is indeed an agent in the ultimate sense; the meaning is that it is not a merely imaginary agent. || 2 ||
Oṃ, from grasping, oṃ.

Because we observe the performance of means such as spiritual practices for the sake of the individual soul's liberation, and because we observe the attainment of that result [liberation] from them, it follows that the individual soul is not a merely imaginary agent even within saṃsāra; this is the meaning. || 3 ||
Oṃ. And because of the designation [of the agent] in the action; for if it were not so, there would be a reversal of the instruction. Oṃ.

In the context of action—in the act of meditation mentioned in the passage, "One should meditate upon the Self alone as the world"—because of this designation and because the individual soul (jīva) is stated to be the agent; for if the jīva were not the agent, and if there were no agency [on its part], there would be a reversal of the instruction. That is to say, there would be a contradiction in the statement regarding the jīva as the agent and the Lord (Īśvara) as the object, resulting in a reversal of the form of the teaching such that it would have to be "the Self alone should be meditated upon" [in a different sense]. || 4 ||
Oṃ, there is no restriction regarding the nature of perception; oṃ.

"Like perception" means as in the case of perception; that is, in the case of the living being's perception, which is knowledge. "Non-restriction" means the failure to obtain knowledge according to one's own will. The meaning is that, likewise, non-restriction is appropriate even with regard to action. || 5 ||
Oṃ, because of the reversal of power, oṃ.

The meaning is that, due to the reversal of power between the Lord (Īśa) and the individual soul (jīva), even agency (*kartṛtva*)—considering the distinction between their powers as being complete or incomplete—is divided into the categories of independent and dependent. Alternatively, the meaning is that because the individual soul lacks complete power like that of the Lord, it does not possess independent agency. || 6 ||
Oṃ, and because of the absence of meditative concentration, Oṃ.
Because that [independent] intelligence does not exist, there is no independent agency for the *jīva*; rather, the meaning is that its agency is solely dependent on another. || 7 ||
Oṃ, and just as a carpenter [acts] in both ways, Oṃ.

The word "ca" (and) serves to include the Dārṣṭāntika view. Just as a carpenter is designated both as one who causes a palace or similar structure to be built by directing others and as its actual maker, so too it can be said that the impulse directed by the Lord is the agent; this is the meaning. || 8 ||
Oṃ, may that [power] protect us from the enemy; Oṃ!

The soul's power of agency exists as dependent upon the Supreme Self, following after Him; it is subordinate to Him alone. Why? Because of the scriptural statement to that effect. The meaning is that in the Pauṅgi-śruti, both agency and instrumentality are heard to be dependent on the Lord, stating that the soul's agency is subject to the Lord. || 9 ||
Oṃ. But [the Lord] takes account of the effort made [by the individual soul], because otherwise the injunctions and prohibitions would be rendered meaningless, and for other such reasons. Oṃ.

The word *tu* (but) is used for emphasis. Since the Supreme Self [is the cause], because otherwise the injunctions and prohibitions would be rendered meaningless, and so forth; the dative case (*tādarthye*) is used here. That is to say, for the sake of making the scriptures of injunction and prohibition non-contradictory, and in order to avoid [the Lord’s] own partiality and cruelty, He impels the individual soul only while taking into account the effort made by the soul—that is, depending upon the fitness of the soul's karma and effort—and not without such dependence. Therefore, the meaning is that although the power of the soul is dependent on the Lord, it nonetheless possesses the capacity for the required activity. || 11 ||
|| Section on the Parts (Aṃśādhikaraṇa) || 18 ||

Om. [The soul] is a part [of Brahman], because of the designation of diversity, and also because otherwise [it would not be possible]; for some [scriptural passages] record that it has the nature of a servant, a fisherman, and so forth. Om.

The individual soul (*jīva*) is indeed a portion (*aṃśa*) of the Supreme Self (*paramātman*). By way of relationships such as father and son, and solely by virtue of being a portion whose nature is dependent upon Him, [the soul] is never anything other than dependent on the Lord. Why? Because of the various designations; for in passages such as "May He protect me," the soul's relationship with the Lord is described in various ways, such as fatherhood, brotherhood, and so forth. Furthermore, because some followers of a particular Vedic school [state], "The other is the Supreme, the other is the individual soul" (*Kāṣāyaṇa Śruti*), thus distinguishing this soul from the Supreme.

Otherwise, they study and recite [the texts] as being distinct. For other followers of the Vedic branches (śākhins) study that Brahman possesses the state of fishermen, hunters, and so forth—meaning the state of individual souls (jīvas) associated with specific castes denoted by the words "fishermen" and "hunters"—which amounts to saying there is non-difference [between them]. Furthermore, they study that fishermen, hunters, and others are not Brahman. Therefore, the meaning is that [Brahman] possesses the nature of being a part (aṃśatva). || 1 ||
Oṃ! From the syllables of the mantra, Oṃ!
And from the scriptural statement, "He has a foot," the meaning is that the individual soul (jīva) is a portion of the Supreme Self (paramātman). || 2 ||
Oṃ, it is also recorded in tradition; Oṃ.
The meaning is that the soul's status as a part (aṃśa) of Kṛṣṇa and others is stated by [Lord Kṛṣṇa] himself in the Smṛti: "He is indeed a part of Me. || 3 ||
