Oṃ. The Supreme is not [subject to change] in this way, just like light and so forth; Oṃ.

The individual soul (*jīva*) is a distinct part (*bhinna-aṃśa*) of the Supreme Self, like light and so forth, or like a portion of fire that possesses the conceit of being its own illuminator. But the Supreme Viṣṇu, appearing in forms such as the Fish and others, is not like this; He is not a distinct part like the individual soul. Rather, the meaning is that He is a non-distinct part (*abhinnāṃśa*) of the Lord, like light and so forth, or like a portion of fire that possesses the conceit of being the cosmic fire at the end of time (*kālāgni*). || 4 ||
Oṃ, and they remember; Oṃ.

The wise declare that the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (īśvara) are both distinct and non-distinct parts [of Him], according to such Smṛti passages as, "These are portions of My own self. This is the meaning. || 5 ||
Oṃ. Permission and prohibition exist due to the connection with the body, as in the case of light and so forth. Oṃ.

Just as in the case of light and so forth, because of the connection with various bodies—such as the devatās residing in the eyeball and other organs who are subject to decline—the activity and so forth of those [organs] occurs by the permission of Sūrya, Varuṇa, and others; likewise, for the *jīva* as well, due to the cause of its connection with various bodies, there is "permission and avoidance" (*anujñā-parihārau*), which refer to the connection with and the avoidance of activity dependent upon the permission of the Supreme Self (*paramātman*). This is not the case for the Fish-incarnation and others.

However, just as those presiding over the sun’s radiance and so forth possess activity and other functions dependent upon that [sun], so too does the individual soul (jīva) have its activity dependent solely upon the Lord; for this reason also, the soul is a distinct part (bhinnāṃśa) of the Supreme Self. The distinction is thus established that while the fish-forms and others are non-distinct parts (abhinnāṃśa), the soul is a distinct part. This is the meaning. || 6 ||
Oṃ, and because there is no continuity [of the self], there is no confusion [of actions and their results]. Oṃ.

Because the individual soul (jīva) lacks the capacity for perfect continuity, whereas fish and other such beings possess it; "non-confusion" (avyatikara) means the absence of any reversal of the stated principle that the soul and the Lord possess parts that are both distinct and non-distinct. || 7 ||
Oṃ, and it is indeed a mere appearance; oṃ.

The word "ca" (and) signifies conjunction. Since the individual soul (*jīva*) is merely a manifestation, that is, a reflection, of the Supreme, whereas the fish and other such beings are not so, for this reason as well there is no reversal of what was stated. This is the meaning. || 8 ||
Section 19: The Topic of the Invisible [Ant-hill] (Adṛśyādhikaraṇa)
Oṃ, because of the rule of being invisible, Oṃ.

Because there is no fixed rule regarding the impressions (*saṃskāra*) of knowledge and action, which are characterized by the state of being invisible. A "rule" (*niyama*) means uniformity of one kind; a "lack of rule" (*aniyama*) means multiplicity of kinds. Thus, there is diversity; and because of this diversity, the diversity among living beings (*jīva*)—who are like reflections—such as gods, demons, and humans, is also logically consistent. This is the meaning. || 1 ||
Oṃ, and it is likewise in the case of the intentional meanings (*abhisandhi*) and so forth; Oṃ.

Since such diversity must be asserted even regarding intentions and the like, as well as defects such as desire and anger, it is precisely due to the diversity of the unseen (adṛṣṭa) that this diversity [of experience] is to be explained. Therefore, because it is necessary, the diversity of the unseen alone is the cause of the diversity among individual souls (jīvas); the meaning is that it is not the diversity of defects and so forth. || 4 ||
Oṃ. If it is argued that [the parts] are distinct regions and so forth, we say no, because they are included within [the whole]. Oṃ.

[Objection: "Surely the diversity among gods, humans, and others arises simply from the diversity of places such as heaven and earth, not from the diversity of unseen forces (adṛṣṭa). [Reply: No. Why? Because it is included within that. When one seeks the cause for the diversity of places—asking what the cause of that diversity is—that cause is included within the very diversity of the unseen; for it is of that nature. Therefore, the meaning is that because it is necessary, the diversity of the unseen alone is the regulator of the diversity among gods, humans, and so forth. || 5 ||
Thus ends the third quarter of the second chapter in the *Sūtradīpikā* composed by the venerable Jagannātha Yati. 2.3.
Section 1: On the Origination of the Vital Breaths (Prāṇas)
Oṃ, likewise the vital breaths; Oṃ.
Just as ether and the other elements arise from Viṣṇu, so too do the vital breaths and the sense organs arise; the meaning is that they are certainly not unproduced. || 1 ||
Oṃ. Because a secondary sense is impossible, Oṃ.

The scriptural statement regarding the beginninglessness of the vital breaths (*prāṇāḥ*)—namely, that they are "without beginning"—is figurative (*gauṇī*), secondary (*amukhyā*), and refers to their non-origination in a subtle form. Why? Because of impossibility; for it is impossible for the senses to be primary (or literal) beginningless, and because the scriptural phrase "from this" would otherwise be inconsistent. This is the meaning. || 2 ||
Oṃ, and because it would contradict his own formal declaration, Oṃ.

The meaning is that, because of the non-contradiction of the proposition "He created all this," and in accordance with that proposition, it must be accepted that the vital breaths (prāṇas) are produced [from Brahman]. || 3 ||
That is the preceding section (Adhikaraṇa) 2.
Om. That [is Brahman], because of the prior scriptural statement; Om.

The word *ca* (and) serves to conjoin the notion of its non-origination. Regarding that mind: because it has arisen prior to—that is, before—the other sense organs; and because of the scriptural statement, "the mind and all the sense organs," [it is heard] from scripture. The meaning is that the mind is indeed subject to origination, and not something unoriginated. || 1 ||
The Section Concerning Having That as its Antecedent (Tatpūrvakatvādhikaraṇa) || 3 ||
Om, because speech is preceded by Om. Om.

Because speech—that is, the organ of speech—is preceded by that [mind], it is said that "the mind alone is the prior form"; for since scripture declares that the mind is its cause, the organ of speech is indeed produced, and not unproduced—this is the meaning. || 1 ||
Section on the Seven Destinies (Saptagatyadhikaraṇa) 4.
Oṃ, and because the seven destinies have been specifically distinguished, Oṃ.

The word "ca" (and) [is used] in the *Pramāṇasamuccaya* [in the sense]: "the seven vital breaths, however, are for the sake of comprehension. Regarding "gate"; that is, of knowledge. The sense organs are the producers [of knowledge], and they are seven—that is, of the number seven—this is indeed a definitive conclusion (*nirṇaya*), not a lack of determination. Why? Because they are specified. The meaning is: because in the Śruti text "seven vital breaths," they are designated as being endowed with specific qualifications, having been placed within the cave for the purpose of the intellect (*buddhi*). || 1 ||
Oṃ, because [the hands and so forth] are already established, it is not thus; Oṃ.

The word *tu* (but) indicates a distinction. For the hands and so forth—namely, the organs such as the hands—are "established in the established action" (*sthite sthitam karma*). The locative case here denotes purpose; thus, they exist for the sake of action. Therefore, because of this distinction from the [other organs], they are not recited together with the organs of knowledge (*jñānendriya*). Consequently, their number as seven is indeed established; this is the meaning. || 2 ||
Section on the Atom (Aṇvadhikaraṇa) 5.
Oṃ, and he is the most excellent; Oṃ!
Just as the other vital breaths (prāṇas) arise, so too the preeminent chief vital breath arises from Viṣṇu; the meaning is that it is certainly not unoriginated. || 1 ||
Oṃ. The vital breath is not a mere function [of the body], because it is taught separately. Oṃ.

The two functions of air—the external wind and the action known as motion—are not what is meant by the phrase "from this [breath]. This is because they are not what is established by the scriptural passage teaching the origin of breath (*prāṇa*). Rather, it is the primary air (the wind) alone that is established by that passage. Why? "Because of the separate instruction. The meaning is that in passages such as "He created breath," the origin of the primary air is heard separately from the origins of the two functions of air. || 2 ||
|| Section on the Eye and Other [Senses] || 7 ||
Om. But it is like the eye and so forth, because of its being taught together with them and for other reasons. Om.

The word *tu* has the sense of *eva* (only/indeed). The principal vital breath (*mukhyaprāṇa*) also, like the eyes and other organs, is dependent upon the Supreme Self and is not independent. Why? Because of its being taught together with them, and so forth; for in the scripture of Gaupavana, "All this indeed [is dependent]," it is stated that the principal breath, along with the eyes and other organs, is subject to the control of another. This is also because of the logical arguments stated in such passages as "the maker of all," and so on. || 1 ||
Oṃ. And because it is not performed, there is no fault; for thus Scripture shows. Oṃ.

Because the chief vital breath (*mukhyaprāṇa*) is an instrument (*karaṇa*); because it is non-different from the instruments such as the eyes, which consist in being employed by an agent; and because the excellence of the chief [breath] over the others is established precisely through this distinction. There is no fault—that is, there is no fault of the scriptural text declaring the independence of the chief vital breath having a different meaning than referring to a subordinate Lord (*avāntareśvara*). If it is asked why it should be interpreted thus, [the answer is: for indeed, the scripture "Tāni ha vā" (Māṇḍūkya Upaniṣad) shows—meaning, makes known—in the manner described above. Therefore is the sense. || 2 ||
The Section on the Fivefold Functioning of the Mind (Prāñcavṛttyadhikaraṇa) || 8 ||
Oṃ, the fivefold activity is designated as being like that of the mind; Oṃ.

"Like the mind" means as if it were the mind; that is, just as the mind is endowed with five functions—namely, those called mind (*manas*), intellect (*buddhi*), ego (*ahaṃkāra*), consciousness (*citta*), and volition (*cetana*)—so too the principal vital breath (*mukhyaprāṇa*) possesses five functions, having the five forms of *prāṇa*, *apāna*, and so forth. Why? Because in the *Kauṇḍiṇya* Śruti it is designated and explained in that way, namely, "Now, [it has] five functions. This is the meaning. || 1 ||
Topic 9: On the Atom (Aṇu-adhikaraṇa).
Oṃ, and the subtle atom; Oṃ.
The chief vital breath (mukhyaprāṇa) is atomic in its form as the individual breath (prāṇa), and it is all-pervasive in its form as air (vāyu); such is the meaning. || 1 ||
Section 10: The Topic Concerning Light and Other [Elements] (Jyotirādyadhikaraṇa)
Om. But [the Lord] is the presiding deity over light and so forth, because of the scriptural teaching; Om.

The phrase "the presiding deity of light, etc. is repeated; its connection is with the word "that" (tat). Thus, that which is the presiding deity of light, etc.—the impeller of the elements such as fire—is Brahman alone. Furthermore, the presiding deity of light, etc., who is the impeller of the eyes and other organs, is not the individual soul (jīva). Why? Because of the scriptural teaching (āmanana) regarding that [Brahman], meaning because it is established as such by passages beginning with, "He who dwells in the eye. || 1 ||
Oṃ, from the sound of that which possesses breath; Oṃ.

The Lord causes the embodied soul (*jīva*), acting as the agent, to perform seeing and other functions by means of those very instruments such as the eyes which are employed by the soul—just as He does through the vital breath (*prāṇa*)—and not by means of instruments employed by the soul. Why? Because of the scriptural statement: "For this [Self] indeed [acts] by means of this" (Bhāllaveya Śruti); this is the meaning. || 2 ||
Oṃ, and because that [Self] is eternal, Oṃ.

The meaning is that although the eyes and other organs are instruments of Brahman, because the individual soul (jīva), the instrument, and the relationship between the two are eternal, the scriptural statement regarding the soul being an instrument is also justified by that intended sense. || 3 ||
|| Section on the Organs of Sense || 11 ||
Oṃ. Those [organs] are the senses (indriya), because they are designated as such; [this is so] because of the excellence of the [supreme] Self. Oṃ.

The senses are those vital breaths other than the chief vital breath; the chief vital breath itself is not among them. Why? Because of that designation; for it is stated in the *Pautrāyaṇa* Śruti that "the senses are indeed twelve. This is the meaning. || 1 ||
Oṃ. [The Self is one] because of the scriptural teaching of difference. Oṃ.

The meaning is that the chief vital breath (*mukhyaprāṇa*) is not non-distinct from the eyes and other senses, because the scripture [the *Pautrāyaṇa* text] states, "For it remains as such," thereby establishing the distinguishing attribute of the chief vital breath—namely, its being the agent and instigator of all actions—and the absence of that attribute in others. || 2 ||
Oṃ, and because of its distinctness, Oṃ.

Furthermore, because there exists a distinction between the principal vital breath (*mukhyaprāṇa*) and the other vital breaths—namely, that the former is dependent solely on the Lord (*īśvara*), while the latter are dependent on both the Lord and the individual soul (*jīva*)—the meaning is that the status of being a sense organ (*indriyatva*) belongs not to the former, but only to the eyes and the other [senses]. || 3 ||
The Section on Designation (Saṃjñādhikaraṇa) 12.
Oṃ. But the fashioning of names and forms belongs to Him who performs the tripartition, because of the teaching; Oṃ.

The word *tu* (but) is used for emphasis. The "formation of names and forms" (*saṃjñāmūrtiklṛpti*) refers to the production of the manifold world consisting of bodies and sense organs, which are of the nature of name and form. This occurs solely from the Supreme Self who performs the "triple-making" (*trivṛtkurvataḥ*)—that is, who effects the intermingling of earth, water, and fire—and not from Viriñca (Brahmā). Why? Because of the teaching; the meaning is that it is so according to the scriptural text: "The Wise One, having fashioned all forms... (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 3.1.3). || 1 ||
|| Section on Meat || 13 ||
Oṃ. [The elements] beginning with flesh are derived from the earth; the others are according to their respective names. Oṃ.

The term "earthy" (*bhauma*) is an illustration; that which in the body is solid, such as flesh and so forth, is indeed earthen or composed of earth, but not the entire body. What then? It is according to the word [of scripture]: following the Vedic text, "That which is solid is earth. One must accept that in the body there is also the effect of the other two—water and fire—in the form of blood, marrow, and so on. Just as flesh and the like are earthen, being the effects of earth, the meaning is that one must likewise accept, in accordance with scripture, the effects of the other two, water and fire, within the body. || 1 ||
Oṃ, but on account of its preeminence, there is that designation; indeed, there is that designation. Oṃ.

The specific designations "earthen," "watery," and "fiery" are appropriate because of the predominance (*vaiśeṣya*) of the respective elements—earth and so forth—in conjunction with their particular bodies. Therefore, there is no contradiction [with other scriptural statements]. This repetition at the end of the chapter is for the purpose of confirming the entire subject matter taught in this chapter. || 2 ||
Thus ends the fourth quarter of the second chapter in the *Sūtradīpikā* composed by the venerable Jagannātha Yati. 2.4.
1. The Section Concerning That Interval (Tadantarādhikaraṇa)
Oṃ. Upon entering the next state, he proceeds enveloped [by the elements], as is established by the questions and the answers. Oṃ.

"In the interval between [deaths], for the sake of attaining another body, the individual soul (jīva) proceeds enveloped—meaning indeed joined with the elements such as earth and the rest. It is known that it departs, leaving this body and going to another world. Why? Because of the question and the explanation: from King Pravāhaṇa’s question to the seer Śvetaketu, "Do you know how...? and likewise from the answer spoken by Pravāhaṇa, "Thus, indeed... This is the meaning. || 1 ||"
Section 2: The Topic Concerning the Nature of Being Consisting of That.
Oṃ, but because it consists of that [the Self] and because of its abundance, Oṃ.

The individual soul (jīva) goes enveloped by all the elements, not by water alone. The specific mention of "water" (āpaḥ) is because [the other elements] consist of that [water], since earth, fire, and air are composed of the essence of water; furthermore, among those [elements], water is predominant due to its abundance. Therefore, there is no contradiction with that [scriptural statement]. This is the meaning.
|| 3 || The Section Concerning the Movement of the Vital Breath (Prāṇagatyadhikaraṇa) ||
Oṃ, and because of the departure of the vital breaths, Oṃ.

Furthermore, because it is heard in scripture that the senses—designated as "vital breaths" (prāṇas) and pervaded by the elements—depart together with the individual soul (jīva), the meaning is that the soul goes forth precisely enveloped by the elements.
|| 4 || [End of] the Section on Fire and the Others (Agnirādyadhikaraṇa).
"Oṃ. If it be argued that [the soul does not go to Brahman] because of the scriptural mention of its destination as Agrya and so forth, we say no, because that is figurative. Oṃ.

If it is argued that the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) do not depart together with the individual soul (*jīva*), because of the scriptural statement regarding their movement toward fire and other elements—namely, the mention of their going toward fire and so forth—we say: no. Why? Because [the statement] is figurative (*bhākta*). The meaning is that the scriptural passage beginning with "wherever" refers only to a portion of the vital breaths. The First Section.

Oṃ. If it be argued that [the meditation on the Self] is not possible in the first [chapter], we say no; for those very [meditations] are indeed possible there, on account of the logical consistency. Oṃ.

"In that first [fire]" refers to the commencement. Because the oblation is heard of in the first fire—namely, the one called *dyu* (heaven)—and because there is no mention of the living soul (*jīva*) accompanying the elements, [it may be argued] that the soul does not go accompanied by the elements. If this is said, we reply: No. Why? Because those very waters under discussion are denoted by the word "faith" (*śraddhā*) occurring at the beginning. Therefore, why is this so? Because of the logical consistency; that is to say, because the concluding statement, "The waters become human-like," is thus logically consistent. || 6 || The Section on the Non-hearing [of the Soul].

Om. If it is argued that [the soul] does not exist because it has not been heard [in the Vedas], we say no, because it is perceived [to exist] among those who perform sacrifices such as the Āgneya. Om.

If it is argued that there is no simultaneous departure of the elements with the individual soul (*jīva*) because such a thing is not heard of—that is, because there is no direct scriptural statement (*pratyakṣa-śravaṇa*) regarding their departure together as there is for speech and so forth in the passage, "Speech merges into fire" (*agniṃ vāgapyeti*)—we say: No. Why? Because of the scriptural text, "Then him... (*athainam iti*, Kauṇḍinya), which refers to those who perform sacrifices and oblations, such as the *iṣṭāpūrta* rites; for from this very [text], the separation and conjunction of the elements is understood through direct perception. This is the meaning. || 7 || [End of] the Section on the Figurative Sense (*bhākta-adhikaraṇa*).

"Or it is figurative because they do not know the Self; for thus [the scripture] shows. (Oṃ) The immortality stated for those who perform works is figurative—that is, secondary. Why? Because they do not know the Self, meaning they lack knowledge of Brahman. By the word "or" (*vā*), the Sūtra indicates two alternative views: that the immortality produced by the desireless works performed by the seeker (*jijñāsu*) and the knower (*jñānin*) is not of the nature of primary immortality, which consists in the cessation of transmigratory existence; rather, it is of the nature of unsurpassed, supreme, and primary immortality, consisting of the excellence of bliss resulting from the purification of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*). Why is this so? Because [the scripture] shows it thus.

The Śruti passages, namely "or [he becomes] immortal," "He [leads] him," "by means of action," and "the Self," demonstrate and establish the aforementioned meanings. Therefore, this is the sense. || 8 || The Section on the Passing Away of What Has Been Done (Kṛtātyayādhikaraṇa).
Oṃ. At the end of [the results of] what has been performed, [the soul] possesses residual karma (anuśaya), as is seen from scripture and from memory. Oṃ.

When there is the exhaustion (*atyaya*) of what has been performed—that is, when the *kṛta* karma has reached its end through experience in heaven and so forth—then one returns to this world again as one possessing residual attachment (*anuśayin*), meaning as one possessing that which remains after being experienced. Why? Because of both scriptural observation (*dṛṣṭi*) and traditional teaching (*smṛti*). The meaning is: because of the scriptural statement indicated by the word "residual" (*śeṣa*), namely, "Then [he descends] with the remainder" (*tataḥ śeṣeṇa*); and because of the traditional teaching (*smṛti*) stating, "Possessing the remainder of what was experienced" (*bhuktaśeṣa*). This concludes the section beginning with *yathetam*.
Oṃ, as it was and not otherwise, Oṃ!

In whatever manner and by whichever path the soul (jīva) has gone—that is, attained—suchness (tathā), and likewise by another path (anevam), the soul returns to this world; such is the meaning. || 10 || [End of] the Section on Conduct (caraṇādhikaraṇa).
Om. If it be argued that [the soul] does not [ascend] because of the mention of "feet," we say no; for Kārṣṇājini holds that this is intended as an indicative mark (upalakṣaṇa). Om.

The going and coming does not result from sacrifice and the like; rather, it results from conduct (*caraṇa*), that is, from conduct which is an auxiliary part of sacrifice. If it is argued that this is because of the *śruti* stating "from conduct" (*caraṇāt*), the answer is no. Why? Because the teacher Kārṣṇājini maintains that the *śruti* teaches both sacrifice and conduct through a secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) that does not abandon its own primary meaning (*ajahatsvārtha*) while being subordinate to that [conduct]. This is the meaning. If it is argued that [the mention of conduct] would be purposeless, we say no, because of the dependence upon that. (Sūtra 3.1.12) Oṃ.

If it is argued that the word *caraṇa* (conduct) would be redundant if it were intended as a mere indicative (*upalakṣaṇa*), because the performance of action can already be indicated by the words "pleasant" (*ramaṇīyaka*) and "foul-smelling" (*pūya*) respectively—[the answer is: no, because that [action] depends upon it; that is, because the nature of an act as being "good" or "bad" depends upon conduct and the like. Thus, the meaning is that the word is purposeful for the sake of making that [conduct] known.
"Bādari, however, says: 'Only good and evil deeds [are taken over]' (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.5)."

The meaning is that the teacher Bādari maintains that "good conduct" (*sukṛta*) and "evil conduct" (*duṣkṛta*) refer specifically to good and evil actions as established in the Śruti, and not to the performance of their constituent parts. By the word "but" (*tu*), he indicates that this very view is his own established doctrine (*svasiddhānta*).
|| 11 || [End of] the Section on Non-Exclusion (*aniṣyādhikaraṇa*).
Oṃ, it is also heard that [liberation] occurs even for those who have committed the five heinous crimes. Oṃ.

The word *ca* (and) serves to include other types of suffering. It is not only those who perform sacrifices and the like who undergo coming and going; rather, this applies even to those who commit sins that are opposed to the acts denoted by the term "sacrifice" (*iṣṭa*). Why? Because it is heard [in scripture]: "Of him, here... (Bhāllaveya Śruti). This is the meaning. **Sūtra:** *Oṃ saṃyamane tvanubhūyetareṣām ārohāvarohau tadgatidarśanāt Oṃ.* But for others, there is ascent and descent after having experienced [the results] in the world of Saṃyama, because their destination is seen [to be so]. **Explanation:** However, for those other than the performers of sacrifices, the process involves first experiencing the fruits of their actions in the world of Yama (Saṃyama), and only thereafter do they ascend or descend, as their specific destiny is observed to be such. Thus, the rule regarding the path does not apply universally.

The word *tu* is used for emphasis. The locative case is used in the sense of the accusative. In the Saṃyamana hell, after having experienced the punishment of being bound, among others—those other than the performers of sacrifices and the like—there occurs for some an ascent (*āroha*), which is rising up from the hell, and for others a descent (*avaroha*), which is a fall into even lower places within the eternal hells. Why? Because their destination is seen; that is, because such a destiny for those who do not perform sacrifices and the like is observed, as stated in the Kauṇṭharavya Śruti: "Some here [fall]... (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 5.10.7). And they remember it. Om. Om. Om.
The meaning is that the authors of the *Smṛtis* establish the stated point through such *Smṛti* passages as "they go," and so forth.
|| 12 || [This concludes] the section consisting of seven [verses].
Oṃ, even seven times, oṃ.
The meaning is that the wise, by means of the *smṛtis*, establish even the seven kinds of hells beginning with Raurava as being designated by the term "Raurava" (in the *Mahābhārata*).
In this regard, there is also an adhikaraṇa.
Oṃ. And even in that case, there is no contradiction because of its operation [therein]. Oṃ.

The word *ca* (and) indicates the sense that [the Lord acts] even without the experience of suffering. Thus, even there—in hell—there is no contradiction because of His activity; for even without the experience of suffering, the activity of that Lord known as "impelling" (*preraṇā*) exists. There is no contradiction between these two types of opposition: namely, that if the Lord were to remain in hell and act as the controller of the living beings situated there, it would contradict the Śruti stating "all [is pervaded by Him]"; whereas if He were their controller, it would imply that He is an experiencer of suffering. [The meaning is: there is no such contradiction. || 14 || [End of] the Section on Knowledge (*vidyādhikaraṇam*).
"Oṃ, but because of the subject matter [of knowledge and action]—thus [it is said]. Oṃ.

The word *tu* (but) is used for emphasis. In the scriptural passage, "Now, of these two paths," the phrase "of these two" refers specifically to knowledge (*jñāna*) and action (*karman*), and not to the two paths beginning with smoke (*dhūma*) and light (*arcis*). [If it referred to the paths,] the soul’s independence regarding the fruit [of its actions] would follow. Why? Because they are the subject under discussion; that is to say, because those two [knowledge and action] are also the subject under discussion in the passage, "But those who live thus... [Chāndogya Upaniṣad 5.10.1]. [End of Section 15] [End of Third Adhikaraṇa]
Oṃ, it is not [the case that the self exists] in the third [state], because it is not perceived there; Oṃ.

In the third [verse], regarding the downward states mentioned as "the darkness of the animal realm," there is no happiness in that third darkness; this is the ellipsis. Why? Because it is perceived as such; the meaning is that it is experienced as such. And it is also recorded in tradition (smṛti) in the world. Om.

The absence of happiness in blinding darkness is both remembered by the author of the Smṛti in the passage, "Not in blinding darkness" (*Bhaviṣyatparva*), and is established by that Smṛti; moreover, this is also proven in the world by inference based on universal observation. *Oṃ darśanācca oṃ*.
The meaning is that the absence of pleasure in the third [state] is established both by reasoning and by the direct perception of Hiraṇyagarbha.
Oṃ. In the third [state], there is the inclusion of sound; this is so for that which arises from sorrow. Oṃ.

The word "third" recurs. In the third darkness; that is, regarding that third blinding darkness, whatever sound [is heard], by that there occurs the obstruction—that is, the attainment—of delusion born of intense sorrow (*saṃśoka*). *Oṃ*, and from remembrance, *oṃ*.

The meaning is that both [the existence of darkness and its capacity to cause delusion] are established by the *Kūrma Purāṇa* Smṛti passage, "Great darkness," which mentions the third type of darkness and the resulting delusion of the listener upon hearing it.
|| 16 || This concludes the section on its inherent nature (*tatsvābhāvya-adhikaraṇa*).
Oṃ. [The soul] attains its own essential nature, because that is logically consistent.

"Attainment of that nature" means the attainment (*prāpti*) of the very nature of that deity, such as smoke, which is a nature similar to [the soul's] own nature. It does not mean identity with it, nor the attainment of its state (*tatpada*). Why? Because of logical consistency (*upapatti*); the meaning is that this alone is reasonable, since the identity of one thing with another is never observed.
[Sūtra 17. This concludes the section concerning "not for too long."
Oṃ, not long after this, by virtue of the distinction; Oṃ.

The transmigrating soul, having departed from its own world, reaches the earth and attains a birth as a Brāhmaṇa or other [caste] before long—that is, very quickly. Why? Because of the specific statement: "Of him, here... (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 5.10.5). This is the meaning of the specific declaration. || 18 || [End of] the Section on Others.
Oṃ. Because of the statement [of the Buddha] regarding one possessed by another, as before, Oṃ.

When a person who has died enters another body—such as that of rice or other grains—which is presided over by another [individual soul] and is considered to have its own life-force, there is merely an entry, but not the assumption of identification with that body; for if there were such identification, there would be suffering. If so, how is it that there is a statement of non-difference in the passage, "Rice and barley"? To this it is said: "As before. Just as in passages such as "Having become smoke," there is a statement of becoming smoke and so forth, so it is here. Why is this? Because of the expression; the meaning is that it is so stated in the *Kauṣītaki* Śruti: "He, from here... (*so 'vāmataḥ*). **Sūtra:** *Oṃ aśuddham iti cet na śabdāt Oṃ.* **Translation:** If it be argued that [the soul's descent] is impure, we say no, because of the scriptural word. *Oṃ*.

If it is argued that because sacrifice is of the nature of violence, its action is unaccomplished and a means to suffering, we say no. Why? Because of the Word; that is to say, because it is enjoined by the scriptural statements. || 19 || [The Section on Semen]

Oṃ. Now, the connection with the "seeder" (retas-sic). First, for the one who performs ritual actions (karmī), there is the connection with the "seeder"—that is, the relationship or union with the father as the seeder of semen; in other words, entry into him. Then, immediately after that, entry into the mother occurs, but not at the very first.
This concludes the section concerning the womb (yony-adhikaraṇa). || 20 ||
Oṃ, from the womb comes the body; Oṃ.

The fifth [case-ending] is used in the sense of *lyap* (the gerund suffix). The meaning is that the soul (*karmī*), having entered the mother’s womb by way of the father, does not [remain there] without that [body].
Thus ends the first quarter of the third chapter in the *Sūtradīpikā* composed by Śrī Jagannāthayati.
|| 1 || The Section on the Twilight Prayers (*sandhyādhikaraṇa*).
Oṃ. For it has been said that creation occurs at the junctions [of time], Oṃ.

For indeed, because the scripture states, "Then [he creates] chariots," the Blessed One’s act of creation occurs in the intermediate state—that is, in the dream state which exists between waking and deep sleep. Therefore, "creation" refers to the creation of the objects of the dream state; the meaning is that they are produced by the Blessed One alone. Oṃ. Some [hold that there is] also a passing away, as well as sons and so forth. Oṃ.

For this reason: some followers of particular Vedic branches (śākhins) declare that this Blessed One is the creator of the objects of dreams, as stated in the passage, "He who [creates] these while they sleep. Others, such as his sons and so forth, say that they are born from Viṣṇu alone. Therefore, the meaning is that the creation of dreams belongs to Viṣṇu alone.
*Sūtra:* But it is mere illusion (māyāmātra), because its nature is not manifested in its entirety. *Sūtra:* Om.

The word *tu* (but) has the sense of emphasis. The intermediate state (*sandhya*) is merely illusion (*māyāmātra*), produced solely by the desire and latent impressions denoted by the term "illusion," which serve as its efficient and material causes; it does not have external causes. Why? Because its nature is unmanifest in its entirety—that is, because its nature is not fully manifested, unlike that of external objects. **Om. And it is indicative, for so says scripture, and those who know it declare it to be so. Om.**

Why is this so? Because a dream-object is indicative, meaning it makes known what is auspicious or inauspicious; for this reason as well, it is not unreal. Why? From the Śruti text: "Because [it is seen]" (*yataḥ*). The word "hi" (for) implies that its fruit is also observed through direct perception. Furthermore, those who know that—that is, Vyāsa and others who know dreams—declare it. The meaning is: from the Śruti text beginning with "When," they state that dream-objects possess causal efficiency (*arthakriyākāritva*);
therefore, for this reason as well, [the dream is not unreal]. || 2 || End of the section on the meditation on the Supreme (*parābhidhyāna-adhikaraṇa*).
Oṃ, but [the Self] is concealed by the meditation on the Supreme; for from that [concealment] arise its bondage and its opposite, Oṃ.

Because, from that Supreme Self, for this individual soul (*jīva*), bondage and its opposite—namely liberation—occur; therefore, through the contemplation of the Supreme, that is, solely by the will of the Supreme Self, the intermediate state (*sandhya*) becomes concealed or dissolved. The meaning is that it does not arise from any other cause.
|| 3 || The Section on Connection with the Body.
Oṃ, because of its connection with the body, even clothing [is included]; Oṃ.

The meaning is that even "dwelling," which consists of remaining in the waking state through the conceit of being the body due to connection with a body, occurs only from the supreme contemplation (*parābhidhyāna*) and not from anything else. || 4 || This concludes the section [dealing] with the absence of that [dreaming].
Oṃ. Its absence [is found] in the channels; its presence is in the Self due to its pervasiveness. Oṃ.

For this individual soul (*jīva*), within the channels (*nāḍī*)—that is, within the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) who resides in the channels—the absence of those [states] occurs; that is, the absence of waking and dreaming arises. Deep sleep (*suṣupti*) is produced. At that time, its entry into that [Supreme Self] takes place. Why? Because of the scriptural statement: "Then, into these channels... (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.6.3); the meaning is that it is so heard in the scripture. With the word "for" (*hi*), he states the logical justification for this point. || 5 || Section on Awakening (*prabodhādhikaraṇam*).
Oṃ; therefore, awakening arises from this.

The awakening of this individual soul (*jīva*)—its rising from sleep—occurs from this Supreme Self alone and not from anything else. Why? Because of the scriptural statement, "This very one," according to the *Kauṇḍiṇya* Śruti; such is the meaning.
|| 6 || [End of] the Section on Action and Recollection (*karmānusmṛtyadhikaraṇa*).
Oṃ, and he alone [is the one who transmigrates], because of the mention of karma, recollection, and the scriptural injunctions; Oṃ.

The word *ca* (and) has the sense of *api* (also). He alone—that is, the Lord alone—is the impeller of all beings at all times and in all states; there is no other [impeller] in another place or at another time. Why? Because of action, remembrance, scripture, and injunction: because of the scriptural statement that actions are dependent on the Lord, namely, "For he alone..."; because of the indicative memory (smṛti) which shows this; because of the word "this" (*eṣa*); and because of the injunction "himself" (*ātmānam*).
|| 7 || End of the section on Attainment (*sampatty-adhikaraṇa*).
Oṃ. For one who has fainted, there is partial attainment [of the fruit] by virtue of the remainder; Oṃ.

"O deluded one, in a state of fainting (*mūrchā*), there is the 'half-attainment' (*ardha-sampatti*) of the individual soul (*jīva*), which is its half-entry into the Supreme Self (*paramātman*). Why? Because of the method of elimination (*pariśeṣāt*); that is to say, by means of inference preceded by the negation of all other possible alternatives.
|| 8 || [This concludes] the section: "Not even from the standpoint of place" (*na sthānato ’pi adhikaraṇam*).
Oṃ. Even from the standpoint of its location, the Supreme has no dual characteristics, for it possesses both everywhere. Oṃ.

Of the Supreme Self (parasya paramātmanaḥ), even from the standpoint of location (sthānataḥ)—that is, despite the difference in locations such as the eye and so forth—there is no dual characteristic (ubhayaliṅgam) or distinct form. Rather, the form situated in all places (sarvasthāneṣu) is one and the same. Why? Because there is the scriptural text (śruti): "In all" (sarveṣu). This is the meaning. *Oṃ. If it be argued that it is not so because of the difference [of locations], we say no, because each [individual location] is declared to be non-different from That.* *Oṃ.*

If it is argued that there is no non-difference among the forms of Viśva and the others because of their distinction—since they are described as being bound by cause and effect due to the heard attribute of being the differentiators that produce the experiences of the dreaming and waking states—the answer is: no. Why? Because each of those forms is [non-different] from one another. This is because of the scriptural statement of non-difference, "This is your Self," which does not speak otherwise. Furthermore, some [scriptures] also state this very thing. Om. 1.4.22. Oṃ. *api caivameke* Oṃ.

Since some followers of certain Vedic schools (śākhins) read in the scripture, "without measure," both non-difference and, by the word "and" (ca), manifoldness; the meaning is that even though there is non-difference, the designation of difference is appropriate due to the difference of locations and so forth.
|| 9 || The Section on Formlessness (Arūpādhikaraṇa).
Oṃ. For that [Brahman] is indeed formless, because it is characterized by that [formlessness]. Oṃ.

Brahman is indeed formless, meaning it is devoid of any material form (*prākṛta-rūpa*). Why? Because it is the primary [subject], that is, because it is superior to primordial matter (*prakṛti*) and so forth; and because of the scriptural statement "not coarse" (*asthūlam*), as indicated by the word "for" (*hi*).
Oṃ. And [its] luminosity exists, lest [the scripture] be rendered meaningless.

It indicates the cause. Just as there is no conventional usage of the term "light" regarding the light of the eyes and other senses—which, though luminous, are distinct from ordinary light—so too [Brahman] is not devoid of purpose. This does not imply the invalidity of the scriptural texts concerning Brahman’s possession of form (*rūpitva*). Why? Because even though it is formless, its possession of a distinctive form is admitted; this is the meaning. *Oṃ āha ca tanmātram oṃ*.

Since the scripture states, "Oneness," the meaning is that it declares—that is, speaks of—the nature of Brahman as consisting solely of that [oneness], having consciousness and bliss as its sole essence. Therefore, there is no failure to define its distinctness; this is the sense of the word "and" (ca). Furthermore, it is shown and also remembered [in the Smṛti]. Om.

"And" (*ca*) signifies conjunction (*samuccaye*). It indicates not only that Brahman consists of bliss and so forth, but the scripture stating "by the knowledge of That" (*tadvijñānena*) also shows and establishes that knowledge itself has Brahman as its essence. Furthermore, the particle *atho* expresses another point. Moreover, the fact that knowledge also possesses the nature of Brahman is recorded in the *Mātsya Purāṇa* by Vyāsa and others in such passages as "like a pure crystal. Therefore, the meaning is that it is not without scriptural authority (*aprāmāṇika*) for both knowledge and bliss to be the very nature (*svarūpa*) of Brahman. || 10 || Section on Simile (*Upamādhikaraṇam*).
Oṃ, for this very reason there is the simile of the reflections of the sun and so forth; Oṃ.

For this very reason—precisely because of the statement regarding the non-difference of the Lord and those [individual souls] who possess His nature; and for this very reason—namely, on account of the reasons such as sentience (*caitanyatva*). "Comparison" refers to the soul's similarity to a fish and so forth. If it is argued that there is non-difference from the Lord just as in the case of a fish and so forth, the answer is "no"—this is the ellipsis. By the word "and" (*ca*), he joins together the similarity in terms of being distinct. Why? Because, like the sun reflected in water and so forth; just as the sun and other objects reflected in water are distinct from the sun and other objects due to their status as reflections, so too the soul is distinct because of its status as a reflection. Alternatively:

For this very reason, because it is stated that the fish and others are not distinct from Brahman in terms of qualities such as knowledge; for this very reason, [the soul is] "like the reflection of the sun and so forth. The comparison is the comparison with the reflection of the sun and so forth. Since the soul possesses a part equal to the fish and others, it would follow that there is no distinction between them; therefore, the meaning is that the comparison is to the reflection of Brahman. For this very reason—namely, because it is a reflection of Brahman—the soul is not non-different from Brahman, unlike the reflection of the sun and so forth; this is the meaning of the word *ca* (and). Alternatively, "for this very reason" means precisely because of the two qualities under discussion: dependence upon Him and similarity to Him.

The analogy is "like the sun and so forth. Because the individual soul (*jīva*) is a reflection of the Lord (*īśvara*), its nature as a reflection does not cease upon the cessation of the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), nor is it dependent upon them; this is the meaning.
|| 11 || The Section on Water (*ambuvad-adhikaraṇa*).
Oṃ. But because it is not grasped like water, it is not so; Oṃ.

The suffix *vati* is used in the sense of similarity (*sādṛśya*). Here, similarity is intended to mean a specific quality known as "affection" (*sneha*). And thus, because of the lack of apprehension [of the Lord] as being like water—meaning, due to the absence of knowledge of His majesty accompanied by affection, which is to say, without devotion—the likeness to the Lord consisting in having the nature of bliss and so forth is not properly manifested. Therefore, since devotion alone generates the full manifestation of His true nature, the meaning is that it must be practiced for that purpose. || 12 || The Section on Increase and Decrease (*vṛddhihrāsādhikaraṇam*).
Oṃ. It possesses increase and decrease because of its internal inclusion [of all things] and because of the consistency of both [states]; thus it is so. Oṃ.

The quality of participating in increase and decrease—namely, the superiority or inferiority among practitioners regarding devotion and so forth—is not to be admitted. Why? Because of inclusion; for those such as Brahmā and others who possess great or small fruits, as well as others, are included within the state of being devotees (*bhakta*). Even so, why would there be participation in increase and decrease? This is possible only when there is such a gradation in devotion.

Because of the consistency of both; that is, because it is consistent for the Lord, the giver of fruits, in relation to both classes of living beings—beginning with Brahmā and others—whether their fruits are great or small, since the granting of fruits according to the gradations of devotion is logical, whereas otherwise it would be illogical. Therefore, the meaning is that this [distinction] must be accepted. *Oṃ darśanācca oṃ*.
The meaning is that what has been stated is correct because the gradation of fruits is seen in the Śruti text beginning with "atha ataḥ" and is also stated in the Smṛti text beginning with "yathā".
|| 13 || The Section on the Nature of the Protector ||
Oṃ. For [the scripture] negates the extent of the world as it has been described; thereafter, it speaks further. Oṃ.

For [the reason is] as follows: the *Śruti* negates—that is, rejects—the notion that "it is only this much," meaning that the nature of the subject under discussion is limited merely to being the agent of creation and so forth. This "limited nature" refers to the state of being restricted solely to the agency of creation and dissolution. It negates this; therefore, because He is the agent of creation and so forth, it further declares His quality of being the Protector (*pālakatva*). Thus, the meaning is that by virtue of His being the Protector, it makes known that Hari possesses yet another glory called "Protectorship," which was indicated by the phrase "creation and so forth. By the word "and" (*ca*) in the phrase "creation and so forth," the *Smṛti* (from the *Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa*) is indicated.
Section 14: The Topic of the Unmanifest (Avyakta)
Oṃ, they say that it is unmanifest; Oṃ!

That Brahman is unmanifest, its nature being such that it cannot be seen through human effort. Why? Because the scripture (the Kauṇṭharavya-śruti) says, "And the unmanifest is partless"; therefore, this is the meaning. Oṃ. Furthermore, [Brahman is perceived] during intense devotion, according to both direct perception and inference. Oṃ.

Even by means of worship devoid of devotion, Brahman cannot be made manifest. Why? Even in "saṃrādhana," that is, even in complete adoration, [Brahman remains unmanifest]. This is because its unmanifest nature is established through both perception and inference—namely, the perception of the wise and the inference based on the subtle cause. Thus: "And like light, there is no distinction. Oṃ.

What is the meaning? Like light—just as fire has manifest and unmanifest states through its gross and subtle forms—so it is not with Brahman; rather, Brahman is unmanifest by its very nature. Why? Because there is no distinction (*avaiśeṣyam*) in Brahman; that is, there is no distinction of grossness or subtlety. This is the meaning. *Oṃ, and like light, because of the repetition in the action, Oṃ.*

"Manifestation" (*prakāśa*) means immediate knowledge (*aparokṣajñāna*). "In the object," namely in Brahman, which is the objective domain. "From practice," meaning from the repetition of hearing and so forth. This is the sense. *Oṃ, therefore [the Self is] with the infinite; for thus there is an indicative mark, oṃ.*

Therefore, since there is evidence for the perceptibility of the Unmanifest (avyakta) despite its unmanifest nature, it is known that through the grace of the infinite and undivided Brahman, the Unmanifest becomes directly perceived; this is established by the fact that such [perception] would otherwise be impossible. But it is not from mere impossibility alone; rather, for [it is so] because the mark (liṅga) has been stated thus: "From meditating upon Him... which indicates that the grace of the Lord is the cause for the cessation of bondage. Furthermore, there exists a means of knowledge indicating that grace is the cause for vision; therefore, such is the meaning. || 14 || The Section on the Serpent and the Coil (Ahikuṇḍalādhikaraṇa).
Oṃ. But because of the designation of both [aspects], it is like a serpent and its coil. Oṃ.

Brahman possesses bliss as its attribute (*guṇa*) and is also of that very nature (*tad-rūpa*). Why? Because of the dual designation (*ubhaya-vyapadeśāt*); for in such scriptural passages as "Bliss is Brahman" and "The bliss of Brahman," Brahman is described both as consisting of the attribute (*guṇātmakatvena*) and as the possessor of the attribute (*guṇitvena*). How is that so? It is like a snake and its coils (*ahikuṇḍalavat*). Just as in the case of a snake (*sarpa*), there is both the state of being a snake and the state of being coiled; the meaning is that it is so because of this distinction. **Sūtra:** *Oṃ, or rather, like light and its substratum, because of its luminous nature.* **Oṃ.**

Just as the sun, which is the substratum of light, possesses both the nature of light and the state of being its substratum, so it is with Brahman as well. To the question, "What is the reason for choosing the illustration of the sun while setting aside other [illustrations]? it is said: "Because of its luminous nature" (*tejastvāt*). The meaning is that since both Brahman and the sun are of the nature of light (*tejas*), the illustration of the sun is employed with that intention in mind. *Oṃ pūrvavadvā oṃ*.

The meaning is that just as time, though not different from "prior," is qualified by the word "prior" as "prior time," so too Brahman is qualified by bliss (*ānanda*). The three examples are stated either for the sake of emphasis or with the intention of addressing those of coarse and subtle intellects.
Om. And because of the negation, Om.
Because of the negation of difference—both of the qualities of Brahman and of Brahman itself—by the statement, "There is no diversity here," the meaning is that Brahman consists of its own qualities.
|| 16 || End of the section concerning the supreme state.
Om. [The Brahman is] different from that [individual soul], because of the designations of being a bridge, of measurement, of connection, and of difference. Om.

The collection of Brahman-attributes is supreme and distinct from the world; why? Because of the designations of being a bridge, measurement, relation, and difference. This is because of the statement of its being a bridge in the passage, "This is the bridge"; because of the statement of fullness denoted by measurement in the passage, "From which words turn back"; because of the statement of the relationship of reflection and original in the passage, "Of this very bliss"; and because of the statement of its distinction from worldly bliss in the passage, "Knowledge is other [than that]. Om. Because it is seen [in scripture]. Om.

The meaning is that because other forms of bliss, such as [sensual] bliss, are established by direct perception and are objects of the mind and speech, whereas the bliss of Brahman (*brahmānanda*) is not so, it is therefore distinct from the world. *Oṃ*, it is for the sake of understanding, like the case of the feet; *oṃ*.

Just as the term "foot" (pāda) is applied to the beings called *jīvas*—which are distinct from the feet of the world—in the statement, "A foot of Him are all beings," for the sake of understanding; that is, to make known that these beings are portions (*aṃśa*) of the Lord; so too is the term "bliss" (*ānanda*) applied even to the super-mundane bliss of Brahman and the like. It is for the sake of understanding; the meaning is that it is intended to make known attributes such as being experienced as agreeable.
|| 17 || [End of] the Section on Specific Locations.
Oṃ. [The soul is all-pervading] because of its specific location, like light; oṃ.

"Like light and so forth": just as there is a variety—such as fire, gold, and so on—in the reflections of the sun and other objects upon the sun-gem (*sūryakānta*) and other substances, which arises from the particularity of the location due to the diversity of qualities inherent in the sun-gem and its substrate; so too, due to the diversity of qualities such as devotion found in the locations of Brahmā and others, a variety among the blissful reflections of the Lord within the states of Brahmā and the rest is likewise established.
This is the meaning. *Oṃ upapatteśca oṃ*.

The meaning is that, because the diversity of bliss among Brahmā and the others is possible solely by virtue of the Lord’s majesty—which serves as the original image (bimba)—it is logical that He is their prototype (tat-pratibimba).
