Oṃ. Likewise, [the self does not exist] because of the negation of anything else. Oṃ.

Just as the bliss of individual souls (*jīva*) and the like is distinct from the bliss of Brahman and the like, so too the object consisting of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) perceived at the time of meditation is other than Brahman; it is different from Him. Why? Because the scripture, in the passage beginning with "That which [is not] by the mind," prohibits anything else from being Brahman—this is the meaning.
|| 19 || [End of] the Section on Omnipresence (*sarvagatatvādhikaraṇa*).
Oṃ, by this [it is established that the Lord is] omnipresent, because of the words "consisting of illusion" and so forth; Oṃ.

By this very Lord alone does creation and so forth occur at all places and times, and not by another at other places and times. Why? Because of His omnipresence, as indicated by such terms as "consisting of Māyā" and others; for there is the scriptural testimony of His omnipresence in the *Bhāllaveya*: "He is omnipresent" (*eṣa sarvagataḥ*). Furthermore, because He is the purpose of creation and so forth, and because of the scriptural passage beginning with "everywhere" (*sarvatra*) which serves as an explanation of the term "consisting of Māyā" applied to Viṣṇu in the *Caturvedaśikhā*. The phrase "and because of the absence of evidence elsewhere," etc., is the meaning of the word "others" (*ādi*). || 20 || [The Section on the Fruit]
Oṃ. The fruit [arises] from that [the Lord], because it is logical. Oṃ.

The fruit is heaven and so forth; therefore, it arises from God alone, not from karma. Why? Because of logical consistency (*upapatti*); that is to say, because it is reasonable for God, being conscious, to be the giver of the fruit.
Om, and because it is heard [in scripture], Om.

And because it is so heard: the meaning is that the Lord alone is the giver of the fruit, because He is declared as such by the scripture in the passage beginning with "He bestows. Oṃ. Jaimini [maintains] that Dharma [is the giver], for that very reason. Oṃ.

The teacher Jaimini states that dharma bestows the fruit; and he considers that very dharma to be produced from the Lord alone. Why? For this very reason—meaning, precisely because of the scriptural text, "For He alone... (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 1.1.7). Om.
But Bādarāyaṇa [holds the view] of the former [position], because of the mention of a cause. Om.

But the teacher Bādarāyaṇa considers both the previously mentioned Brahman and Dharma to be the cause of the fruit. In this regard, the meaning of the word "tu" (but) is that there is a distinction: Brahman is the cause by way of being the agent (*kartṛ*), while Karma is the cause by way of being the instrument (*karaṇa*). Why? Because of the designation of the cause; the meaning is that in the scriptural text "by merit" (*puṇyena*), the causality of both Brahman and Karma is stated in the form of agency and instrumentality.
Thus ends the second quarter of the third chapter in the *Sūtradīpikā* composed by Śrī Jagannātha Yati.
|| 1 || The Topic Concerning All the Vedas.
Oṃ. All Vedānta texts convey the same meaning, because there is no difference in their injunctions and so forth. Oṃ.

In the preceding sūtra, Brahman—described by the first member [of the compound] as being recognized by all Vedāntas—is a *bahuvrīhi* compound. It is the object of the knowledge produced by the determination arising from hearing (*śravaṇa*) and other means concerning all the Vedas, performed according to one's capacity. Why? Because of the non-difference of the injunctions and so forth; that is to say, because there is no difference between the injunctions such as "The Self," etc., indicated by the word "etc.," and the logical arguments stated in passages such as "For here [they] merge," etc., indicated by the phrase "and so forth. The meaning is: because they are common to all qualified aspirants. **Sūtra:** *Oṃ bhedānneti ced ekasyām api oṃ.* (If it be said that [the Vedāntas do not have the same purport] because of differences, [we reply: no, even in the case of a single [Veda]).

The words "if" (*ced*), "not" (*na*), "because of difference" (*bhedāt*), "also" (*api*), and "thus" (*iti*) are repeated; the words "then" (*tarhi*) and "in the branch" (*śākhāyām*) are likewise understood. And so: if, because of the difference—that is, the distinctness—of the matters taught in all the branches, it is said that one [person] need not know everything taught in every branch, but only what is taught in their own respective branch, then even what is taught in their own branch would not be known. Why? Because even within a single branch there is difference, as differences in meaning are observed.

Now, if it is argued that the refutation [of the objection] lies in the fact that there is a distinction of attributes (dharma-bheda) because different attributes are enjoined for a single substratum (dharmin), and because there is a distinction of the resulting consequences (prasaṅga-bheda), the meaning is that this [refutation] applies equally even when one has full knowledge of what is stated in all the Vedic branches (śākhās). *Oṃ svādhyāyasya tathātvena hi samācāre 'dhikārācca oṃ.* (Sūtra 3.3.3) The meaning is as follows: The Vedic text is indeed to be studied in its entirety, because the traditional practice (samācāra) of those who know the Veda prescribes the study of all branches, and because the qualification (adhikāra) for Vedic study extends to the whole. Therefore, since the injunction to study one's own Veda (svādhyāya) implies the study of all its constituent parts, the same rules of application apply across all branches. Thus, the objection regarding the difference in attributes and consequences is neutralized by the fact that the entire Vedic corpus is subject to the same authoritative injunction.

Regarding *svādhyāya* (Vedic study), it refers to the injunction "The Veda is to be studied. This is because it prescribes study as something common to all. Regarding *samācāra* (traditional practice), it refers to the performance of all Vedic rites. Regarding *adhikāra* (qualification), it is because the qualification exists for everyone. Furthermore, by the word "hi" (for), there is the Smṛti text indicated: "The entire Veda is to be mastered. The meaning is that Brahman is to be known through the study of all the recensions (*śākhās*) even by each individual practitioner.
Om. And like water, that rule [is universal]. Om.

The word *ca* is used in the sense of emphasis (*avadhāraṇe*). In the phrase "that restriction" (*tanniyama*), there is a genitive tatpuruṣa compound followed by an avadhārya. "Like water" (*salilavat*) means like water. That restriction is as follows: just as for all waters, there is a restriction that they have the ocean as their sole receptacle only in dependence upon the absence of any obstruction, so too here, that restriction exists only in dependence upon the power of the Person (*puruṣa-śakti*). The meaning is that there is a restriction that Brahman must be known through meditation in the manner prescribed by all the Vedas. **Sūtra:** *Upasaṃhāro 'rthābhedād vidhiśeṣavatsamāne ca* (Oṃ). [This sūtra establishes] the synthesis [of details from different sources], because the purpose is not different, as in the case of supplementary injunctions, and because [the object] is the same. Oṃ.

"Like a subordinate element of an injunction" (*vidhiśeṣavat*) means like that which is enjoined by an injunction. Just as the twilight worship (*sandhyāvandana*) and other such rites must necessarily be performed because they are enjoined by an injunction, so too [is there no distinction] because of the non-difference of meaning. "Distinction" (*bheda*) means division; [the phrase] "because of the non-difference" means because of the non-distinction among the qualities such as bliss and the absence of defects such as being free from sin, which constitute the meaning of all the Vedas. "He does not divide them" is the sense. "Synthesis" (*upasaṃhāra*) means the synthesis consisting in the ascent of all qualities into a single cognition.

Because it is enjoined in the Bhāllaveya Śruti, "One [should be] worshipped," this must be performed. Furthermore, that [worship] applies only when the objects are similar and the scope is identical; it concerns only those qualities that are appropriate for Brahman and do not contradict its perfection. It does not concern inappropriate things such as weeping and the like, for if it were so, it would lead to misfortune—this is the meaning. *Sūtra:* "If it be argued that there is a difference because of the word 'and,' we say no, because there is no distinction. (Brahma-sūtra 3.3.6)

“Otherwise-ness” (*anyathātva*) means that what was stated—that there should be a collection of all qualities—becomes otherwise; its non-performance must necessarily be accepted. Why? Because of the scriptural statement (*śabda*): “One should meditate [on Brahman] as the Self alone” (*ātmetyevopāsīta*), which indicates a lack of such collection. If this is argued, we say no. Why? Because there is no specific authority (*aviśeṣāt*) to the effect that these qualities are not to be collected. For while there is an absence of specific authority regarding the non-collection, there is the existence of specific authority for the collection of all qualities without distinction. This is the meaning. Furthermore, the sense is that the particle *eva* in the phrase “as the Self alone” (*ātmetyeva*) serves to exclude non-connection (*ayogavyavacchedaka*). **Sūtra:** *Na vā prakaraṇabhedāt parovīyastvādivat.* (Or rather, no, because of the difference in context, as in the case of ‘being higher than the high,’ etc. **Commentary:** Or rather, there is no such rule of non-collection. Why? Because of the difference in context (*prakaraṇabheda*). Just as in the case of the qualities such as “being higher than the high” (*parovīyastva*) and so on, which belong to different meditations, so it is here. The word “or rather” (*na vā*) sets aside the previous position. The meaning is that the qualities mentioned in one context are not to be combined with those mentioned in another context, because they belong to distinct meditative sections. As in the case of the qualities like “being higher than the high,” which are not combined across different meditations, so it is here. Thus, the conclusion is that there is no mandatory collection of all qualities in every meditation.

As in the case of the attributes such as being "higher than the high" (*parovarīyastva*), there is no combination of all attributes; rather, only those qualities such as being higher than the high—which consist in being the unsurpassed supreme of all—as stated in the passage "He is this," are to be combined for the purpose of meditation. Similarly, a combination of all attributes need not be performed. Why? Because of the difference in context (*prakaraṇabheda*); that is, because of the difference in context between the section on the "Higher than the High" (*parovarīya*) and the section on Vaiśvānara. Otherwise, that [distinction] would not exist. [Objection: If it is argued that they are one because of the identity of name (*saṃjñā*), that has already been answered. However, that [identity of name] does indeed exist. (Sūtra 3.3.7)

Because, O Blessed One, by virtue of being the name of all sciences (*vidyā*), it consists in the description of their qualities. If it is argued that the qualities mentioned in all the sciences must be combined [here], the response to that objection is stated: "That is indeed desired there. This means that this was stated by the *Upasaṃhāra-sūtra*. This is not established merely by reasoning; rather, there is also scriptural authority for this point, namely the *Kauṇḍinya-śruti*: "Or these are names" (*nāma vā etā*). Indeed, such is the meaning. || 3 || The Section on Attainment (*Prāpty-adhikaraṇa*).
Oṃ, and because [the fruit] is attained, it is consistent; Oṃ.

The necessity of performing both the inclusion (*upasaṃhāra*) and the non-inclusion (*anupasaṃhāra*) is appropriate and logical. Why? Because they are established according to the distinction between individuals suited for each, and because no contradiction arises; such is the meaning.
|| 4 || The Section on the Non-difference of All.
Oṃ, because of the non-difference of all things, these others are also [included] Oṃ.

These [meditations]—beginning with that of Brahmā which brings together all qualities—are "elsewhere," meaning they are elsewhere than those meditations that do not bring them together. They result in a great fruit distinct from the fruits of those others; that is, they become partakers of that [great fruit]. Why? Because of the non-difference of all [qualities], meaning because of the meditation performed by bringing together the qualities declared in all the Vedas without distinction.
|| 5 || The Section on Bliss (Ānandādhikaraṇa).
Oṃ. Bliss and the other [attributes] belong to the Pradhāna. Oṃ.

Bliss and the others: bliss, knowledge, that which is denoted by the word "Being," and faultlessness—these four qualities, as well as lordship denoted by the word "Self," are to be meditated upon for the sake of liberation, the primary goal, by all those seeking release. This is the meaning. || 6 || The Section on Having Bliss as the Head.
Oṃ. [The opponent argues: "There is no attainment of the beloved head and so forth, for increase and decrease occur only where there is difference. Oṃ.

The qualities such as having pleasure as the head (*priya-śirastva*) and so forth, mentioned in the Śruti passage beginning with "Pleasure indeed is its head," are not attainable by all qualified aspirants (*adhikārin*); rather, they belong to only some. Why? Because there exists the *Vārāha-smṛti* which states that a distinction among them—namely, a difference in results or a gradation of fruits—is well-known, and not applicable to all. Furthermore, for the sake of establishing this difference in results upon such a distinction, increase and decrease—that is to say, growth and diminution—in the meditation must be admitted; therefore, [these qualities are not for all]. This is the meaning.
|| 7 || The Section on Others ||
Oṃ. But [the other] is [a designation] because of the commonality of its meaning. Oṃ.

The word *tu* has the sense of *eva* (only/indeed). Because of the commonality of their purpose (*arthasāmānyāt*), the ablative case is used on account of the elision of the suffix *-lyap*. With reference to the equality of the fruits obtained by each respective [meditation], the meaning is that all other qualities—the "intermediate" (*madhyama*) ones, which are distinct from all others—are to be combined by the gods and others. || 8 || End of the section on meditation (*ādhyānādhikaraṇam*).
Oṃ. [The meditation] is for the sake of higher contemplation, because there is no other purpose. Oṃ.

The mention of qualities associated with heaven (*svarga*) in the Vedas and their subsequent withdrawal (*upasaṃhāra*) are intended for meditation—that is, for the purpose of meditating upon perfect knowledge. This is established because there is no other purpose; the meaning is that there is no purpose for the mention of qualities and their withdrawal apart from meditation.
Om. And because of the word "Self" (*ātman*). Om.

In the passage, “One should meditate [on him] as the Self” (*ātmetyevopāsīta*), the word “Self” (*ātman*) is primarily intended to denote the state of being the Self (*bhāvapradhāna*) and is used with emphasis. The word “Self” (*ātma-śabda*) is the term that enjoins meditation on the mere state of being the Self; it is the phrase “one should meditate [on him] as the Self. Therefore, the meaning is that because this word enjoins meditation on the state of being the Self while excluding other qualities, the non-combination (*anupasaṃhāra*) [of these qualities with others] is established. || 9 || [End of] the Section on the Comprehension of the Self (*Ātmagṛhītyadhikaraṇa*).
Oṃ. The Self is grasped [as the object of knowledge], as in other cases, because of what follows. Oṃ.

Because, as in other cases, just as in the passage "Truth, Knowledge," and so forth, the qualities such as Truth and the rest are understood through their respective words, so too in the sentence "The Self alone," the grasping of all four qualities is possible by means of the word "Self. Why? Because of what follows, namely the subsequent statement, "For here these [qualities are present]. Therefore, there is no contradiction with that [teaching], since the meditation on the four qualities is indeed taught; this is the meaning. || 10 || The Section on Conjunction (Anvaya-adhikaraṇa).
If it be argued that [the self exists] because of its persistence through transmigration, we reply: it may be so, because of the restrictive definition. Oṃ.

[Objection: Is it not improper to claim that the statement "Or rather, the Self" lacks the status of a concluding summary? Why? Because of the connection (*anvaya*); that is to say, because all qualities are connected with the word "Self," and thus that word conveys them. If this were the case, then what has been stated by the opponent would indeed be so. Nevertheless, there is no inconsistency. Why? Because of the restriction (*avadhāraṇa*). This is because of the restriction: "The Self alone. Nor is there a lack of determination; for the meaning is that the word "Self" denotes all qualities only in relation to Brahman and the like, and not in relation to others—thus, a definitive conclusion is possible. || 11 || [End of] The Section on the Effect (*kāryādhikaraṇam*).
Oṃ. [The Self] is beyond [the body], because it explains the effects; Oṃ.

Because of the description of the effect, and because liberation as the body of meditation is stated to be non-worldly; the meaning is that a collection of qualities never before known—that is, non-worldly—is to be meditated upon. || 12 || This is a coordinate construction (samānādhikaraṇa).
Oṃ, it is indeed the same because there is no difference; Oṃ.

And thus, even so: although the qualities of Brahman are supramundane (*alaukika*), the synthesis (*upasaṃhāra*) of speech applies only to those objects that possess corresponding qualities, and not to actions that lack such correspondence. However, in that case, because there is no difference—taking non-difference into account—the occasional actions such as the "three-striding" (*trivikrama*) and so forth may be included within the eternal strides and similar acts of the same genus; this is the meaning. *Oṃ. On account of the connection, it is the same elsewhere too. Oṃ.*

But for Hiraṇyagarbha, even in other specific actions such as the three strides (*trivikrama*) and so forth, the withdrawal of all [powers] is thus appropriate. Why? Because of the connection of these actions with Brahman; the meaning is that this is due to their eternal nature through a relationship consisting of identity (*tādātmya*).
|| 13 || The Ninth Topic of Discussion ||
Oṃ, or rather not, because there is a distinction; Oṃ.

It is not accepted that by the word "Self" (ātman) occurring in the sentence, all qualities are grasped. Why? Because of the distinction; the meaning is that, depending on the specific qualification of the seeker, that word denotes only those qualities for which he is fit. Oṃ, and scripture also shows this. Oṃ.
The meaning is that the *Śruti* passage from the Bhāllaveyas, "all," establishes the point stated by [the author] himself.
|| 14 || The Section on Accumulation (*Sambhṛtyadhikaraṇa*).
Oṃ! Furthermore, from this [point], there is the accumulation, the manifestation, and the pervasion; Oṃ!

By the word "ādi" (and so forth), the negative particle (*nañ*) is drawn back [from the previous sūtra]. The word "ca" (and) has the sense of "only" (*eva*). "Accumulation and pervasion" (*sambhṛti-dyuvyāptī*) mean perfect filling and luminous pervasion. These do not apply to every object of meditation; rather, they apply only to the meditations on deities and the like. Why? Because of this very reason—that there exists a specific distinction in the fitness of the qualified aspirant. || 15 || End of the Section on the Person (*puruṣādhikaraṇam*).
Oṃ. Also because [the details] of the other [Vedas] are not mentioned in the Puruṣa-vidyā, Oṃ.

Even in the case of the *puruṣavidyā*, although it is asserted to be the highest of all sciences, since it is taught as such only for certain [qualities] and because other qualities not mentioned therein are not enumerated, the meaning is that the collection of qualities from all sciences must indeed be performed. || 16 || End of the section on piercing (*vedhādhikaraṇa*).
Oṃ. [This is established] because of the difference in meaning starting with "piercing" (vedha), Oṃ.

Because of the difference in purpose—the fruit of meditations such as "piercing" (*vedha*) and so forth being distinct from the fruit appropriate for ascetics and others, such as non-violence (*ahiṃsā*) and so forth—the meaning is that practices like piercing, which are mentioned in the *Bṛhattantra* as "pierce," "penetrate," and "cut," are not to be practiced by all worshippers. || 17 || [This concludes] the Section on Omission (*Hānyadhikaraṇa*).

Oṃ. But [the word "going"] refers to the act of departing, because it is subordinate to the word for "approaching," as in the cases of the *kuśa* grass, the meters, the hymns, and the chanting; this has been stated [in the Sūtra]. Oṃ.

The word *tu* (but) serves as a restriction. Because in the case of abandonment—that is, in liberation, which consists of the abandonment of bondage—it has been stated in the scripture that for those who are liberated, there is meditation [on the Self] in the words, "This is the Sāman. Therefore, even in liberation, their meditation must certainly exist. Yet, even that is not by way of an injunction, but rather like the *kuśa*-grass, the meters, the hymns of praise, and the chanting; it is just as when twice-born men who are bound to the obligatory *brahmayajña* study both names at will, even after the obligatory twilight worship (*sandhyopāsana*), using *kuśa*-grass and according to the meters, as in the case of hymns of praise and chanting.

Likewise, [the soul proceeds] by its own will alone, not by injunction. Why? Because of the subordinate status of the word "attainment" (*upāyana*). The meaning is that "attainment" refers to liberation (*mokṣa*), since the injunctions for meditation are supplementary to the statements concerning liberation. And thus, if the injunctions for meditation are intended for the sake of liberation, how could they enjoin those [meditations] even in that [state]? **Sūtra:** *Oṃ sāmparāye tartavyābhāvāttathā hyanye oṃ.* **Commentary:** At the time of departing [from the body], [the soul proceeds] by its own will, because there is nothing further to be crossed over; for so say others. The meaning is as follows: When the soul departs from the body at the time of death, it proceeds according to its own desire, not under the compulsion of scriptural injunction. Why? Because the term "attainment" (*upāyana*)—referring to the attainment of the state of liberation—is subordinate to the statements regarding liberation. That is to say, the injunctions for meditation are supplementary to the passages concerning liberation. Consequently, since these injunctions for meditation are directed toward the goal of liberation, how could they possibly enjoin such meditations with respect to the state of liberation itself? **Sūtra:** *Oṃ sāmparāye tartavyābhāvāttathā hyanye oṃ.* At the time of departure (*sāmparāye*), the soul proceeds by its own will, because there remains nothing further to be crossed over (*tartavyābhāvāt*). For other teachers maintain this view. This is because once the soul has reached the state of liberation, there is no longer any obstacle or distance to be traversed. Therefore, the movement of the soul at that stage is spontaneous, not governed by ritual injunctions. Thus, the conclusion is that the soul departs according to its own volition.

"In the hereafter" means in liberation (*mokṣa*). It must be accepted that meditation (*upāsana*) occurs by one's own will, and not for the purpose of avoiding what is undesirable. Why? Because there is nothing to be crossed over; for those who are liberated, there is simply no undesirable thing to be avoided. And why is that? Because other followers of different *śākhās* recite the scriptural text: "For he has crossed over. This is the meaning. || 18 || [End of] the Section on the Metres (*chandādhikaraṇa*).
By choice, because there is no contradiction between the two; Oṃ.

The liberated ones perform actions solely according to their own will (*chandataḥ*), following their own desire, and not according to scriptural injunction (*vidhi*). Why? Because there is no conflict between both; that is to say, because there is an absence of the bond of injunction and the sin of transgression regarding both the performance and non-performance of action. *Oṃ. The movement [of the soul] has the nature of free will, for it is in both ways; otherwise, there would be contradiction.* *Oṃ.*

The word *hi* indicates the reason. For in both cases, it is precisely because of the absence of bondage (*bandha*) and transgression (*pratyavāya*) that liberation (*gati*) constitutes the goal of human endeavor (*puruṣārthatva*). Otherwise, if bondage and transgression were present in liberation, there would be a contradiction regarding liberation; the meaning is that there would be a contradiction in the form of liberation being non-teleological (*apuruṣārthatva*), as it would be equivalent to worldly existence (*saṃsāra*). **Sūtra:** *Upapannaḥ tallakṣaṇārthopalabdher lokavat* (It is logical, because an object characterized by those [qualities] is perceived, as in the world). **Commentary:** It is logical that the Self possesses the qualities of omniscience and omnipotence, because objects characterized by such qualities are indeed perceived, just as in the world. Just as in the world we perceive that a person who possesses the knowledge and power to build a palace actually builds one, so too the Lord, possessing the characteristics of omniscience and omnipotence, creates the universe. Thus, the attributes of the Lord are established as real. The doubt raised was whether these attributes are merely figurative or real; this sūtra establishes them as real. The term "logical" (*upapannaḥ*) implies that the Lord’s possession of these attributes is not only possible but necessary for His creative activity. The phrase "as in the world" (*lokavat*) provides an analogy: just as in the world we observe that a king who has the power and knowledge to rule actually rules, so the Lord’s attributes are real. Therefore, the Lord is endowed with the characteristics of omniscience and omnipotence. This concludes the section on the Lord's attributes. *Note: The provided text contains the commentary on the first part of the sūtra, explaining the necessity of liberation being free from bondage and transgression, followed by the full sūtra and its commentary establishing the reality of the Lord's attributes.*

Just as in the world there is no rule for the performance of the Viṣṇukramaṇa rite—which is an auxiliary of the sacrifice—that must be carried out immediately after the completion of the sacrifice, but rather it is performed only at certain times; so too, it is logical and appropriate that liberated souls perform actions only occasionally, and not otherwise. Why is this so? Because of the perception of the goal characterized by that [liberation]; that is to say, because liberation, which is achieved through action in a traditional sequence, is perceived as having been attained. || 19 || The Section on Non-Restriction (Aniyamādhikaraṇa).
Om. There is no restriction for all [aspirants], because there is no contradiction with scripture and inference. Om.

There is no fixed rule (*aniyama*); that is, it is known that among those possessing direct knowledge (*aparokṣajñānin*), for some there is liberation and for others there is not—such a lack of settled distinction is understood. Why? Because liberation occurs for all of them; because there is no contradiction, as there is no evidence to the contrary. Furthermore, it is known from both scripture and inference: from the scriptural statement, "No one [is excluded]" (*na kaścit*) [from Kauṇḍinya], and from the inference based thereon. This concludes the section.
Oṃ. Those who hold office remain in their positions for as long as their term of authority lasts. Oṃ.

The meaning is that for those who hold offices—such as Brahmā and others—who are habituated to meditation according to their fitness, there is a state of abiding in liberation precisely in accordance with their respective offices. For those so abiding, the fruit of liberation occurs according to the very gradations of their meditative practice.

*Om. But there is no contradiction regarding the cognitions of the Imperishable (akṣara), because of the commonality and the presence of that [state], as in the case of the Aupasadā; this has been stated.* *Om.*

The word *tu* (but) has the sense of *api* (also). Regarding those who possess knowledge of the syllable (*akṣaradhiyaḥ*), that is, those who know Brahman: even in the case of inequality [of status], there is no contradiction; that is, no conflict exists. Why? Because they possess the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmadhītvāt*). Furthermore, because of the general rule and the presence of that [knowledge] in all, there is an absence of defect in everyone, and because there is a state of being helpful from the superior to the inferior. How so? Like the *aupasada* [sacrifice], and like a good disciple. Moreover, that which was stated—that there is no contradiction despite inequality—is expressed in the *Tura-śruti* by the word "various" (*nānā*); therefore, for this reason also, there is no contradiction. This concludes the section on the "Recollection of this much" (*iyadāmananādhikaraṇa*).
Oṃ. [The Self is Brahman] because of the repeated consideration of this much. Oṃ.
The gradation of eligibility extends only as far as the vital breath (*prāṇa*). Why? Because of the scriptural statement:

"The vital breath indeed [is the self]" (Kauṇṭharavya Śruti). This is the meaning. [Sūtra: "If it be argued that [the gradation] exists within [the body], like the aggregate of elements, we say: that has already been answered. [Sūtra: Oṃ. "That has already been stated. Oṃ.

[Objection: "Just as in the case of a group of living beings (*bhūtagrāma*), where among a collection of vital breaths (*prāṇa*) and so forth, one is seen to be superior to another; likewise, since there is no mention of Śrī or the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) in between, [the individual soul] must be superior even to the vital breath. [Reply: This is not so; such is the remainder [of the argument]. For that which was stated there—namely, that in the absence of anyone superior to the vital breath—"no" (*na hi*)—is the authoritative proof (*pramāṇa*) cited [by Kauṇṭharavya]. Therefore is the meaning. [Objection: "If it were otherwise, the distinction [between the stages] would be untenable. [Reply: This is not so, because it is like the instruction [regarding the stages of meditation]. (Oṃ. *Note: The "Oṃ" at the end marks the conclusion of this specific scriptural citation or section.*

If it be argued that otherwise—given the absence of anything superior even to *prāṇa*—the distinction between *prāṇa* and the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) would be untenable, we say: no. Why? Because it is accepted as it is taught in scripture (*upadeśavat*). Therefore, the aforementioned defect does not apply. This is the meaning. || 22 || The Section on Exchange (*vyatihārādhikaraṇam*).
Oṃ. There is an exchange [of attributes], for they distinguish [the two] as in other cases. Oṃ.

The exchange (*vyatihāra*)—the supplying of questions and answers—should be performed immediately after the section on Prāṇa and before the section on Viṣṇu. Why? Because, just as those who speak of Prāṇa begin with names such as Speech (*vāk*) and so forth, the Chandogas who speak of Viṣṇu under the name Satya distinguish [themselves] from them by means of the word "but" (*tu*) in the phrase "But he indeed... (*eṣa tu vā*); that is the meaning.
Thus ends the section on Satya (*satyādhikaraṇa*). || 23 ||
Oṃ, for she alone is indeed Truth and the rest; Oṃ.

For indeed, from "truth" (satya) up to the "I-self" (aham-ātman), these are the categories [of the self]. That very same one is the supreme deity called Īśvara. Therefore, there are not many [deities] superior to Prāṇa; rather, the meaning is that there are only Śrī and Dhīśa.
|| 24 || The Section on Desire (Kāmādhikaraṇa).
Oṃ! [The fruit arises] from desire, and in other cases from the sense-bases and so forth; Oṃ!

Lakṣmī, while remaining there in the presence of the Blessed One, also manifests incarnations elsewhere, such as upon the earth and so forth, solely by desire—that is, by the will of the Lord. Why? From the scriptural passages beginning with "having all as her abode," which establish her omnipresence; this is the meaning.
"Om, there is no omission [of the rites] because of respect, Om."

"Out of reverence" means due to an excellence of unconditional devotion toward the Blessed One. "There is no loss of prosperity" means that there is no absence of the practice of worshiping the Blessed One.
"Om, because of its presence, on account of the statement regarding it, Om."

It is logical that Śrī is eternally liberated. Why? Because of her *upasthiti*—her constant presence in the vicinity of Hari. Furthermore, Śrī’s state of being eternally in his proximity is known from the statement of that [scripture]: "These two" (from the Gaupavana Śruti), which declares their eternal relationship. This is the meaning. || 25 || [End of] the Section on Determination (*nirdhāraṇādhikaraṇa*).
Oṃ. There is a restrictive rule for the purpose of determining that [object], and its fruit is seen in that very object. Oṃ.

Because the restriction for the purpose of determining that [Brahman] consists of the ascertainment of the meaning of the Vedas and the restriction regarding the meaning of the Vedas; this is the fruit of hearing (*śravaṇa*) and reflection (*manana*). [The realization] resulting from meditation (*dhyāna*) arises from the vision of Brahman (*brahmadarśana*), which is indeed distinct and separate from it. Therefore, the meaning is that the vision of Brahman does not arise through hearing and the other [means]. Nevertheless, hearing and reflection are not useless. Why? Because there is "non-obstruction," meaning the removal of the obstacles to the vision of Brahman.

The ascertainment of that [Self] is the fruit of hearing (*śravaṇa*) and reflection (*manana*) by way of its restriction. Therefore, although realization (*dṛṣṭi*) is to be accomplished through meditation (*dhyāna*), it becomes something to be accomplished through hearing and so forth by way of the removal of obstacles. The meaning is that for that purpose, hearing and the rest must indeed be performed. By the word "hi," the Śruti passage "The Self, verily, O Maitreyī... is indicated. || 26 || The Section on Bestowal (*pradānādhikaraṇa*).
Oṃ, for it has been stated that this is indeed like a gift; Oṃ.

Just like a gift, the means for attaining knowledge—such as hearing [the scriptures] and so forth—must be performed properly, preceded by devotion, and in accordance with the teacher’s instruction; it is not sufficient merely to do so alone. Why? Because it has been stated that such knowledge is dependent upon the grace of the teacher. This is the meaning of the scriptural statement, "He who has a teacher" (*ācāryavān*).
|| 27 || [End of] the Section on the Abundance of Indicative Marks (*liṅgabhūyastvādhikaraṇa*).
Om. Because of the abundance of indicatory marks; for that is more powerful. That also, Om.

That [attainment] consists merely of the gift preceded by the grace of the Guru; it is *balīyaḥ*, meaning exceedingly powerful. Why? Because of the abundance of indicative marks (*liṅga-bhūyastvāt*). From the words of Satyakāma—who, despite possessing Vedic learning, spoke regarding those who are Wind, Fire, and Varuṇa in the forms of the Bull, the Swan, and the Water-Crow—there is seen an abundance of indicative marks consisting of the gift from the Guru and so forth. Nevertheless, even that [study and hearing] must be performed. Why? Because of the scriptural statement, "He is to be heard" (*śrotavyaḥ*); this is the meaning. The word *hi* indicates the Śruti.
[This concludes] the Section on the Alternative View (*Pūrvavikalpādhikaraṇam*).
Oṃ. The prior conceptualization [of the self] must exist because of the context, just as in the case of ritual action and mental activity. Oṃ.

As in the case of ritual action (*kriyā*) and mental action (*mānasa*), so too in meditation (*dhyāna*) which consists of mental action, there may be a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*). Just as there is a prior conceptual construction regarding the teacher previously attained, there may subsequently arise a conceptual construction concerning the teacher newly attained—namely, the doubt as to whether he is to be accepted or not. However, this is not a mandatory injunction (*vidhi*) that he must necessarily be accepted. Why? Because, having been drawn from the context, the sense is that acceptance of the teacher depends upon his grace (*anugraha*). *Oṃ* and because of the extended application (*atideśa*). *Oṃ*.

Because the previous teacher himself extends [the rule] for the acceptance of a teacher who is equal to or superior to oneself; since it is extended by the Pauṣyāyaṇa Śruti with the words "just as," the subsequent acceptance is indeed proper—this is the meaning. || 29 || The Section on Knowledge (Vidyādhikaraṇa).
Om. But knowledge alone [is the means], because of the definitive determination; Om.

Because of the definitive statement, "There is no other path," which excludes all else, it is certain that knowledge alone is the means to liberation; the meaning is that knowledge itself is the means to liberation, and not ritual action (*karman*) or the like. The word "tu" (but/only) serves to highlight the superior authority of the Śruti. Oṃ, and because it is seen [in scripture], Oṃ.

Liberation does not result from the knowledge of the nature of the Self as something merely beyond the senses; rather, it results also from "darśana," that is, from the direct realization of Brahman. Therefore, the meaning is that meditation is not purposeless. || 30 || [The Section on Revelation] (Śruty-adhikaraṇam)
Om. And because of the greater authority of direct Vedic statement and so forth, there is no sublation. Om.

There is no contradiction with the Smṛti stating that liberation is achieved by karma alone when liberation is actually accomplished through knowledge; why? Because the Śruti and other sources are more authoritative. The meaning is that since the Śruti, indicative marks (*liṅga*), and so forth—such as the passage beginning "Having known thus"—are extremely powerful in establishing that knowledge is the means to liberation, the word *eva* (alone) found in the Smṛti can be interpreted as having the sense of excluding non-connection (*ayogavyavaccheda*). And the word *ca* (and) is used to indicate this. || 31 || [End of] Anubandhādhikaraṇa.
Oṃ, [this is] from the *Anubandha* and other [works]. Oṃ.

The vision of Brahman does not arise through mere hearing and so forth, nor even by the powerful grace of a guru; rather, it arises from intense devotion to the guru—termed "anubandha"—as well as from tranquility (śama) and other such qualities. This is the meaning. || 32 || End of the section on the difference in knowledge (Prajñāntarādhikaraṇa).
Oṃ. It has been stated that [the soul] is like the distinctness of cognitions; Oṃ.

*Prajñāntaram* means a distinction in wisdom; that is to say, *dhyāna*. Like its diversity—that is, like its having many varieties—so too, according to that [diversity], the vision of Brahman (*brahmadṛṣṭi*) is also of many kinds and is not of a single form for all. Furthermore, it has been stated: the meaning is that the manifold nature of that vision is also declared in the Śruti, namely in the passage beginning with "the internal visions" (*antardṛṣṭayaḥ*).
|| 33 || It is not a case of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānyādhikaraṇya*).
Oṃ. Even from perception based on generality, there is no falling into the world, just as in the case of death; Oṃ.

Just as there is no liberation immediately after death, but only after the specific final death, so too here, although the forms of the Lord are identical, liberation does not occur for all upon the perception of those forms—that is, upon the direct knowledge of the common form due to the similarity with the Lord's vision—but rather only from the sight of one’s own respective reflection. And it is not the case that such a general perception [is sufficient].

[The objection is that there is] fruitlessness [of meditation on the heart-lotus], because it is a means for attaining worlds such as Maharloka. And by this much alone, its being a cause of liberation does not follow; for it is a means for attaining worlds such as Maharloka. Indeed, because "attainment of worlds" (*lokāpatti*) is merely the reaching of a world and not liberation—this is the meaning of "therefore. By the word "hi" (indeed), the well-known authority of the *Nārāyaṇatantra* beginning with "through general vision," etc., is indicated.
|| 34 || [End of] the subsequent section.
Oṃ. And by the subsequent [scriptural passage], the nature of the word is such; however, because of its abundance, there is a connection. Oṃ.

Even though [the realization of Brahman] is by the Supreme alone—that is, by the Supreme Self alone—nevertheless, because of the scriptural statement, "Devotion alone leads him" (*Māṭhara*), it is appropriate that devotion possesses such a nature as being the cause of the realization of Brahman through its own independence, just like the Supreme Self. Why? The reason must be supplied: "because of its being the cause in [the process of] realization and so forth. Alternatively, the meaning is that because of the scriptural statement, "Devotion belongs to the word by means of the Supreme, which is the denoted object," its possessing such a nature is logical.

If one asks, "In that case, how is it said that devotion (bhakti) is the 'concomitant' (anubandha) by means of the statement [in the scripture], even though other means exist?"—it is for this reason that it is stated: "Because of its abundance" (bhūyastvāt). This means: because of the abundance—that is, the preeminence—of that [devotion] among the means. The sense is that, with reference to that, devotion is specifically designated as the concomitant. || 35 || [This concludes] the section on the single topic.
Oṃ. [The self is one] because it exists in the body. Oṃ.

The meaning of the terms "part" (aṃśa) and "possessor of parts" (aṃśin) is one and the same. There is indeed identity between the part and the possessor of parts. Why? Because of the existence of the part—such as Arjuna and others—within the body of the possessor of parts—the Self—namely Indra and others, in that body produced by karma; the meaning is: because of its presence through the state of identifying with it. *Oṃ. [The soul's] distinction [from the Lord] is due to its being conditioned by the states of that [body], but not [an absolute difference], just like perception.* *Oṃ*.

Just as there is a mutual distinction between cognition, pleasure, and so forth, [so too is there a distinction] because the part experiences the fruit produced by the meditation (upāsanā) designated as "the state of being made into parts" (aṃśikṛtabhāva). Otherwise, that would not be possible; this is the meaning. || 36 || The Section on Those Bound to the Limbs (Aṅgāvabaddhādhikaraṇa).
Oṃ, for indeed, the [limbs] are bound to the body, not to the branches of each Veda; Oṃ.

The word *tu* (but) indicates a distinction. "Bound to the limbs" (*aṅgāvabaddhāḥ*) means those who reside upon the limbs of Hari. Although these deities are also worshipped by the gods as being part of His retinue, there is a distinction in their withdrawal (*upasaṃhāra*). What is that distinction? It means that among the hosts of qualities bound to the limbs of Brahmā and the other deities, which are described in every branch (*śākhā*) of all the Vedas for each respective Veda, none of that is to be withdrawn into Rudra and the others; rather, only what is appropriate [to them] is to be so. By the word *hi* (for), the traditional authority of the *Brahmatarka*—namely, "or because of equality"—is indicated. **Sūtra:** *Oṃ, mantrādivad vā 'virodhaḥ, Oṃ.* (Or, like the case of the mantras and so forth, there is no contradiction.)

The meaning is that, as in the case of mantras and so forth—just as there is no contradiction in mantras and vidyās addressed to lower deities such as Agni having the capacity to denote higher deities such as Brahmā—likewise, even when the qualities of lower [deities] are combined with higher ones, it is accepted that there is no contradiction.
This concludes the section on "Various Words" (Nānāśabdādhikaraṇa).
Oṃ. [The Self is one] because of the diversity of various sounds and so forth; Oṃ.

Because, as stated in the *Kamaṭha-śruti* ("Just as by a king..."), it is taught that action, which has liberation as its superior fruit, serves as a cooperative factor (*sahakārin*) for knowledge; such is the meaning.
|| 5 || End of the Section on the Two-fold Characteristics (*Ubhayaliṅgādhikaraṇa*).
Oṃ. But in every way, they alone [are the cause], because of both kinds of scriptural evidence. Oṃ.

In every way, even when there is a perfection of various means such as place, time, and the instruction of a teacher, only those who are fit for knowledge attain that knowledge; the unfit do not. Why? Because of the evidence of both. That is to say, because of the indicative sign consisting in the attainment of correct and contrary knowledge respectively by both—the fit and the unfit—namely Indra and Virocana, despite the equality of their instruction by Viriñca. Oṃ, and it shows non-overpowering. Oṃ.

Why is this so? Because of the scriptural statement: "Only the divine [nature]," and so forth. It does not merely show the nature of the fit and the unfit; rather, it shows—that is, establishes—both non-overpowering and overpowering by the suppression of one's own nature. Therefore, the meaning is that those who are unfit do not attain knowledge.
Oṃ. And also because of the observation of that in the intermediate state, Oṃ.

The word *ca* (and) is used for emphasis; the word *tu* (but) is for the sake of distinction. "In between" (*antarā*) means in the interval between right knowledge (*samyag-jñāna*) and contrary knowledge (*viparīta-jñāna*). For those who abide therein—even for the eternally transmigrating beings (*nitya-saṃsārin*) whose nature is mixed—there is indeed no suppression [of the contrary]. Why? Because it is observed in them (*tad-dṛṣṭeḥ*); the meaning is that this aforementioned [mixture] is seen (*dṛṣṭi*) in them precisely in that state of mixed knowledge. **Om. It is also recorded in Smṛti. Om.**

In the *Gītā*, [the Lord] states that His own nature is not overcome by Kṛṣṇa and others; furthermore, it is recorded in the *Skanda Purāṇa* that "Asuras" [do not overcome Him]. Therefore, the meaning is that the natures of gods, Dānavas, and humans do not overcome Him.
Om, special favor! Om.

The word *ca* (and) serves to aggregate the logical reasons. For, by the scriptural text "He hears and sees," it is shown—that is, established—that the Supreme Lord bestows special grace upon the gods. Therefore, the meaning is that perfect knowledge and its fruit belong to the gods alone, and not to others. *Sūtra*: "But therefore the other [attains] what is inferior, and because of the indicative mark. (Oṃ).

The word *tu* (but) is used for emphasis. Therefore, because the portion belonging to the Asuras is never less than the portion belonging to the Devas, the other [portion]—namely, the host of Asuras alone—is greater (*jyāyaḥ*) or more numerous than the portion of the Devas. Why? From the inferential mark (*liṅga*) consisting of the otherwise inexplicable statement prohibiting entry into a crowd of people, namely: "Therefore, one should not go among the crowd" (*tasmān na janatām iyāt*). And the meaning is that this is also supported by the scriptural text indicated by the word *ca*, namely: "From that, he becomes smaller" (*tataḥ kanīyasā*). **Sūtra:** But for one who has become such [a state], there is the attainment of that [state]; so Jaimini also thinks, on account of the restrictive rule, the absence of that form, and so forth. (Oṃ) **Translation of the Sūtra:** However, for one who has attained such a state [of being a Deva or an Asura], there is the persistence of that very nature; thus Jaimini also maintains, based on the restrictive rule regarding the absence of the former form and other reasons. (Oṃ)

But for one who has become that—that is, for one who has indeed become a deity—the state of being that (tadbhāvaḥ) is the state of being a deity; likewise, for an asura, it is the state of being an asura. This is established even for the teacher Jaimini. Why? Because of the restrictive rules, the absence of that form, and the scriptural statement indicated by the word "ca" (and), namely: "They are not asuras," which implies the scriptural teaching that "whoever has what form [remains] that form," meaning there is no absence of the form of another for one who is not of that form. "Absence" (abhāvaḥ) means non-existence (abhūtiḥ). This refers to the scriptural statement regarding gods and asuras: "Their [is] existence" (te bhūtiḥ), where the word *bhāva* signifies existence. || 6 || [End of] the Section on Those Holding Office.
Oṃ. Nor is there [a loss of status] even for one holding an office, because of the inference of falling [from grace] and because that [office] is incompatible [with such a state]. Oṃ.

The word *ca* (and) indicates another procedural requirement (*itikartavyatā*), namely, the avoidance of improper desire by those seeking knowledge. The word *api* (also) indicates that even the status of a presiding deity (*adhikārika*)—let alone the divine sovereignty of the Lord—is not to be desired by others. Why? Because of the inference of falling; for it is established by Smṛti reasoning that falling results from desiring what is unfit. Therefore, because of that impossibility—the meaning being that it is improper to act upon an improper desire—it is said:
"Some say 'even preceded by *upa*,' as in the case of the pacification of [evil] intent; so it was stated. (Oṃ).

"Just as there is the pacification of existence, so too is there the pacification of the mind within existence; those for whom this is the final goal (niṣṭhā) are the seers who have attained the pacification of existence (bhāvaśamanā ṛṣayaḥ). That state is not even to be desired—how much less so the state of gods and others? This is indicated by the word "api" (even). Thus some followers of the Vedic branches (śākhinaḥ) believe. Why? Because for those seeking knowledge, it is said "just as" in the *Indradyumna-śruti*. That which was stated [in the previous Sūtra] is stated here as well; such is the meaning. *Sūtra*: "But outside [the village], in both ways, according to Smṛti and custom. (Oṃ bahistūbhayathāpi smṛterācārācca Oṃ)

"Outside" means other than the states of being a deity and so forth. "In knowledge" refers to the object of devotion and the like. In both cases—whether there is a desire [for results] or no desire—there is no fault. Why? Because of the traditional teaching (smṛti) that "he is a divine sage" and because of established practice; the meaning is that this is also due to scriptural words that enjoin auspicious conduct.
|| 7 || The Section on the Declaration of Fruits.
Oṃ. Ātreya [maintains] that [the fruit belongs] to the master, because of the scriptural declaration of the fruit. Oṃ.

The singular number in the word *svāminaḥ* ("of the master") is used because the collective group is intended. Thus, the fruit of knowledge belongs only to the masters, the gods, and not to the subjects (*prajā*). Why? Because they alone possess ownership of knowledge, as indicated by the passage "whatever [there is]" (*yadu kiñca*), and because the scripture declares the fruit for them alone; such is the view of the teacher Ātreya.
"Om, the clarified butter is yours," says Auḍulomi, for that [butter] is indeed prepared for them. Om.

For this reason—because knowledge is produced through the medium of the subjects for the sake of the king by the gods—he is "to be served" (*ārtvijyam*), meaning he is like one who is to be served by officiating priests (*ṛtvij*). The meaning is that the venerable Ācārya Auḍulomi considers that just as there is a fruit of the sacrifice for the officiating priests, so too there is a fruit consisting of limited knowledge for the subjects.
Om. There is an injunction for an auxiliary factor in the alternative view; the third [case] belongs to one who possesses that [auxiliary], just as in the case of the beginning of an injunction. Om.

[This applies] to the king who possesses subjects and to the teacher who possesses disciples. "Like the injunction and so forth" means like the injunction and its fruit. Just as there is an injunction and a fruit regarding the protection [of subjects] and the exposition [of knowledge] for the sake of the subjects and disciples respectively, through their cooperation with the king and the teacher—wherein the injunction and fruit primarily belong to those two alone—so too, in the case of bestowing the knowledge ordained for oneself, there is an injunction for the subjects to provide another form of assistance, acting as a further auxiliary in the form of being favored by the gods. "By way of a side" (pakṣeṇa) means by way of being an alternative position. "The third" refers to the third in relation to the positions of Ātreya and Auḍulomi; the meaning is that this alone is the position of Bādarāyaṇa.
|| 8 || The Section on the State of Being Entirety (Kṛtsnabhāvādhikaraṇa)
Oṃ. But because of the totality of its nature, there is a withdrawal [of the path] for the householder. Oṃ.

Since the Śruti statement, "In the family," concludes by declaring that the fruit of liberation belongs specifically to the householder (gṛhin), the gṛhastha, on account of his complete state—that is, in comparison to the gods who possess the full duties of a householder—and because there is no contradiction with the Śruti, the meaning is that the ascetic alone is the highest among those in all stages of life (āśrama). Om. As with the vow of silence (mauna), so too for others, because of the teaching [of their duties]. Om.

Just as silence is [a duty] for the ascetic, so too are the duties of the other stages of life. This is because of the teaching in the *Kauṇṭharavya* Śruti, which states, "The gods themselves are celibate students. The meaning is that the gods possess superiority over those belonging to all the stages of life.
|| 9 || Section on Concomitance (*anvayādhikaraṇa*).
Oṃ. Because it follows from the fact that [the self] does not manifest itself. Oṃ.

The teacher, without manifesting [his learning] in assemblies and the like—that is, without displaying it—should impart knowledge to his disciples. Why? Because of the consequence (*anvaya*); that is to say, because of the undesirable contingency (*atiprasaṅga*) that even those who are unfit would obtain knowledge.
|| 10 || The section concerning this-worldly results (*aihikādhikaraṇa*).
Om. That which pertains to this life [occurs] when there is no obstacle to what has been commenced, because that is observed. Om.

In the absence of obstacles—whether to what has not yet begun, to what is currently beginning, or to what is expressed by the word "begun"—direct knowledge (*aparokṣajñāna*) resulting from hearing and other means arises in that very life; however, if there is an obstacle, it arises in another birth. Why? Because such is seen in scripture; the meaning is that this is established as such in the *Śauparṇa* Śruti passage beginning with "having heard. || 11 || This concludes the section on the fruit of liberation (*muktiphalādhikaraṇa*).
Oṃ. Thus, there is no restriction regarding the fruits of liberation, because that state is definitively established; because that state is definitively established. Oṃ.

Thus, just as there is no fixed rule regarding knowledge, so too there is no fixed rule regarding the fruit of liberation. Even with respect to the fruit called liberation, there is no rule that for the knower, liberation occurs immediately after the fall of that body. Rather, if *prārabdha* karma is absent, liberation occurs immediately after the fall of that body; but if *prārabdha* is present, liberation occurs at the conclusion of that body’s life. To the question, "Why is this postulated? it is said: "In that [scriptural passage]," namely, in the Śruti text "He who is established in Brahman" (*brahmasaṃsthaḥ*), which refers to one who abides in that Brahman.

"Of those who know that" means up to that point. "Because of the determination" means because of the determination of the fruit of liberation, namely, "one attains immortality indeed. The sense is that, therefore, there is no assumption of an obstacle. The repetition is for the purpose of indicating the well-known nature of all this subject matter of this chapter. Thus ends the fourth quarter of the third chapter in the *Sūtradīpikā* composed by the venerable Jagannātha Yati.
1. The Section on Speech and Mind.
Oṃ. [The intermediate state] merges into speech and mind, because of the scriptural statement and because of the word "and. Oṃ.

Speech—namely Umā, who presides over speech, as well as Vāruṇī and Sauparṇī—is merged into the mind. The mind is merged into Śeṣa, who is designated by the term Rudra and presides over the mind, and also into Garuḍa. Why? Because speech is dependent on the mind; this is the sense. How so? Because it is observed, meaning it is established by direct perception. Furthermore, "and from scripture," meaning because it is heard thus in the sacred texts. "Om, for this very reason, all [the others] follow. Om.

The word *ca* has the sense of *api* (also). All the deities as well, according to their respective suitability (*anu*), dissolve into their own appropriate deities. Why? Precisely for this reason, on the basis of the scriptural statement (of Gauṣapana), "In Agni" (Chāndogya Up. 5.9.2); such is the meaning. || 2 || [End of] the Section concerning Mind and Breath.
Oṃ, that mind; breath from the north, Oṃ.

That mind—the presiding deities of the aforementioned mind, namely Śeṣa and Suparṇa—is dissolved in the vital breath (prāṇa), that is, in the four-faced Brahmā denoted by that term. Why? Because of the subsequent [scriptural] statement; the meaning is that this follows from the subsequent sentence, "mind [is merged] in the vital breath.
|| 3 || This concludes the section concerning the Overseer (adhyakṣādhikaraṇam).
Oṃ. He [attains the Supreme Self] in the Overseer, because of the scriptural statements concerning his approaching that [Self] and so forth. Oṃ.

That four-faced one (Brahmā) merges into the Supreme Self, who is the presiding overseer and Lord. Why? Because of such passages as "all," etc., which establish the attainment of the Supreme Self and so forth; this is the meaning. || 4 || [End of] the Section on the Elements (Bhūtādhikaraṇa).
Oṃ! Because of its pervasion among all beings, Oṃ!

The gods [dissolve] into others distinct from those already mentioned; they dissolve into the elements—that is, into the five gross elements. Why? Because of that statement: the meaning is that it is so because of the Vedic scripture (*Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad*) stating, "The gods [dissolve] into the elements.
[Objection: Is it not the case that [the gods] dissolve into one [element]? [Reply: No, for the two [scriptures] show this. Om.

All the gods do not dissolve into one horse alone; rather, they dissolve into all beings according to their respective fitness. Why? Because the *Mahopaniṣad* and the *Caturvedaśikhā* demonstrate this, establishing it thus: "The Ṛbhus are in the earth" and "The Ṛbhus are in the earth. This is the meaning. || 6 || [End of] the Section on Similarity.
Oṃ! And [the soul] departs together with the mind, even without having cultivated immortality through the practice of the path; Oṃ!

The first *nañ* (negative particle) has the sense of drawing [the previous statement] forward. The second is the conjunction based on the Vedic revelation (*śruti*) stating "or both. Thus, Lakṣmī does not dissolve. Why? Because, without having approached—that is, without having worshipped—the Supreme Self, she possesses immortality, which is the state of being eternally liberated. Why is that? Because of the beginning with creation; there is never any commencement of her transmigratory existence. Why is even that so? Because she is *samanā*; the meaning is: because she belongs to Him who is equal (*sama*) in respect of space and time, the Supreme Person (*puruṣa*). **Sūtra:** *Oṃ, [She is] subtle, because of the process of emanation and because it is perceived as such, Oṃ.* **Bhāṣya:** She is subtle. Why? Because of the process of emanation (*pramaraṇataḥ*). For it is from Her that the entire universe proceeds. Furthermore, it is perceived as such in scripture. As it is said: "Subtler than the subtle, greater than the great. And again: "From Whom all this world arises. Therefore, She is indeed subtle. Moreover, because of the perception of Her as such: for in the state of deep sleep, when one has entered into Her, one perceives no other object whatsoever. As it is said: "When a person sleeps here, as it were, he becomes united with this [Being]; he has gone to his own self (*svam ātmānam apītaḥ*). Therefore, She is subtle. Furthermore, because of the teaching regarding Her as the cause of the world. For it is taught that She is the cause of the origin, subsistence, and dissolution of the world. As it is said: "From whom all this world arises, by whom, once arisen, it is sustained, into whom it dissolves—know that as Brahman, and know that as the highest goal. Therefore, She is indeed subtle. Furthermore, because of the absence of any other cause. For apart from Her, no other cause of the world is perceived. As it is said: "There is nothing higher than Her. Therefore, She is indeed subtle. Furthermore, because of the impossibility of another cause. For it is impossible for anything else to be the cause of the world, since it would entail the faults of non-eternality and the like. Therefore, She alone is the cause. Furthermore, because of the denial of others. For the Śruti denies any other cause: "There is no other seer but He," and so forth. Therefore, She alone is the cause. Furthermore, because of the teaching of Her as the inner controller. For it is taught that She is the inner controller of all: "He who dwells in the earth, yet is within the earth, whom the earth does not know, whose body the earth is, and who controls the earth from within—he is your self, the inner controller, the immortal. Likewise: "He who dwells in the water... in the fire... in the ether... in the air... in the sun... in the quarters... in the moon and stars... in the darkness... in the light... in all beings... in the breath... in the speech... in the eye... in the ear... in the mind... in the skin... in the understanding (*vijñāna*)... in the semen. Since it is thus taught that She is the inner controller of all, therefore She is indeed the cause. Furthermore, because of the teaching of Her as the source of liberation. For it is taught that liberation results from knowing Her: "Knowing Him, one transcends death; there is no other path to the goal. Therefore, She is indeed the cause. Furthermore, because of the teaching of Her as the supreme goal. For it is taught that She is the supreme goal: "That which is beyond the darkness, that which is beyond death, that which is the highest light, that which is the supreme goal—knowing that, one attains immortality. Therefore, She is indeed the cause. Furthermore, because of the teaching of Her as the supreme bliss. For it is taught that She is the supreme bliss: "That which is the bliss of Brahman, that which is the bliss of liberation, that which is the bliss of the infinite—knowing that, one attains peace. Therefore, She is indeed the cause. Furthermore, because of the teaching of Her as the supreme reality. For it is taught that She is the supreme reality: "Truth is Brahman. Truth is knowledge. Truth is bliss. That which is truth, that is Brahman. That which is Brahman, that is the supreme. That which is the supreme, that is the goal. Therefore, She is indeed the cause. Furthermore, because of the teaching of Her as the supreme witness. For it is taught that She is the supreme witness: "He who witnesses all, who knows all, who is the witness of all, who is the knower of all, who is the inner witness, who is the supreme witness—He is your self, the inner controller, the immortal. Therefore, She is indeed the cause. Furthermore, because of the teaching of Her as the supreme ruler. For it is taught that She is the supreme ruler: "He who rules all this from within, who rules all this from within, who rules all this from within—He is your self, the inner controller, the immortal. Therefore, She is indeed the cause. Furthermore, because of the teaching of Her as the supreme refuge. For it is taught that She is the supreme refuge: "To Him, the refuge, we go; to Him, the protector, we go; to Him, the support, we go; to Him, the ultimate resort, we go. Therefore, She is indeed the cause. Furthermore, because of the teaching of Her as the supreme light. For it is taught that She is the supreme light: "The light beyond darkness, the light beyond death, the light beyond the finite, the light beyond the infinite—knowing that, one attains immortality. Therefore, She is indeed the cause. Furthermore, because of the teaching of Her as the supreme purity. For it is taught that She is the supreme purity: "Purity is Brahman. Purity is knowledge. Purity is bliss. That which is purity, that is Brahman. That which is Brahman, that is the supreme. That which is the supreme, that is the goal. Therefore, She is indeed the cause. Furthermore, because of the teaching of Her as the supreme freedom. For it is taught that She is the supreme freedom: "Freedom is Brahman. Freedom is knowledge. Freedom is bliss. That which is freedom, that is Brahman. That which is Brahman, that is the supreme. That which is the supreme, that is the goal. Therefore, She is indeed the cause. Furthermore, because of the teaching of Her as the supreme sovereignty. For it is taught that She is the supreme sovereignty: "She who is the sovereign of all, the ruler of all, the mistress of all, the queen of all—She is your self, the inner controller, the immortal. Therefore, She is indeed the cause. Furthermore, because of the teaching of Her as the supreme majesty. For it is taught that She is the supreme majesty: "Majesty is Brahman. Majesty is knowledge. Majesty is bliss. That which is majesty, that is Brahman. That which is Brahman, that is the supreme. That which is the supreme, that is the goal. Therefore, She is indeed the cause. Furthermore, because of the teaching of Her as the supreme glory. For it is taught that She is the supreme glory: "Glory is Brahman. Glory is knowledge. Glory is bliss. That which is glory, that is Brahman. That which is Brahman, that is the supreme. That which is the supreme, that is the goal. Therefore, She is indeed the cause. Furthermore, because of the teaching of Her as the supreme splendor. For it is taught that She is the supreme splendor: "Splendor is Brahman. Splendor is knowledge. Splendor is bliss. That which is splendor, that is Brahman. That which is Brahman, that is the supreme. That which is the supreme, that is the goal. Therefore, She is indeed the cause. Furthermore, because of the teaching of Her as the supreme radiance. For it is taught that She is the supreme radiance: "Radiance is Brahman. Radiance is knowledge. Radiance is bliss. That which is radiance, that is Brahman. That which is Brahman, that is the supreme. That which is the supreme, that is the goal. Therefore, She is indeed the cause. Furthermore, because of the teaching of Her as the supreme effulgence. For it is taught that She is the supreme effulgence: "Effulgence is Brahman. Effulgence is knowledge. Effulgence is bliss. That which is effulgence, that is Brahman. That which is Brahman, that is the supreme. That which is the supreme, that is the goal. Therefore, She is indeed the cause. Furthermore, because of the teaching of Her as the supreme luminosity. For it is taught that She is the supreme luminosity: "Luminosity is Brahman. Luminosity is knowledge. Luminosity is bliss. Brahman is subtler than even Prakṛti according to the means of valid knowledge, and it is superior to her in terms of the magnitude of its qualities such as knowledge and bliss. Why? Because it is perceived as such, and because of the scriptural text, "from everywhere" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad). Therefore, the meaning is that Brahman has no equality with Prakṛti.
Om. Not by sublation, therefore, Om.

Therefore, since both similarity and its absence have been established, there is no sublation [of the qualities] by means of annihilation; that is to say, there is no sublation of the qualities such as independence (svātantrya) and so forth. The meaning is that the similarity of Prakṛti with the Supreme Self consists precisely in its eternal liberation and other such attributes.
Oṃ, and because of this very reasoning, there is heat (ūṣman). Oṃ.

The Śruti passage from the *Sauparṇa* Upaniṣad, "For this is twofold," which teaches both the possession of heat and the absence of heat, also serves as a supporting proof for the consistency of this very point, namely that the meaning consists of a certain degree of similarity. Om. If it be argued that [the self] is not [the object of the prohibition] because of the denial [of agency], we say no, because [the denial refers only] to the embodied self. Om.

Because of the prohibition; that is, because of the prohibition of the Lord's equality with anything else. If it is argued that there is no equality of the Supreme Self even with *prakṛti* due to the latter’s pervasion of space and time and so forth, we say no. Why? Because the equality of the Lord is prohibited only with respect to the embodied soul (*jīva*), not with respect to *prakṛti*. This is the meaning. "Om, for some [scriptures] declare He is to be touched, Om."

For indeed, because in the branches (*śākhā*) of some [Vedic schools], such as the Mādhyandina, there exists a clear statement regarding the equality or inequality of the *prakṛti* (the archetype), that is the meaning. And it is also recorded in the Smṛti: "Om."
The meaning is that it is recorded in the *Vārāha-purāṇa* as "Matsya" with respect to the matter stated by Kṛṣṇa and others.

Oṃ, those [are] beyond, for thus it has been said: Oṃ.
All those deities merge into the Supreme Self through the four-faced one (Brahmā). Why? Because the Śruti (Kauṣītaki Upaniṣad) says "all," meaning that for this reason it is so stated.

Oṃ, there is no division, because of the scriptural statement; Oṃ.

The non-differentiation between the will of the Blessed One and the will of His devotees refers to the identity of their objects, not to a lack of contradiction. Why? Because of the scriptural statement: "These are the gods," according to the *Gaupavana* Śruti; this is the meaning.

Oṃ. [The soul] has its abode there; [there occurs] the flaming up of the tip of the heart; the door [of the skull] is illuminated by that [flame]; by the power of knowledge (vidyā), and by the application of recollection of the path which is the remainder of that [knowledge], and being favored by the one dwelling in the heart (the Supreme Lord), [the soul departs] through the artery that exceeds the hundred. Oṃ.

At that time of departure, there is a flaming of the tip of his abode; that is, there is a flaming at the tip of the heart, which is the abode—the locus—of that Supreme Self. Then, with its door illuminated by that light—that is, having the path made radiant by that light—the individual soul (jīva) departs from the body. But how is this possible? It is possible through the power of knowledge (*vidyā*), through the power of wisdom (*jñāna*), and through the conjunction of the recollection of the path remaining as a residue of that knowledge—that is, through the accompaniment of the memory of what is to be attained as a limb of that knowledge.

Moreover, being favored by the one within the heart—that is, being favored by the Blessed Lord residing in the heart—he goes. By what? By the hundred-and-first channel, namely the *suṣumnā*; this is the meaning.
Om, he follows the rays; Om.
The meaning is that the individual soul (jīva) departs following the rays, being guided by the light of the sun situated within. [Sūtra 10:
"If it be argued that this does not happen at night, we say no, because of the connection. [Sūtra 11: "Om."

[Objection: But surely, because the rays of the sun are absent at night, there can be no departure [of the soul] for one who possesses knowledge. [Reply: This is not so. If you say it would not occur, we say no. Why? Because of the connection; that is to say, because the rays of the sun are connected [to the body] at all times. Om. [The Lord] shows this because [the connection] persists as long as the body exists. Om.

Because the connection with the rays exists as long as the body exists—that is, for as long as the body persists—it is logical that the departure [of the soul] of the knower occurs even at night. Why? Because the scripture shows it; for the *Mādhyandināyana* Śruti, stating "having united," demonstrates this, and the meaning is that it establishes it thus. **Sūtra:** And therefore, also during the southern course, for there is indeed [a path]. (Oṃ) **Commentary:** Therefore, because the connection with the rays persists as long as the body, the departure of the knower is possible even at night. Why? Because the scripture shows it; the Śruti text "having united" (*saṃsṛtya*) demonstrates this, and thus it is established. Furthermore, the knower may depart even during the southern course of the sun, for there is indeed a path available. Oṃ.

The word *ca* (and) serves to conjoin two propositions. Even though there is a Smṛti text stating "even in the southern [course] at the time of death," the departure (*utkrānti*) of the knower is appropriate during the southern course, that is, at the time of the sun’s southern transit. Why? Because of this: because even then, the connection with the thousand solar rays within the channels remains. For this reason—namely, because of this—it follows that one should not say that there is no departure at night based on the illustration of the southern course.
