Oṃ, these two are enjoined with reference to Yogins, and they are based on Smṛti. Oṃ.

Why is this? These two paths—the path of Brahman and the path of the Moon—are mentioned (*smaryete*) by way of tradition (*smṛtyā*) with respect to yogins, that is, with respect to those who practice the yoga of knowledge and the yoga of action. And they are "traditional" (*smārte*), meaning they are to be accomplished through one's own remembrance (*svānusmṛti*). By the words "the paths," etc., they are mentioned in the context of the inner self (*adhyātme*). Therefore, the meaning is that these two do not have time and so forth as their sole cause. Thus ends the second quarter of the fourth chapter in the *Sūtradīpikā* composed by Śrī Jagannātha Yati.
|| 1 || Section on the Path Beginning with Light (Arcirādyadhikaraṇa) ||
Oṃ. [The soul departs] by way of the path beginning with light, because that is well-known from scripture. Oṃ.

The knower who has departed travels by way of the path beginning with light (*arcis*). Why? Because that [path] is well-known; the meaning is that this fact is established by the scripture: "They reach the light" (*te 'rciṣam abhisambhavanti*). || 2 || The Section Concerning the Word "Wind" (*vāyu-śabdādhikaraṇa*).
Oṃ. [The proof of the existence of air] is from the sound of wind, by means of both the general and the particular. Oṃ.

Because of the scriptural statement that air is both "without distinction" and "with distinction," and through the consideration of both [aspects], the meaning is that air possesses a second kind of reachability (*prāpyatva*). || 3 || This concludes the section on Lightning (*taṭidadhikaraṇa*).
Oṃ, Varuṇa presides over lightning due to their connection; Oṃ.
After lightning—that is, immediately upon reaching lightning—Varuṇa is to be reached. Why? Because of the connection; the meaning is that Varuṇa is connected with what follows lightning.
|| 4 || The Section on the Conductors (Ātivāhikādhikaraṇa).
Om. [The soul] is of a transportable nature, because of the scriptural indication of that. Om.

The air (vāyu) previously mentioned as the second stage to be reached is indeed the *ātivāhika* (conveying) air, not the primary element. Why? Because of its characteristic mark (*talliṅgāt*). This means that from the word "air" used in the context of being the first stage to be reached, it follows that [the soul] goes to the flame (*arciḥ*), because it possesses those attributes and so forth. **Sūtra:** Oṃ. On account of the delusion of both, that is established. Oṃ.

The ablative case is used in the sense of the locative. Because there is a doubt—due to the confusion regarding both—as to whether the previously mentioned wind is the primary *ativāhika* (conductor) or the subsequently mentioned wind is the primary *ativāhika*, [the author says: "Because of its establishment"; that is to say, by that qualifying attribute of being the lord of Śiva, the primacy of that subsequently mentioned wind is established, and thus there is no lack of determination.
|| 5 || The Section on the Lightning (*Vaidyuta-adhikaraṇa*).
Oṃ, then that [is established] by means of the lightning itself; Oṃ.

The knower of Brahman goes to Brahman by means of lightning and indeed by means of Vāyu, the lord of lightning; there is nothing else to be reached between those two. Why? Because of that [scriptural] statement: the meaning is that from the scripture stating that Vāyu alone is the one who leads them to Brahman, namely, "He leads them to Brahman. || 6 || [End of] the Section on the Effect (Kāryādhikaraṇa).
Oṃ. Bādari [holds that the soul] goes [to the world of Brahman], because this is logically consistent with its movement; Oṃ.

The teacher Bādari maintains that the meaning of the scriptural passage "Vāyu leads him" is that Vāyu leads Brahman, known as the four-faced one (Caturmukha), who is the effect and characterized by origination. Why? Because for this very four-faced one, the movement is logical; that is to say, his status as the goal to be reached is logical.
"And because of being specifically distinguished. (Oṃ viśeṣitatvācca oṃ).
The meaning is that the statement is correct because, in the *Kauṣītaki* Śruti, the Brahman to be attained is specifically qualified by the term "four-faced" (*caturmukha*).
Oṃ. But the designation [of Brahman] is due to proximity. Oṃ.

Because there is the designation [of the knower] as "one who knows Brahman," which is a scriptural statement regarding the attainment of the Supreme Brahman; and because of proximity—meaning that having attained the four-faced Brahmā, one attains the Supreme before long—it proceeds precisely by following that [attainment of Brahmā]. Therefore, there is no contradiction with that. Om. Upon the dissolution of the effect, [the soul goes] together with its presiding deity to the Supreme, because of the declaration [to that effect]. Om.

"At the destruction of the body," that is, at the great dissolution (*mahāpralaya*), "together with its presiding lord," the four-faced Lord of effects (Brahmā); "beyond" that four-faced one is the Supreme Brahman. The knower goes there; this is the meaning based on the designation and the scriptural testimony.
Om. And from Smṛti, Om.

Furthermore, because the traditional teaching (smṛti) stating "O Brāhmaṇa" exists, it is established that the knower of Brahman attains the Supreme together with the four-faced Brahmā; this is the meaning.
Oṃ. Jaimini [holds that he attains] the Supreme, on account of its being primary. Oṃ.

The knower attains the Supreme Brahman alone, and not the effected (kārya) Brahman. Why? Because of the primacy [of the term]; that is to say, Master Jaimini considers that the word "Brahman" has its primary meaning only in reference to the Supreme Brahman.
Om. And because of the vision, Om.
The knower goes to the Supreme Brahman itself. Why? Because by means of hearing and so forth, it is the Supreme Brahman alone that is perceived; this is the meaning.
"And there is no intention toward the effected [Brahman] for the sake of reaching [the goal]. Oṃ.

For this reason as well, the attainment of the effected Brahman (kāryabrahma) by the knower is untenable. Why? Because: regarding the effected Brahman as the object, the knower has no intention of "attainment" (pratipatti). "Attainment" (pratipatti) means worship (upāsti); there is no desire for "intention" (abhisandhi), that is, the wish "may I reach [it]. This is the meaning. || 8 ||
"Oṃ, Bādarāyaṇa [maintains that the Lord] leads those who have no support other than the Imperishable; for there are defects in both cases, and because of the nature of their resolve. Oṃ.

The teacher Bādari maintains that the meaning of the scriptural passage "He leads them" is as follows: Vāyu leads those qualified aspirants who meditate upon the pervasive [Brahman] and are not dependent on symbols (*apratīkālambana*) to the Supreme Brahman; he leads others—those who meditate on symbols (*pratīkālambana*), meaning those whose meditation is limited to the body designated by the symbol—to the effected Brahman (*kāryabrahma*). Why? Because there would be a fault in either alternative.

If one does not accept this established rule and instead accepts that everyone attains each [of the two goals], then the faults mentioned regarding both the attainment of the effected Brahman (*kāryabrahman*) and the supreme Brahman (*parabrahman*) would follow. Now, it might be argued: "Since the *Padma Purāṇa* states, 'One attains that which one desires to attain,' the attainment of various things is possible through mere desire for them; therefore, the aforementioned rule need not be accepted. To this, he says: "And [the soul] has that as its resolve" (*tatkratuśca*).

By this, the Śruti passage beginning with "as is his desire, so is his resolve" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 3.14.1) is understood. The word "ca" (and) has the sense of "yataḥ" (because). Because that Śruti passage—beginning with "as is his [desire]"—negates the attainment of those respective objects through the mere wish for their attainment, and instead declares that their attainment occurs only through the direct realization resulting from the knowledge and meditation upon them; therefore, the meaning is that attainment is not accomplished by the mere wish for them alone. || 9 ||
Oṃ, and he demonstrates the distinction; oṃ.

The scripture (*śruti*) [of the *Caturvedaśikhā*], stating "because they are luminous within," shows—that is, establishes—the distinction or difference that some have non-symbols as their support while others have symbols as their support. Therefore, what was stated is logical; this is the meaning. || 10 ||
Thus ends the third quarter of the fourth chapter in the *Sūtradīpikā* composed by the venerable Jagannātha Yati.
|| The Section on Attainment (*sampadyādhikaraṇam*) ||
Oṃ, [the soul] departs from its own body, because of the scriptural statement; Oṃ.

Having become a knower—that is, having attained Brahman—without leaving Brahman and without transcending Brahman, he remains established in his own manifested true nature and enjoys enjoyments. Why? From the scriptural statement: "He who knows thus... (Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa, Sauparṇa-kāṇḍa). This is the meaning. || 2 || [End of] the Section on the Liberated One.
Oṃ, he is liberated because of his declaration; Oṃ.

"He wanders there"—in this scriptural passage, it is the liberated one alone who is spoken of. Why? Because of the initial proposition (*pratijñā*). Having denied divine enjoyment to anyone other than the liberated, the *Bṛhadāraṇyaka* scripture states, "Day after day," that it is the liberated one alone who attains Brahman and thereby experiences divine enjoyment; such is the meaning. || 3 || [End of] the Section on the Self (*Ātmādhikaraṇa*).
Oṃ, the Self [is the subject] because of the context. Oṃ.

By the term "supreme light," it is the Self, that is, the Supreme Self alone, which is denoted, and not the sun. Why? Because of the context; the meaning is that this passage belongs to the context of the Supreme Self. || 4 || The Section on Non-Differentiation.
Oṃ. Because it is perceived as non-differentiated, Oṃ.

The enjoyments already experienced by the Supreme Self are enjoyed in due order by the liberated souls without distinction. Why? Because they are objects of perception, according to the scriptural statement from the *Caturvedaśikhā*: "Those very [enjoyments] which I... (5). This concludes the section concerning Brahman (*brāhmādhikaraṇam*).
Oṃ. Jaimini [holds that the Self is known] through the Vedic [scripture], because of the introductory passages and so forth. Oṃ.

By means of the *brāhma* body—that is, by means of a body connected with Brahman—he enjoys the objects of experience. Why? Because of the introductory passages (*upanyāsa*) and so forth; for the Mādhyandina recension of the Śruti says, "by Brahman" (*brahmaṇā*). By the word "and so forth," the Smṛti passage "he is given [by Brahman]" (*ādatta*) is intended, as well as logical reasoning (*yukti*). This is the meaning: the teacher Jaimini considers that he enjoys them in this way. **Sūtra 4:** **Oṃ. [The soul enjoys] by mere consciousness, because its nature is that [consciousness]; thus [says] Auḍulomi.** The meaning is: [the liberated soul] experiences through mere consciousness alone, because his essential nature consists of that [consciousness]. Thus says the teacher Auḍulomi.

By means of pure consciousness—that is, by having a body whose sole nature is knowledge—the liberated one enjoys objects of experience. Why? Because that is his very essence; for the state of liberation consists precisely in having a body of pure consciousness alone, and because that [body] is not a cause for transmigratory existence. This is the view of the teacher Auḍulomi. *Oṃ. Even so, because of the introductory statement and because of the prior state, Bādarāyaṇa maintains there is no contradiction.* *Oṃ.*

Thus, regarding the manner stated by Jaimini; because of the introduction [of the topic] in the *Śaunaka* (Sāuparṇa) Śruti, "He indeed is this... (*sa vā eṣaḥ*); and because of its existence in the prior state—that is, because there is the presence of valid evidence even in the former position stated by Jaimini—[Bādarāyaṇa] considers the non-contradiction, meaning the lack of contradiction between the two positions. This is the sense. || 6 || The Section on Volition (*Saṅkalpādhikaraṇa*).
Oṃ, and because of the scriptural statement that [the creation] occurs from mere volition, Oṃ.

The word "ca" (and) is for the purpose of excluding the opposing view. Released souls enjoy their respective portions solely through *saṅkalpa*—that is, according to their own will. Why? Because of the scriptural authority; the meaning is that this is established by the Śruti text beginning with "If he [desires]" (*sa yadi*) regarding that matter.
7. The Section on the Sovereignty of No Other.
Oṃ, for this very reason, he has no other lord; oṃ.

The word "ca" (and) serves to exclude the suspicion of contradiction. "Having no other lord" means he is liberated and not possessed of another superior lord over himself. Why? For this very reason; that is to say, precisely because of his power of true resolve (*satya-saṃkalpa*).
|| 8 || The Section on Non-existence (*abhāvādhikaraṇa*).

Oṃ. Bādari maintains that there is non-existence [of the body], for thus it is said. Having accepted the absence of the natural body, the liberated one possesses enjoyment by means of a body consisting of pure consciousness alone. Thus the teacher Bādari thinks. Why? Because—*hi*—since the scripture says, "Verily, he is bodiless" (Kauṇṭharavya), meaning the absence of the natural body. Therefore is the sense. Oṃ. Jaimini maintains that there is existence [of the body], because of the mention of an option. Oṃ.

Jaimini maintains that for those who are liberated, there exists a state in which a body remains distinct from pure consciousness (*cinmātra*). Why? Because of the scriptural mention of alternatives; that is to say, because scripture mentions both types of bodies, as established by the *Chāndogya* (Uddālaka) passage stating "either with consciousness or without consciousness. **Sūtra:** *Oṃ dvādaśāhavadvobhayavidhaṃ bādarāyaṇo'taḥ oṃ* || 4.4.12 || **Translation:** Oṃ. Therefore, Bādarāyaṇa holds that [the state of the liberated] is of both kinds, like the twelve-day sacrifice (*dvādaśāha*). Oṃ.

Bādarāyaṇa considers his own view to be twofold, namely, the presence and absence of the natural body. Why? Because there is evidence for this. How is this appropriate? It is like the twelve-day sacrifice (*dvādaśāha*); just as the twelve-day sacrifice consists of both the *ahīna* and the *sattra* types, so it is here. *Sūtra:* "In the absence of a body, [the soul's existence] is possible, as in the case of the twilight [meditation]. (Oṃ)

As in the case of the twilight [state], just as in the state of dream there is a connection with experience even in the absence of an external body, so it is in liberation as well. "Even in the absence of a body" means even in the absence of a material body. "Because of the possibility" means because experience is logical; the meaning is that the position of the absence of a body is tenable. *Oṃ, as in the waking state, when there is existence, Oṃ.* Just as in the waking state there is the occurrence of experience even while the body exists, so it is in liberation as well. "When there is existence" means that experience is appropriate even when a material body exists. *Oṃ, the entry is like a lamp, for thus Scripture shows, Oṃ.*

It is like a lamp: just as when a lamp enters a house or similar place, there occurs both the consumption of the oil and so forth contained therein, as well as the manifestation of its blackness and other qualities; in the same way, there is the entry of liberated souls into inert bodies. In that state, there is the experience of auspicious enjoyments and the non-experience of suffering and the like. Why? Because of the Śruti text: "For he who has crossed over... (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.7). It shows it thus, it establishes it thus; therefore is the meaning. **Sūtra:** *Oṃ svāpyaya-sampattyor anyatarāpekṣam āviṣkṛtaṃ hi Oṃ.* **Commentary:** [The state of the soul after death] depends on either deep sleep (*svāpyaya*) or union with the Supreme (*sampatti*), for this is clearly declared [in scripture]. *Oṃ*.

The phrase "in the heavenly world" (svarge loke) refers to either of the two states—deep sleep (svāpyaya) or union [with Brahman] (sampatti)—depending on the context. Why? Because, by the scriptural statement, "And here his father is no longer his father," it is revealed—that is, made manifest—that this refers to the state of deep sleep and liberation. This is the meaning. || 9 || [End of] the Section on the Activity of the World.
Oṃ, [the Buddha's activity] is devoid of worldly involvement; oṃ.
The meaning is that the liberated one attains all desires in such a way as to be devoid of activities such as the creation of the world.
Om; because of the context and because [the liberated one] is not present [in those activities], Om.

The word *ca* (and) serves to include the object to be established [in the preceding argument]. In the scriptural passage, "all desires," the individual soul (*jīva*) is spoken of. Why? Because of the context; for this statement belongs to the section concerning the individual soul. And thus, in that case, the enjoyment of all desires by the individual soul is not applicable in an unrestricted sense, but only in a restricted sense. Why? Because they are not in proximity; the meaning is that the individual souls are far removed from the capacity for the governance of the universe. *Sūtra:* "If it be argued that [the soul's enjoyment of all desires] is due to direct scriptural instruction, we say no, because [the scripture speaks of] one who abides in the sphere of authority. (Oṃ).

If it is argued that one must accept that liberated souls possess sovereignty over the world—on the grounds that the scripture "He who knows them" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 7.1.5) clearly establishes that the liberated soul is worshipful to all deities—we say no. Why? Because this refers to those situated in the spheres of authority (*ādhikārika-maṇḍala-stha*). The meaning is that in this passage, it is specifically the liberated Hiraṇyagarbha who is declared to be worshipful to the host of deities appointed to their respective offices.
**Sūtra:** *Oṃ vikārāvarti ca tathā hi darśayati Oṃ.* And [the Lord] does not abide in the realm of modification, for thus the scripture shows. (Brahma-sūtra 4.4.17)

The particle *ca* (and) is for the purpose of drawing [the previous point] forward. Regarding the phrase "not existing in the modifications of the liberated" (*muktānāṃ vikārāvarti*): that which causes one to revolve (*āvartayati*) in modification—that is, in *saṃsāra*—is "existing in modification" (*vikārāvatī*). There is no activity pertaining to the sphere of *saṃsāra*. Why? Because of the scriptural statement, "this" (*imam*); thus it shows, that is, it establishes [this], and therefore [it is so]. || 10 || The Section on Abiding (*sthityadhikaraṇam*).
Oṃ. Thus he states the stability of both perception and inference as they demonstrate [the object]. Oṃ.

The state of the liberated one is indeed of a single uniform nature, and there is neither increase nor decrease. Why? Because the Śruti, beginning with "He is this very one" (Jābāla Upaniṣad), declares his station to be a state of existence in precisely that one way. Not only this much, but both perception and inference—namely, the mark consisting in the absence of causes for the perception of a knower—also demonstrate and make known the meaning stated by the Śruti. This is the sense. Om. And because of the mark indicating equality in respect to enjoyment alone, Om.

Except in the case of a difference [in nature], even though there is a difference in mere enjoyment (*bhoga*), there is no difference in enjoyment for the liberated one because of the indicative mark (*liṅga*) consisting of the statement that they are of a single mode, designated as "equality. Therefore, increase and so forth are not the cause for such a distinction; thus, the meaning is that the liberated one does not possess increase and so forth.
|| 11 || The Section on Non-return (*anāvṛttyadhikaraṇa*).
Oṃ, there is no return, on account of the scriptural statement; there is no return, on account of the scriptural statement. Oṃ.
For one who is liberated, there is no returning again; why? Because of the scriptural statement: "And he does not return," which is the meaning of the Śruti.
The repetition is for the purpose of emphasizing that the stated matter is exactly so.
[He is] directly beheld by Hari, who dwells within the lotus of my mind.
Through this bestower of prosperity, may Kṛṣṇa, whose abode is the lotus, be pleased.

Thus ends the fourth quarter of the fourth chapter in the *Brahmasūtradīpikā* composed by the ascetic Jagannātha, disciple of the venerable Paramahaṃsa Parivrājaka Ācāryas, the holy Raghunāthatīrtha. || 4 || 4 ||
